#1. Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.

TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.

Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.

TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.

However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.

“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”

AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.

“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.

But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.

Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:

Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.

While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.

Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

#2. LatAm Startup Funding Jumps 26% In Q3 As VCs Begin ‘Rediscovering’ The Region

A continued boom in late-stage and growth funding combined with a surge in seed-stage funding helped buoy venture investment in Latin America for the third quarter of 2026, Crunchbase data shows.

All told, startups in Latin America raised a combined $1.3 billion across seed- and growth-stage deals in the three-month period ending Sept. 30. That was up 26% year over year but down 9% from the second quarter.

For perspective, we charted out total investment, color-coded by stage, for the past 12 quarters below.

Of the quarterly total, $757 million went into late-stage and growth deals, up 74% compared to the $435 million that flowed into such deals in the third quarter of 2025. However, that is down 21.3% from the $962 million in late-stage and growth rounds raised by LatAm startups in the second quarter. (Although it’s worth noting that Q2 2026 represented the most raised at that stage since the second quarter of 2022.)

Mexico startups have raised $1.52 billion in venture funding during the first three quarters of 2026, per Crunchbase data. Notably, that’s about 40.7% more than the $1.08 billion Brazil’s startups raised in the same period. This is unusual as Brazil has historically been the largest recipient of venture funding in Latin America.

Still, Brazil continues to attract a broad range of investors.

“Over the past year, we have seen investments into Brazil from firms including Sequoia, Founders Fund, NEA, Battery and Tidemark,” Allen Taylor, managing partner of Endeavor Catalyst, told Crunchbase News. “For several, this marked either their first investment in Latin America or their first in a long time.”

Igor Piquet, Endeavor Catalyst’s vice president and head of Latin America, noted that Mexico drew more venture funding in the first half of 2026 than Brazil. But much of Mexico’s funding went to a few startups, he pointed out, while Brazil recorded many deals.

“Investors are concentrating on a few Mexican winners, while Brazil retains the breadth,” Piquet said, adding that Brazil also leads in realized exits.

Several mega-raises took place in Latin America in the third quarter. And notably, the two largest funding deals were not for companies in Brazil or Mexico, which have historically raised the largest share of venture capital in the region. They also weren’t to fintech, which typically has the most funding recipients in the region, but rather to energy-related startups.

Black Giant, the Chilean project company for EnergyX’s Black Giant lithium project, raised $225 million in a July round at a reported $900 million valuation. And Colombia’s Erco Energía, a clean energy company that builds and operates solar power systems for homes and businesses, landed a $129 million Series C in August at a reported $600 million valuation.

Mexico’s Kapital, an AI-powered financial services company, raised a $125 million Series C in September at a $1.6 billion valuation. Tru Arrow Partners led the financing, which included a senior debt funding facility provided by Fasanara Capital.

And in August, Brazilian fintech Kesh Bank brought in $106.9 million in an equity and debt seed round at a $626 million valuation.

Also in August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI-native wealth advisory company, landed $85 million in  what Crunchbase data shows is the largest seed funding deal ever raised for a Latin American startup. Founded by Vitor Olivier, former CTO of Nubank, and Felipe Meneses, founder of Hyperplane AI, the startup is backed by Benchmark, Greenoaks, Diffusion, Norte Ventures and Atlantico.

Latin America experienced a marked surge in very early-stage funding totals in the third quarter, largely thanks to the seed rounds mentioned above.

Of the $1.3 billion raised by Latin America’s startups in the third quarter, about 20.5% — or $266 million — was raised across the angel and seed stages.

That’s up 128% from the $117 million raised across those stages in the second quarter of 2026, and up 62% from the $165 million in the same quarter last year.

Just over 22%, or $288 million, was raised at early stages, down 18.9% from $355 million in the second quarter and 34% from $437 million in the same period last year.

We expect the Q3 deal counts to rise somewhat over time; however, as seed rounds in particular are commonly reported weeks or months after they close.

Latin America is drawing renewed interest from international venture investors, according to Endeavor’s Taylor. He said international VCs were more active in the region, particularly Brazil, during the first three quarters of 2026 than in 2024 and 2025 combined, through both new investments and follow-on funding.

“I joke that investors from the U.S. ‘rediscover’ Latin America every five or six years, and I think we are approaching another rediscovery moment,” Taylor told Crunchbase News.

Liquidity is improving, although acquisitions and secondary transactions are providing more opportunities than public listings, Piquet said. He pointed to approximately 60 private Latin American technology companies that have each raised at least $150 million as a potential pipeline for future IPOs.

“The exit door is open, although it is not primarily opening through IPOs yet,” Piquet said.

Taylor expects more exits could help bring global investors back consistently, with potential New York Stock Exchange listings by companies such as Wellhub, CloudWalk or Creditas contributing to another “rediscovery moment” in 2027.

International investors remain interested in Latin America but have become more selective about deploying capital, according to Ana Cristina Gadala-Maria of QED Investors. Firms with a longstanding presence in the region remain engaged, while many that entered during the 2020–2021 investment boom have shifted toward AI opportunities elsewhere and are concentrating on existing portfolios, she noted.

“Global investors are increasingly investing behind themes rather than geographies,” she said, putting Latin American startups in more direct competition with companies in the U.S. and other markets.

Investor interest is increasingly centered on AI-native businesses and financial infrastructure, particularly stablecoins and cross-border payments. Gadala-Maria said more founders are targeting global markets from the outset, marking a departure from the previous wave of startups that adapted established business models to underserved local markets.

“Increasingly, we’re seeing founders build globally competitive technology companies from Latin America, rather than necessarily for Latin America,” she said.

Gadala-Maria agrees that Brazil and Mexico remain the region’s largest markets, with Brazil offering a deeper, more mature startup ecosystem and Mexico providing substantial room for financial services innovation. She pointed to Argentina as an overlooked market, citing its strong technical talent and founders building companies for global customers.

Correction: Details regarding Kapital’s Series C were updated. The deal was a debt and equity raise.

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026.

Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year.

Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted.

Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less.

Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million.

Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round.

Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.)

#3. The 1 Question I Ask in Every Leadership Meeting to Uncover Problems Before It’s Too Late

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This simple leadership practice reveals hidden risks, creates accountability and turns uncomfortable truths into better decisions before problems become crises.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every executive has sat through the familiar project review. A dashboard flashes green, yellow and red. Leaders move from one initiative to the next, assuming the colors tell the story. They don’t.

I remember sitting in a leadership meeting reviewing a major project. The status was green. The completion percentage was 20%. The deadline was the next day.

I said, “Walk me through how we’re going to finish the remaining 80% by tomorrow.”

The response caught me completely off guard.

Technically, that was true. The deadline hadn’t passed. Operationally, it was disconnected from reality.

That meeting reinforced something I’ve seen throughout my career. Leaders can become so focused on reporting status that they lose sight of what is actually happening. Green, yellow and red tell you almost nothing by themselves. A project can appear healthy while serious risks are quietly building beneath the surface. Teams can update every dashboard and complete every status report while moving steadily toward a missed commitment.

From that point on, I changed how I ran leadership meetings. Instead of asking people to explain the dashboard, I started asking one question: “What am I missing?”

That question has consistently improved the quality of decisions, strengthened accountability and helped teams execute more effectively because it uncovers information a status report never will. The real value, however, comes from what happens after full transparency is provided.

When I ask, “What am I missing?” I’m not asking for opinions. I’m asking for information. I want to know what risks haven’t surfaced, what assumptions we’re making, what dependencies could derail the timeline and what decisions are preventing progress.

If your meetings consist of everyone reporting that everything is on track, you’re probably missing something important. When you think about it, what does a green status tell you about what’s really going on? Instead, ask questions that reveal what’s actually happening.

Those questions move the conversation beyond reporting and into problem-solving.

Finding a risk is only the beginning. When someone raises a concern, don’t move on to the next agenda item. Ask them to walk you through it.

What evidence supports your concern? What happens if we do nothing? What options do we have?

This is exactly what happened during that project review. Once we walked through the work that remained, everyone could clearly see the project wasn’t green at all. We still had time to respond because we identified the problem before the deadline arrived.

Leaders don’t create value by discovering problems. They create value by discovering them while options still exist. Time is a precious resource; get to the heart of your issues early, and you will have more room to work out a solution or do damage control.

One of the biggest mistakes leaders make is allowing someone to identify a problem without asking them to help solve it. Whenever someone raises an issue, I follow with another question.

That shifts the discussion immediately. Instead of simply pointing out what’s wrong, people begin thinking through priorities, tradeoffs, resources and execution. They become invested in the outcome because they’ve contributed to the solution. Ownership grows when people articulate their thinking and help shape the path forward. Ownership is a way to reward people for providing transparency.

Every concern raised in a meeting should end with a decision or an owner. If additional resources are required, decide who will secure them. If priorities need to change, make the tradeoff before the next meeting. If an issue needs to be escalated, assign someone to do it.

Meetings should never end with everyone agreeing there is a problem. They should end with clarity about who is doing what next. That discipline turns discussion into execution.

This process only works if people believe it’s safe to speak honestly. Too many organizations unintentionally reward good news, and that can have unintended negative consequences. People learn to protect themselves by reporting green until the evidence becomes impossible to ignore.

I reward something different. I reward transparency. Silence can be deadly, never mind expensive.

When someone surfaces a risk early, my first question isn’t, “Who caused this?” It’s, “What decision do we need to make now?” That response teaches the organization that identifying problems early is valued because it gives us time to solve them. Over time, people stop hiding issues and start bringing them forward while options still exist. That is how trust accelerates execution.

Leadership today is very different from when I started my career. Technology evolves rapidly. AI is changing how organizations operate. The pace of business continues to accelerate, and no leader has all the answers.

The leaders who succeed are the ones who consistently uncover the information they don’t have. At the beginning of your next leadership meeting, try this simple process. Ask, “What am I missing?” Listen carefully before offering your own conclusions. Turn concerns into ownership by asking how people would solve the problem. Leave the meeting with clear decisions, clear owners and clear next steps.

Better leadership rarely begins with having the smartest answer. It begins with asking the question that unlocks clarity, better judgment and stronger decisions.

Every executive has sat through the familiar project review. A dashboard flashes green, yellow and red. Leaders move from one initiative to the next, assuming the colors tell the story. They don’t.

I remember sitting in a leadership meeting reviewing a major project. The status was green. The completion percentage was 20%. The deadline was the next day.

I said, “Walk me through how we’re going to finish the remaining 80% by tomorrow.”

#4. Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks.

IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “It still worked,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”

Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded Wabi.

The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as Muse and Instinct, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals.

our launch video from 2015 – Luka later pivoted into @replika. we were building personal agents 11 years ago! https://t.co/OBQqCF1MeW pic.twitter.com/rIS3ljEZFq

On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread.

The launch is something of a pivot for Wabi, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app.

Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.”

With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads.

“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.

App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.

“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”

The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.

Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats.

“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.”

Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next.

In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese.

Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.

“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.

On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said.

“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”

Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

#6. Seattle ag-tech startup Carbon Robotics reduces workforce, citing economic conditions

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 19, 2026 at 6:34 pmOctober 19, 2026 at 6:34 pm

Carbon Robotics, the Seattle-based agricultural technology startup known for its AI-powered, laser-weeding farm implements, has trimmed its workforce.

The company did not disclose the total number of layoffs, but confirmed to GeekWire on Monday that the cuts affected employees across multiple departments both in the U.S. and internationally.

Carbon Robotics currently employs 275 people worldwide, according to Brett Goodwin, vice president of marketing, who attributed the decision to a need to “realign costs due to broader economic conditions.”

The cuts come after a period of rapid momentum for the startup. The company raised $20 million last year to support the development of an undisclosed AI-powered farm robot. Carbon also unveiled an autonomous tractor kit in 2025.

The company’s signature product is its LaserWeeder, a machine which can be pulled behind a tractor and uses AI to detect and map plants in fields and then target and eliminate weeds with lasers. The most recent iteration is the LaserWeeder G2.

Founded in 2018 and led by CEO Paul Mikesell, Carbon Robotics has raised about $177 million to date from investors including BOND, NVentures, and Anthos Capital.

In a recent interview with AgFunder, Mikesell noted that the startup crossed the $100 million revenue threshold, stating, “We intend to keep scaling from there — it’s our intention to get to the point that we’re an independently publicly traded company, so that would involve going through an IPO.”

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. secretary of health and human services, earlier this year touted Carbon Robotics’ machines on an episode of “The Joe Rogan Experience” as a possible solution in cutting pesticide use.

Carbon Robotics was named Next Tech Titan at the 2026 GeekWire Awards earlier this year. The company is currently ranked No. 8 on the GeekWire 200 index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

#7. Ex–OpenAI engineer accused of bugging office stays in jail as prosecutors allege Saudi ties: ‘Once he leaves, there’s no getting him back’

A federal judge on Monday ordered a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an executive conference room to stay in jail, after questioning whether a $1 million bond the Saudi government offered to guarantee would bring him back if he fled.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the 35-year-old former OpenAI engineer, appeared in court today wearing an orange jumpsuit and white face mask while escorted by two U.S. marshals. He will remain in federal custody until his next court date, a preliminary hearing on Nov. 6. He has been in jail since the FBI arrested him on Oct. 9, alleging he planted the device in a conference room where executives, and sometimes government officials, discussed sensitive information, on Sept. 28.

Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse said a $1 million bond had to be weighed against the possibility that Alfozan “potentially has access to much greater wealth.”

“Once he leaves, there’s no getting him back, and that’s why this is a bigger case,” Tse said in the courtroom Monday morning.

OpenAI terminated Alfozan’s employment on Oct. 9, although Alfozan’s lawyer said Monday in court the company never formally told him that. However, per his defense motion, he was told before his arrest that he had been placed on administrative leave. Tse noted that OpenAI would not have fired him if it had no concern about what it found.

Fortune was in the San Francisco courtroom for the hearing, as were about 60 others, including a group of high school students who had come to witness a case involving one of the most prominent companies in the world.

Ahead of the court hearing Monday, both prosecutors for the federal government and the defense, Alfozan’s attorney William Pernik, filed court documents revealing new details about the case. Alfozan sought release from federal custody, with supervision, such as an ankle monitor, while the U.S. argued there was reason to believe he would leave the country and that he posed a danger to the community and to U.S. national security.

Alfozan faces one count of using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, which carries a maximum of five years in prison. He was charged by criminal complaint and has not been indicted or entered a plea. The complaint does not charge him with espionage, theft of trade secrets, or acting as an agent of a foreign government, a point his defense stressed in its motion. OpenAI has said it has “no indications” that he inappropriately accessed or took model weights, source code, or customer data.

The filings reveal far more than has been known to date about Alfozan and some of the most controversial details of the case, including why Alfozan had a one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia three days after his arrest. Alfozan’s lawyer said he is a citizen of Saudi Arabia, although he has been in the U.S. for 15 years; got his green card in 2020; and joined OpenAI in 2025.

Alfozan booked the flight to Saudi Arabia on Sept. 13, according to the defense motion, along with his wife, also a Saudi national, and 3-month-old baby. The economy fare for all three cost $1,897.59 and could be changed for a $180 fee, the defense said, adding this wasn’t unusual for its client: Alfozan often books one-way tickets to allow for scheduling flexibility around his work schedule, the defense motion says. In fact, 70% (96 of 138) of the airline bookings “in his email since January 2021 were one-way tickets.” His naturalization application lists 25 trips abroad between 2020 and 2025, 20 of which included Saudi Arabia, and he returned from every one, according to the defense.

As for the date of Oct. 12, Alfozan booked it for then because that’s the day his wife’s 60-day grace period ended after her work permit in the U.S. expired on Aug. 13. Since giving birth, she has “struggled with postpartum depression and anxiety,” the defense motion says. Alfozan filed for paternity leave from OpenAI, set for Oct. 19 to Dec. 20, after which he planned to return to the Bay Area and his role at OpenAI.

After Alfozan’s arrest, his wife allegedly told authorities that she and their baby intended to permanently move to Saudi Arabia, according to the court filing. She told them her husband intended to move there at some point to be with them, but for now, was spending two months of his paternity leave in the country before returning to the U.S. In court Monday, however, the defense said she now plans to return to the U.S. on a temporary, short-term B-1 visa. The defense also said she left the U.S. rather than overstay her visa.

That is consistent with a letter one of Alfozan’s friends submitted for the defense motion, in which the friend says he spoke to Alfozan about his plan to continue working in the U.S. and supporting his wife and baby when they returned to Saudi Arabia.

As further evidence of Alfozan’s intent to return to the U.S., his lawyer notes that on Sept. 26, two days before he allegedly planted the device, Alfozan registered to attend the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), a convention in Las Vegas scheduled for early January 2027.

In court, Pernik argued that Alfozan stayed in the country for about eight to 10 days after OpenAI confronted him. “If he really were an agent of a foreign government … why wouldn’t he just leave right away?” Pernik said in court.

The U.S. filing also reveals the results of a federal search of Alfozan’s home and cell phone. They found “several electronic components similar” to the recording device Alfozan allegedly installed behind a TV in the conference room, and a second one OpenAI security staff found in his bag.

On Alfozan’s iPhone were several photographs, dated from Sept. 22 to Sept. 28, 2026, of another recording device. Other photos showed what appeared to be the input and output panels on televisions and other devices in “various locations in OpenAI buildings” including another conference room where “sensitive meetings” frequently occurred, according to the filing. This suggested Alfozan “had done reconnaissance at OpenAI to determine where he might install additional devices,” the U.S. filing says.

Also on Alfozan’s iPhone was a note he had deleted from September 2026, which had links to different recording devices, including ones made by Seeed Studio, the type of device Alfozan allegedly put in the conference room and which had been found at his residence.

Two other notes stood out. One titled “Riyadh tasks,” last modified Sept. 13—the day he booked the flight—listed finding an apartment and a job for his wife and getting a Saudi passport for his son. Another, titled “OpenAI leave” and last modified Oct. 7, suggested he planned an “early … pick up” of the devices and extending his leave “to full,” according to the U.S. filing. His wife also told FBI agents she had seen her ChatGPT account open on her husband’s laptop, the filing says.

In court, Pernik disputed the government’s account of the room. “This was an open room where anyone could walk in,” he said, adding that Alfozan held meetings and led teams there. The complaint, however, says Alfozan had no authority to enter the room or take part in meetings there.

“OpenAI encouraged Mr. Alfozan to be involved with Saudi Arabia,” Pernik said.

Prosecutors said in court they don’t know what information Alfozan may have tried to take out of OpenAI and the U.S. “That is the concern, that something is going to leave OpenAI and the U.S., and quite frankly we don’t even know what that is,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick Parker said.

The court filings also reveal Alfozan’s browser history, which allegedly shows he accessed a folder called “Saudi Gov Docs” on Oct. 4, 2026. Between July 6 and Sept. 21, 2026, he queried an internal OpenAI productivity tool about which OpenAI staff could be suitable to attend a high-level informal meeting with ministers in Saudi Arabia, and about planned OpenAI visits to Saudi Arabia. He also asked the tool on Sept. 7 who at OpenAI might be likely to attend a meeting with the Saudi state–backed AI company Humain and the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) of Saudi Arabia.

He asked the tool about matters related to MCIT again on Sept. 8, such as an upcoming Saudi MCIT visit on Sept. 9, as well as on Sept. 21. Alfozan’s base salary at OpenAI was $385,000, (up from $325,000 when he was hired) plus a $2.2 million new-hire equity grant.

“OpenAI encouraged Mr. Alfozan to be involved with Saudi Arabia,” Pernik said in court.

Alfozan’s wife and child left the U.S. within 36 hours of his arrest. They did not take the originally planned Oct. 12 flight. Instead, the Saudi government first booked and paid for another one-way ticket for her and their son to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on Oct. 11. However, they also did not take that flight, but rather left a day earlier on Oct. 10 on another business class flight to Qatar booked and paid for by a member of the Saudi military, court documents say.

In court Monday, the defense specified that Alfozan’s brother-in-law (his wife’s sister’s husband) booked the flight. He works in the Saudi government, and paid for the flight with his own money.

The Saudi Consulate General in Los Angeles said in an Oct. 14 letter, filed with the defense motion, that it stands ready to cover the full amount of any bail bond the court requires. It also told Pretrial Services in writing that it “will not issue any travel documents” to Alfozan while he is on release. In court, Pernik said the Saudi government was willing to guarantee $1 million, “giving their full faith and credit,” and would notify the State Department. Tse asked whether the offer amounted to Saudi Arabia keeping him in the U.S. so it wouldn’t lose its money. Pernik said the relationship mattered more than the $1 million.

Alfozan was “in frequent communication via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family,” the U.S. alleges in its motion. The unnamed royal allegedly tried to recruit Alfozan for an AI initiative being launched in Saudi Arabia, and asked Alfozan when he would leave OpenAI. Alfozan allegedly said he wouldn’t leave until his stock vested, the government’s detention memo read.

Alfozan communicated with the unnamed royal as recently as Oct. 5, 2026, court documents say. In May 2026, the royal told Alfozan, “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!” Alfozan responded, “100,” indicating agreement.

Alfozan had applied in July to a program for young Saudi Arabian leaders, the Misk Foundation’s 2030 Leaders program, according to the U.S. filing. He had proceeded to the second stage of the process, and checked the status of his application, as recently as Sept. 4, filings say. The program would have required him to take part in person in Riyadh, the filing says.

At the same time, Alfozan was on the “verge” of getting U.S. citizenship, the defense motion says. A day after OpenAI found the device, on Oct. 1, 2026, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services notified him that his citizenship interview was set for Nov. 6, 2026. This was “a long-held dream for the Alfozan family, as it is for so many immigrants,” reads the defense motion. That interview has since been postponed because of the case, and his next court date is set for Nov. 6, the date of the originally scheduled interview. The defense also told the court that Alfozan had worked and paid taxes in the U.S. for years, and had disclosed even traffic tickets on his citizenship application.

“His plan was always to return to the Bay Area, where his home, his career, and his community are,” the defense motion says. “The evidence shows that Mr. Alfozan planned to accompany his wife and son to Saudi Arabia for his paternity leave and then return.”

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#8. The FDE Bubble: Silicon Valley’s Most Expensive Game Of Pretend

Congratulations to the enterprise AI company that just raised another nine-figure round to solve a problem software is supposed to solve by itself: getting humans to use the product.

You know the one. Won’t name it. Don’t have to. You’ve read the press release — “autonomous,” “agentic,” “category-defining” in paragraph one, and then, a few paragraphs down, where the money is actually going: hiring an army of engineers to sit inside customer offices and manually make the “autonomous” thing behave.

Nothing says “we’ve built the future of work” quite like raising half a billion dollars to hire more people to do the work.

Here’s how it works, in case the deck was too artfully vague:

This is not a flywheel. This is a payroll with a pitch deck.

And the industry has stopped even pretending otherwise — it’s fundraising on it, loudly.

OpenAI pledged up to $1.5 billion into a deployment joint venture valued at $10 billion, with another $4 billion from TPG, Bain Capital, Advent, Brookfield and Goanna. The vehicle, DeployCo, has been reported with more than $4 billion in investment.

Meanwhile, job postings for “forward deployed engineer” are up somewhere between 800% and 1,000% year over year. Lightcast data reported by Fortune put the increase at more than 1,000% from January to August 2026. Financial Times data carried by PYMNTS put listings up more than 800% from January to September 2025, and Indeed data showed postings rising from 643 in April 2025 to 5,330 in April 2026. Total comp is pushing past $300,000 in the U.S. Employer postings list Anthropic at $280,000 to $320,000 base pay and OpenAI at $185,000 to $300,000 base, plus equity. Fortune reported some Anthropic roles reaching $400,000 in total compensation.

Somewhere, a VC is calling this “operating leverage” with a completely straight face.

It is not operating leverage. It’s a staffing agency that learned to say “agentic.”

Ask the one question the pitch deck conveniently never answers: “If you pulled the embedded engineer out tomorrow, does the customer still get what they paid for?”

If the honest answer is “well, no, but the ARR is real” — that’s not product-market fit. That’s people-market fit, and people-market fit has a brutally unglamorous ceiling: You can only hire humans so fast, and you can never hire them cheap enough to earn a software multiple. Every new logo doesn’t get more profitable to serve. It gets another headcount request.

Two companies, same $20 million ARR. One needs 10 engineers to keep the lights on. The other needs 100. Both slides say, “AI software company.” The difference shows up in gross margin, cost to onboard the next customer, and whether that cost falls as the company scales.

Here’s the thing about people-market fit: it feels great right up until someone asks the unfashionable questions: What does it actually cost, fully loaded, to onboard the next customer? Does that number go down as the company scales, or does it just grow the org chart? What happens to gross margin if the first year growth slows and the headcount can’t hide behind hypergrowth anymore?

Companies funding their FDE armies with fresh nine-figure rounds are betting nobody asks these questions until after the round closes and the confetti is swept up. That’s a fine bet in a hype cycle. It’s a terrible one in a market that’s about to start reading the fine print.

Because eventually, someone always reads the fine print. A CFO builds a cost-per-deployment model. A CIO benchmarks time-to-value against three vendors instead of trusting one demo. An investor finally does the unglamorous work of separating software ARR from human-powered ARR on the same balance sheet.

The distinction buyers and investors can test is on the numbers. Software ARR should get cheaper to deliver as it scales. Human-powered ARR does not. OpenAI guaranteed the private-equity backers of its deployment vehicle an annual 17.5% return over five years, which is a different structure from a growth thesis.¹

So no, your AI isn’t autonomous. But your business model might be — autonomously transferring the cost of a services company onto a software valuation, for as long as the music plays.

Enjoy the round. Hope the org chart was worth it.

#9. America's offshore wind detour

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Trump administration is paying offshore wind developers billions to abandon projects, raising questions about energy costs and taxpayer money

Patrick Pleul/picture alliance via Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration agreed to pay offshore wind developers nearly $4 billion to not build wind farms. Nine states sued on Sept. 22 to unwind some of the deals.

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

The lawsuits targeted Invenergy, which was to get $653 million for three leases, and Bluepoint Wind, which was to get $765 million for one. They were the latest in a string that began in March with TotalEnergies, which got $928 million back for two leases. California filed a separate suit over Invenergy's Morro Bay lease, tied to another $111 million.

Each deal worked the same way. Interior refunded what the company had paid for its lease, which it described as dollar for dollar, and the lease was canceled. In exchange, the company promised to invest the same amount in gas and other energy projects.

Interior called the deals settlements of legal claims, which let it pay out of a federal fund meant for that purpose. The states said there was nothing to settle. California said Invenergy had never sued, and the New York-led coalition said the deals weren't real compromises.

Other countries had been building offshore wind for decades with much less drama. Denmark put up the world's first offshore wind farm in 1991, 11 small turbines off the island of Lolland that together could power about 2,200 homes. By 2024, offshore wind alone produced 28 percent of the electricity generated in Denmark.

America's first came in 2016, five turbines off Block $SQ Island, Rhode Island, enough for about 17,000 homes. The next wave, approved under Biden, was meant to close the gap. Biden officials argued the country needed proofs of concept in the water. It arrived at a bad time.

Regulators began approving big projects a year into the pandemic, as supply chains seized up and interest rates climbed. Eleven won approval.

Trump moved on his first day back in office, freezing federal permitting and leasing for wind. Stop-work orders followed, first at Empire Wind off New York and then at Revolution Wind off Rhode Island.

The One Big Beautiful Bill, signed July 2025, cut short the credits wind depended on. In December, Interior halted all five farms under construction. Courts kept ruling against the orders, so Interior turned to buyouts.

Three big farms were finished anyway: South Fork off Long Island, Vineyard Wind 1 off Massachusetts and Revolution Wind off Rhode Island. Empire Wind and Sunrise Wind are still due to come online in 2027. Even so, BloombergNEF cut its forecast for U.S. offshore wind in 2035 from 39 gigawatts to six.

The Trump administration has a lot of arguments against offshore wind, and the strongest on is about money. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said such projects were "only viable when propped up by massive taxpayer subsidies."

Gas and wind are paid for in opposite ways. A gas plant was cheap to build and then paid for fuel for decades. A wind farm got its fuel free but spent nearly everything upfront, on turbines, foundations, cable and ships, so the interest on its loans showed up immediately in every megawatt hour.

A federal tax credit covered up to 30 percent of that bill. When Congress shortened the deadline to qualify, BloombergNEF's modeling put the price of power from a new project about a third higher, before tariffs.

Support like that was common in energy. Oil and gas drillers claimed depletion allowances and nuclear plants got a production tax credit, though analysts disputed which breaks counted as subsidies. What set offshore wind apart was the risk. The money was spent before the rules could change, so changing them midway hurt more than it would for a gas plant.

The administration also questioned reliability, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright arguing that power arriving at unpredictable times was not really dependable. But offshore wind has already provided examples of helping during times of stress. Vineyard Wind and South Fork performed well during Winter Storm Fern when the grid was strained trying to keep people warm. In July, offshore wind also helped displace oil-fired peaker plants during a heat wave.

Almost everything big in energy got more expensive to build. Data centers drove up demand and supply chains lagged, and BloombergNEF found the cost of a new U.S. gas plant rose 66 percent from 2023 to 2025.

The administration decided offshore wind was the one that cost too much. So far, it has spent almost $4 billion to make sure some of it never gets built.

#10. Hiring a Speaker for Your Next Event? Ask These 6 Questions Before You Sign a Contract

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Ask these six questions that separate a keynote speaker people remember from one they forget before they return home.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Last year, an executive at a tech company asked me whether I could keynote their employee resource group event. I knew there were speakers out there who were better aligned with their women’s program, so I kindly passed on the opportunity and sent several other names instead. I’m an ally, but I was also the wrong person for that stage. Their audience deserved someone who could speak from lived experience.

I’ve delivered hundreds of keynotes, workshops and retreats on workplace mental health, burnout and boundaries, communication and conflict for organizations like Amazon, Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, LinkedIn and WebMD, but I still keep a running list of speakers I refer organizers to, because the right speaker serves everyone better. Disappointing sessions usually trace back to a good speaker standing in front of the wrong room.

The following six questions will help you decide what you want to actually receive for your investment in a speaker, and how to make sure you get the right one.

Organizers usually start their event planning process by focusing on a topic. I’d rather you start with the question of what needs to be different when people walk out of the room.

The speaker who raises the professional caliber of your conference isn’t necessarily the one who re-energizes a room after lunch. If you just want to attract registrations with a marquee name like Michelle Obama, that’s one thing, but if you want to run a workshop that gives managers practical tools for navigating employee mental health, that’s another.

Before you shortlist any particular speaker, answer these questions:

When I ask an organizer what success looks like to them, and the conversation goes quiet, I usually find that they’re not really ready to book a speaker.

Do you want lived experience, academic depth or someone who does the work daily? Those are three different speakers, yet organizers treat them as interchangeable.

I once spoke at a university and it turned out that the audience really wanted an academic. They had come for theory and peer-reviewed research, and I showed up as a practitioner with tools and exercises. Within 10 minutes, I could feel my presentation wasn’t what they were expecting.

The same thinking applies to diversity. I ask every organizer who else is speaking at their event, and I’ve declined invitations that would have put me on an all-white, all-male panel. I believe that your speakers should reflect the audience in front of them.

Speaking fees generally range from a modest honorarium to well into six figures. What that covers is rarely obvious from the outside, but it’s customary to include the calls before the event, the design work that turns those calls into a real session, the day itself and the debrief afterward. I also consider travel days to be working days, particularly for a multi-day offsite or leadership retreat.

Your speaker’s reputation is part of how your event gets marketed, too. Attendees have told me they registered for a conference because they saw my name on the agenda. Professional development budgets are tight, and HR leaders who can attend one conference a year regularly choose based on the speaker roster.

Still, organizers tend to lean too heavily on public visibility when choosing a speaker. A large social media following only tells you someone can market themselves, which is a very different skill than holding a room’s attention for 90 minutes. A bestselling book only tells you they can write. Neither tells you how a speaker handles questions they don’t see coming.

I once sat in the audience at an industry conference and recognized that the keynote was giving the exact same speech they’d given at another event I’d attended. In fact, someone I knew leaned over partway through to mention that fact to me.

To avoid stale or irrelevant material, ask what the speaker’s customization process actually involves. Dropping your logo onto a deck isn’t the same as targeting their content. They need to understand what you actually want. I once designed a conflict inventory workshop for the people team at an enterprise software company then realized in the prep call that they didn’t even want me to do conflict training. Rather, they wanted to me to equip them to deliver the training themselves. Understanding that in advance helped me reshape the entire build, from the exercises down to the facilitator notes.

Another time, I was mid-session in a workshop on boundaries and self-care, about to launch into a delegation activity, when audience feedback revealed they didn’t know how to prioritize. You can’t hand work off until you know which work matters most, so how were they supposed to delegate?

So we stopped. I set the slides aside, picked up a flip chart and markers and built a prioritization exercise on the spot. We returned to delegation afterward, and it landed because we’d cleared the roadblock.

Plenty of speakers just keep clicking through their deck regardless of what’s happening in the room. While that can work for a large keynote audience, managers and executives in a training session can tell when a facilitator is just delivering a script and not addressing their needs.

It’s hard to know in advance whether a prospective speaker can adapt on the fly, which is why it’s important to go beyond the one-sheet and check references and try to watch a full-length video of their past presentations.

Strong speakers fill their calendars a year out, so booking late narrows your options to whoever happens to be available. Try to start looking for speakers as far ahead of time as possible. This allows you to get good prices on travel and engage in planning calls to help the expert tailor their content to your needs.

Of course, you don’t always have enough time to plan ahead, but you can still make a better decision by working closely with the speaker on their content. I once accepted a booking with under two weeks of lead time, but it went well because we were honest about what was possible.

If you’re up against a tight timeline, you might also consider hosting a virtual session, which opens up your options, though I’d press hard on whether that speaker can truly engage people remotely. Otherwise, your attendees will experience your event as just one more meeting on their calendar.

The organizers I most respect approach this process as if they were making a hiring decision. They talk with several prospects before choosing one. They call references. They ask what the post-event survey data from the person’s last speech actually said rather than relying on testimonials. When they approach it this way, some conclude they don’t need an outside speaker at all, which can be the right answer.

When you address the questions above before you sign anything, you’ll walk into your event knowing exactly who and what you booked. That way, your audience will have a productive and engaging experience. Remember, you’ve got this!

Last year, an executive at a tech company asked me whether I could keynote their employee resource group event. I knew there were speakers out there who were better aligned with their women’s program, so I kindly passed on the opportunity and sent several other names instead. I’m an ally, but I was also the wrong person for that stage. Their audience deserved someone who could speak from lived experience.

I’ve delivered hundreds of keynotes, workshops and retreats on workplace mental health, burnout and boundaries, communication and conflict for organizations like Amazon, Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, LinkedIn and WebMD, but I still keep a running list of speakers I refer organizers to, because the right speaker serves everyone better. Disappointing sessions usually trace back to a good speaker standing in front of the wrong room.

The following six questions will help you decide what you want to actually receive for your investment in a speaker, and how to make sure you get the right one.

#11. 4 VC Firms for B2B Tech Startups in 2027: Product Signals or ARR?

B2B tech startups receive funding from venture capital firms that evaluate early evidence through different diligence lenses.

Some firms use product signals to understand adoption, engagement, and product-led demand before financial metrics fully mature, while others place more emphasis on ARR, go-to-market progress, team quality, market opportunity, or enterprise execution.

That distinction matters at pre-seed and seed, when annual recurring revenue (ARR) may be limited or absent. Choosing an investor starts with understanding what the business can demonstrate today.

How Do Investors Evaluate B2B Tech Startups?

Investors evaluate B2B tech startups by matching the company’s current evidence to the stage of the round. At pre-seed and seed, that evidence may include product adoption, customer feedback, usage depth, GTM progress, team quality, market timing, and early revenue where available.

Product signals show how customers respond to a tool: how quickly adoption spreads, how deeply users engage, whether they recommend it and how usage translates into interest in paying.

Financial indicators show the commercial results of that behavior. ARR measures recurring revenue on an annualized basis. Revenue growth, customer retention and sales efficiency help investors assess whether demand supports a sustainable business. GTM progress shows how a company reaches and converts customers.

Product behavior can reveal momentum before financial patterns mature. Adoption velocity, engagement depth, user advocacy and conversion behavior can all provide useful evidence at this stage. Repeated use can provide stronger evidence than registrations followed by inactivity. ARR remains important as the business develops.

At pre-seed, founder insight, market timing, customer feedback and early product behavior may carry considerable weight because little revenue history exists.

At seed, investors may have more adoption, retention and commercial data to examine. Expectations still depend on the business model and product maturity. An enterprise tool with long purchasing cycles will produce evidence differently from self-service software.

Founders should ask which proof points matter to the specific partner evaluating their company. The same startup can present differently through a product-usage, SaaS-metric or GTM lens.

Mighty Capital, a16z, Bessemer, and Accel each show a different way investors assess early B2B tech momentum, from product signals to ARR, GTM progress, and enterprise execution.

Mighty Capital is an early-stage, B2B-specialist venture capital firm built for B2B tech founders raising from pre-seed through Series A. That focus matters because pre-seed and seed founders need investors whose check size, lead role, and support model match the stage where product evidence often develops before ARR fully matures.

Mighty Capital invests at pre-seed through Series A in B2B technology companies with enterprise ambitions, writing checks from $200K to $5M+ and leading most rounds, providing founder-friendly terms and direct operational support from the product leadership network, a specialist alternative to generalist multi-stage funds.

Its evaluation model supports that early-stage focus. Mighty Capital is a venture capital firm that invests in B2B technology companies using the Product Alpha Effect™, a proprietary methodology that reads product signals from 600,000+ product leaders to identify outlier companies before traditional investors do. Its Product Signal Stack examines adoption velocity, engagement depth, community advocacy and product-qualified lead (PQL) conversion patterns.

Through its exclusive Products That Count partnership, Mighty Capital reads early product signals from 600,000+ CPOs and product managers. The community also provides structured buyer distribution for portfolio companies, helping founders sell more and faster.

Andreessen Horowitz is a broad, multi-stage technology investment platform operating from seed through growth across areas including enterprise software, AI, infrastructure and fintech. Its scale brings operating resources spanning talent, marketing, legal and policy support.

For B2B founders, that breadth can be useful when the pitch depends on a large market, a strong founding team, technical differentiation and the potential to scale across a major technology category. Available traction helps explain the opportunity, but early-stage investing does not require waiting for mature ARR.

a16z is generalist and platform-driven rather than built around a proprietary product-signal methodology. Founders should establish which team fits their business and what evidence that team expects at the current stage.

The practical attraction is brand recognition, portfolio breadth and access to a wide operating network. Its fit is strongest for founders who want multi-stage platform support rather than a specialist pre-seed-through-Series-A B2B investor.

Bessemer Venture Partners brings established cloud, SaaS, and B2B software expertise to this comparison. Its strength is not a product-signal methodology, but a long-running software investment lens that helps founders frame commercial performance once customer and revenue data begin to matter.

For B2B software startups with emerging ARR, Bessemer’s SaaS and cloud guidance can make metrics more legible. Repeatable sales cycles, retention, acquisition efficiency, and net revenue retention help show whether demand is turning into a scalable business rather than remaining early interest.

That makes Bessemer especially relevant when a startup’s strongest evidence includes SaaS economics, cloud-market fit, and early commercial execution. It can suit founders ready to explain how customer demand is becoming measurable revenue, particularly as the company moves beyond initial product adoption into a more repeatable growth motion.

Accel brings B2B and enterprise investing experience to startups where go-to-market progress, customer targeting and early commercial execution are becoming central to the story. Its strength in this comparison is not product-signal diligence before metrics mature, but a broader enterprise lens for understanding how product demand turns into repeatable growth.

For B2B founders, that makes pilot outcomes, purchasing behavior, early revenue and sales motion useful evidence in the pitch. A company can show who uses the product, who pays for it, how customers are being reached and whether that route to market is becoming more consistent.

Accel’s early-stage activity also includes pre-product and pre-revenue companies through programs such as Atoms, so it is not limited to startups with mature ARR. Still, its positioning fits founders whose evidence is moving toward GTM traction, enterprise adoption and commercial development rather than primarily early product behavior.

How Should Founders Choose Between Product-Signal and ARR-Focused VCs?

The right fit depends on what the startup can already prove and which type of evidence an investor is best equipped to assess.

If a founder needs a specialist B2B tech investor for pre-seed through Series A, Mighty Capital writes $200K to $5M+ checks, leads most rounds and uses the Product Alpha Effect™ to evaluate early product evidence before ARR fully matures.

A founder looking for a broad multi-stage platform will find a16z suitable because of its scale, operating resources and coverage across multiple technology categories.

If a startup already has enough recurring-revenue and customer data for SaaS metrics to be meaningful, Bessemer’s cloud expertise helps frame retention, growth and commercial performance.

When GTM progress, pilot results or early revenue are the strongest proof points, Accel fits founders looking for enterprise and B2B experience tied to commercial execution.

Founders should start with their strongest evidence, then ask which investor is most likely to understand it.

Before sending a pitch, founders can assemble usage data, customer feedback, GTM progress and available financial results into a clear account of what the company has proved.

Match that evidence to the investor’s questions, then establish what the partnership would contribute to the next stage of development. The strongest fundraising target is usually the investor whose diligence lens matches that evidence.

What Product Signals Do VCs Look at Before Revenue?

Investors may examine adoption velocity, engagement depth, user advocacy, retention and conversion behavior. They also look at who uses the product and which problem it solves. Repeat usage and customer recommendations can reveal demand, but different investors weigh these signals differently.

ARR is not universally required for seed funding. Expectations vary with the investor, business model, stage and product maturity. A company without recurring revenue may demonstrate its potential through customer validation, retention, technical progress or a credible market opportunity.

What Is the Difference Between Pre-Seed and Seed Funding for B2B Tech Startups?

Pre-seed often supports initial product development and validation, with evidence centered on the team, market and early customer response. Seed generally involves more proof of adoption, GTM development or commercial traction.

#13. Dream Labs raises $90M to help build more intelligent robots with simple video feeds

Dream Labs, a startup trying to make robots more intelligent and capable of performing many different tasks, has raised $90 million in seed funding to coincide with the launch of a public application programming interface that provides access to its universal robot foundation model.

Today’s round was jointly led by B Capital and Kindred Ventures and saw the participation of others including A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, Wing VC, SV Angel, Scribble VC and angel investor Adrian Aoun.

Dream Labs is taking aim at the lack of intelligence in today’s robots, which might be fairly numerous in many environments but are also fairly limited. The startup believes there are more than 5 million industrial robots working inside factories and warehouses globally. These robots surely do perform useful work, otherwise their owners wouldn’t have invested in them, but Dream Labs co-founder and Chief Executive Joel Jang believes they should be able to do so much more.

What’s stopping them is a lack of expertise and knowledge. Almost all of those 5 million robots are designed to perform a single task, which they do very well. But they cannot be trained to do any other task, nor can they pass on their acquired knowledge to train other robots and machines.

Though the costs of robotic hardware have fallen dramatically, with extremely dextrous robotic arms now selling for just a few thousand dollars, those products don’t ship with any intelligence. Rather, the onus is on the buyer to teach that robotic arm how to do a specific job, and that’s a process that can take many months, because it involves lots of tedious and highly specialized programming work. Worse, whenever new robotic hardware is introduced, that entire process has to be redone from scratch.

Today, Dream Labs is coming out of stealth with Dream-1, a robot foundation model that controls bimanual robots it has never seen, on tasks it was never shown, in places it has never been, from $3/hour.

Dream API is live for everyone, today. 🧵 pic.twitter.com/MB1snhUOAJ

— Dream Labs (@dreamlabs_ai) October 19, 2026

Jang believes there should be an easier way to train robots to perform new tasks, and his solution is a highly versatile foundation model called Dream-1, which is designed to be a “universal brain” for robots. Dream-1 treats robotic skills as simple video prediction problems. It teaches robots using what Jang calls “human egocentric training data,” which is a fancy term for videos of people performing physical tasks such as stacking shelves and packing items in boxes.

By studying these videos, Dream-1 learns to predict what should logically happen next and based on that, it will then determine the physical action the robot needs to perform to ensure it actually happens. The big advantage of teaching robots this way is that video-based data is much easier to accumulate than specialized machine-specific datasets. It means Dream-1 can quickly amass the data it needs to teach robots new skills, transferring intelligence seamlessly across different types of robotic hardware.

Jang said Dream-1 has been designed to work with any two-armed robot that’s equipped with parallel grippers. The only thing required to get started is a video feed and natural language instructions – basically, someone to tell it what to do.

“The hardware is ready, but what’s been missing is a brain any robot can use,” Jang said. “When you get into a rental car, you don’t relearn how to drive. You find the controls and your past driving experience does the rest. Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so it can do useful work in minutes, not months.”

The next step is making this intelligence universally accessible to developers, and that’s where today’s API launch comes in. Through the Dream API, developers can access Dream-1 and instantly start translating visual inputs and natural language prompts into robotic actions. Dream Labs is charging developers $3 per hour to access the most powerful version of Dream-1, with prices dropping to just 75 cents per hour for a lightweight version.

Dream-1 can also be used to teach robots entirely new skills that the model hasn’t come across before through the startup’s Fine-Tuning-as-a-Service offering. All developers have to do is submit video demonstrating a new task — the more video footage there is, the better — and Dream Labs will turn that into a highly customized version of Dream-1 within a few hours.

To showcase the capabilities of its model, the company has also launched the Robot Playground, which can be accessed by anyone through a web browser. Simply type a command and watch a live robot respond in real time.

Dream Labs is currently working with more than 20 robotic hardware companies whose machines cost anywhere between $2,000 and $10,000. While Dream-1 is designed to work with any robotic arm, the company works with these partners to optimize the model for their specific hardware. This work gives it a better ‘grasp’ of what each robot can do, enabling better performance.

Jang said Dream-1 is already highly capable at tasks such as picking up and placing objects and folding clothes, but he has much bigger ambitions in the long term. For instance, he plans to teach the model to support mobile robots that use wheels and also robots with fully dextrous or humanlike hands. The money from today’s round will help to pay for the necessary compute power to get this done, he said.

Daisy Cai of B Capital said robotic arms can now be bought for the same price as a high-end laptop. “What they need now is intelligence,” she continued. “This team did some of the defining work in robot learning at Nvidia, and now anyone with an API key can build on it.”

#16. ‘Don’t wait for somebody else to fix it’: T-Mobile exec Deeanne King on cutting CO2 and costs

The Sustainability Spotlight profiles individuals who are impacting the future of our planet by turning visionary climate tech concepts into real-world solutions.

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 19, 2026 at 7:57 amOctober 19, 2026 at 7:57 am

When Deeanne King came to the Pacific Northwest in 2020 — relocating from Kansas after Sprint merged with Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile — she fell in love with the region’s natural beauty. In her role as executive vice president and chief people officer, she also helps lead sustainability efforts for the telecom giant.

“The outdoors is my happy place,” King said. The region’s lakes, inland sea and trails, she added, are “a good reminder of what we’re all working to protect.”

T-Mobile has been ranked among the greenest companies in the U.S and globally. It’s making notable progress toward climate goals at a time when numerous corporations are scaling back or abandoning their carbon targets.

Keep reading to learn more about King’s sustainability journey. Her quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

People. Hands down. I get to work with some incredibly smart, curious, and committed people, and one thing I’ve learned is that when you put a hard problem in front of people who care, they find a way. They challenge the status quo, they try something new, they learn, and they keep going. I’ve never seen our teams walk away from a problem because it was hard.

I’m also encouraged by the growing recognition that sustainability and good business can, and should, go together. Building more efficiently, using resources more thoughtfully, and reducing waste can make a business more resilient while also being better for the planet. Those things don’t have to compete.

And I see that mindset in our employees. People want their work to matter. They want to contribute to something bigger than themselves. When you combine that sense of purpose with ingenuity and a willingness to work together, I think there’s tremendous reason for hope.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

I’ve gotten much more intentional about cutting down on single-use things, and my reusable water bottle is probably the simplest example. It goes everywhere with me now.

It sounds small, but I think that’s actually the point. Once you make one change part of your routine, you start noticing other opportunities: what you throw away, what you reuse, what you buy, and what you probably didn’t need in the first place. Those small choices add up.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I’d choose Chief Sustainability Officer Kara Hurst at Amazon. T-Mobile joined Amazon and hundreds of other companies in signing the Climate Pledge, committing to reach net-zero carbon by 2040. And there’s something Kara has said about that work that really resonates with me: “We cannot go at this alone.”

I couldn’t agree more. The biggest challenges we face aren’t going to be solved by one company, one industry, or one really smart person. We have to find common ground, share what we’re learning, and be willing to work together toward something bigger than any one of us.

I’d love to sit down with Kara and compare notes on what’s working, where we’re getting stuck, and where companies like ours can work together to move faster. And knowing me, we’d probably end up talking about people and leadership too, because ultimately, ambitious goals only become real when you have people who are willing to question how things have always been done and figure out how to get there.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Making sustainability practical. Sometimes we gravitate toward the giant, breakthrough idea, and we absolutely need those. But there is also enormous opportunity in doing the basics really, really well and using data to figure out where small changes can add up to a very big impact.

Take buildings. They aren’t necessarily the first thing people think about when they think about climate innovation, but managing HVAC systems more intelligently produced nearly $5 million in estimated energy savings for T-Mobile in 2025. As of 2025, we have 132 community solar projects in our portfolio, providing an estimated lifetime total savings of $60 million in energy costs. You can reduce energy use, lower costs, and do something positive for the planet.

What’s one metric you watch obsessively as a sustainability leader?

I don’t know that I would use the word obsessively, but I absolutely believe in measuring whether the work is actually making a difference. One number I’m particularly proud of is that in 2025, T-Mobile’s total emissions were 50% lower than our 2020 baseline. That’s meaningful progress, especially because our business hasn’t been standing still.

The scope of the climate challenge is daunting — how do you approach this work?

You can’t let the size of the problem become the reason you don’t start. That’s true of climate change, but honestly, it’s true of almost every really hard problem I’ve encountered in my career. When something feels enormous, I focus first on what we can control. What’s the next decision? What’s the next action? What can we make better today? Then you keep going.

I’m also a big believer in being willing to learn along the way. Take smart risks, look at the data, listen to people, adjust and keep moving.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

As a mom, I think about the world we’re handing to the next generation. Of course I want my children, and someday, their children, to inherit a healthy planet. But I also want them to inherit the belief that when something matters, you don’t wait for somebody else to fix it. You figure out what you can do, you bring people together and you get to work.

Data and science guide us. Passion and invention drive us. We work backward from ambitious targets because that’s where progress happens, bringing innovation to the planet’s biggest challenges. Every package delivered, every data center powered, every product designed is an opportunity to make tomorrow better—and we share what we learn to help accelerate collective climate action.
