#18. The AI productivity boom has bosses asking what’s in it for employees

Good morning! Fortune reporter Emma Burleigh here, filling in for Kristin.

AI is helping employees get more done in less time. As companies race to capitalize on those efficiency gains, some executives are rethinking how they measure the technology’s success—and what it should ultimately deliver for their businesses and workers.

From unlocking creativity and innovation to protecting employees’ brain health, leaders are taking a broader view of AI’s impact on the workplace. The stakes are growing: U.S. employees who frequently use AI report higher burnout rates than those who don’t, according to 2026 data from Quantum Workplace.

For Athina Kanioura, global chief strategy and transformation officer and CEO of PepsiCo Latin America, rethinking AI’s value means challenging the pressure to prove immediate financial returns. Speaking with panelists from Indeed, Dropbox, and Bristol Myers Squibb at the Fortune Most Powerful Women conference last week, Kanioura argued that requiring a business case for every AI application risks overlooking benefits that are harder to quantify. She described the relentless pursuit of ROI as “death by a thousand cuts.”

At Indeed, AI is already delivering measurable productivity gains, helping software engineers write 50% more code and saving employees six hours a week, according to chief revenue officer Maggie Hulce. The company is looking to put that newfound time toward creative thinking and innovation, giving employees more opportunities to do work they enjoy. “We’re moving faster, we can innovate faster, we can invent faster, we can do fun work more and more,” said Hulce.

Other leaders are exploring how to keep employees mentally sharp. Dropbox chief people officer Melanie Rosenwasser said the $8 billion cloud company is examining the risk of “cognitive atrophy” as workers increasingly outsource their thinking to AI. Dropbox has introduced memory exercises, attention-span training, and puzzles. It also experimented with device-free “analog” offsites and brought in a breath-work specialist for its executive team.

“When you outsource your thinking to AI, you become less intelligent in the process,” Rosenwasser said, referencing research from MIT professor Eric So. “So we need to be very deliberate about how we’re using these tools.”

At Bristol Myers Squibb, EVP and chief people officer Amanda Poole is weighing how much of the productivity gained from automating “joyless” work should go back to employees to support their well-being. The company has begun exploring a “well-being quotient” to decide how to split those gains between the business and its workforce.

“Let’s say we’re going to get 20% productivity [with AI]: What part are we going to take back as a company, and what part are we going to give back?” Poole said, adding, “We haven’t solved it, so more to come.”

Emma BurleighFortune Success Reporteremma.burleigh@fortune.com

This week, Crystal Barney, chief talent officer at public affairs firm APCO, answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: We have an employee—we’ll call him Steve—who's been a solid performer for six years. After he was passed over for a promotion, his wife emailed HR demanding to know why. When we said we couldn't discuss his employment with her, she emailed his manager and our CEO. Steve was mortified and said he'd asked her to stop.

After his annual review, she emailed us again, attaching screenshots of internal messages Steve had forwarded her. We told Steve he couldn't share confidential communications.

Then Steve took several sick days. His wife called his manager, blamed work for his anxiety, and demanded paid medical leave. A leave request later arrived from Steve's work email, which he admitted his wife had sent.

She then posted on LinkedIn accusing the company of destroying his mental health, publicly accused his manager of retaliation, and threatened legal action.

Steve says he had no idea she'd do any of this, but his performance is now slipping.

We can't discipline Steve because his wife is difficult, but he has shared confidential information and let her use his work account. When does a spouse's behavior become the employee's problem? How do we handle this without creating a retaliation issue around his leave?

A: Steve can’t control his wife, and you can’t discipline him for her LinkedIn posts or her questions at a conference. But sharing confidential messages and letting someone else use his work account are his actions. Those are fair to address, the same way you would with any employee.

I’d have a direct, compassionate conversation with Steve. Make clear you aren’t asking him to manage his spouse. You’re asking him to protect company information and keep his account to himself. Put expectations in writing and offer support.

On leave, treat the request like any other. If it’s unclear who submitted it, ask Steve to confirm directly, then let the process run.

I’m speaking from a U.S. perspective, and specific legal requirements vary by country, but the principle holds anywhere. To avoid a retaliation claim, keep decisions about Steve’s role, performance, and development consistent and documented, and loop in someone beyond his manager. Discomfort is human, but it can’t drive outcomes. And talk to employment counsel early, especially with a legal threat on the table.

#20. FDA updates Salata's jalapeño avocado dressing recall to highest-risk category

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Class I designation means exposure to the product could cause serious harm or death; no illnesses have been reported

Salata Dressings received a Class I recall designation from the Food and Drug Administration for its Jalapeño Avocado Dressing, the agency's most serious recall category, covering more than 1,700 cases distributed across three states over potential salmonella contamination.

The Houston-based company initiated the voluntary recall on August 6 and announced it publicly on August 11. The FDA assigned the Class I classification on September 29, according to Newsweek. Under FDA guidelines, a Class I recall means the agency has determined a reasonable probability exists that contact with or consumption of the product will lead to serious adverse health consequences or death.

In total, 1,724 cases of the dressing are subject to the recall, packaged in either 12.5-fluid-ounce bottles or one-gallon jugs. The affected bottles carry best-by dates of November 5, 13, 18, or 25, 2026. The one-gallon jugs have best-by dates between October 6 and October 26, 2026. The product was distributed in Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas, the FDA said.

According to Newsweek, the recall was triggered when Salata's jalapeño supplier alerted the company that the diced jalapeños incorporated into the dressing may carry salmonella and could have a connection to a broader FDA investigation into a multistate jalapeño outbreak. When Salata first went public with the recall, it covered only 12-ounce bottles that had been on sale at HEB grocery stores in Texas from July 13 through August 5.

Neither the company nor the FDA has reported any illnesses connected to the recalled dressing.

The broader jalapeño outbreak affected 488 people across 34 states and led to 65 hospitalizations, the FDA said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the FDA declared that outbreak over last week, according to The New York Times. The probable source of the outbreak was traced to a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, whose identity has not been disclosed publicly, operating as a supplier to Coast Citrus Distributors.

Consumers who have the recalled product should not eat it. Salata is advising customers to return affected bottles or jugs to the place of purchase for a full refund. Any surfaces or containers that may have come into contact with the dressing should be thoroughly cleaned to reduce the risk of cross-contamination, the company said.

According to the FDA, illness from salmonella generally sets in within 12 to 72 hours of eating tainted food and tends to run its course over four to seven days. Young children under five, elderly individuals, and those whose immune systems are compromised are at heightened risk of developing severe complications.

#21. Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.

The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.

Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.

That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.

Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.

“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.

Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.

“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.

Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.

Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.

The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.

Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.

Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).

Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.

Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.

In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.

Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.

“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

#22. What Investors Should Know Before Investing in Canadian Physical Silver

Silver doesn’t pay a dividend. You can’t buy anything in the grocery store with it, and if it is kept in the house it won’t grow. But people still buy it.

Why? Partly because it’s something they can have to themselves. But investing in real silver is a little more complicated than just picking out a coin and hoping its value rises.

Silver is a commodity you can invest in and is traded on the market in troy ounces. That will change through the trading day and it may not be the amount you really pay if you go out and acquire the metal.

If you want to buy silver in Canada you will find coins and bars of different sizes and even if they have the same silver content they will cost different amounts.

Premiums can blow the deal. Dealers also charge for manufacturing, handling and other commercial costs. Buyers love certain things more. And that’s what they charge you for extra. For example, a 1 ounce coin could cost more per ounce than a larger bar. But that doesn’t mean the bar is the better choice. Depends on what you want to do with the silver and what you are willing to spend.

If you walk into a bullion shop you will find silver in all shapes and all sizes. Coins are easy to identify, and there are only so many different ones. And what makes them hot. For example, the Royal Canadian Mint makes Canadian Maple Leaf silver coins. Another choice is bars, particularly for larger purchases. They can be cheaper per ounce but who knows?

The Royal Canadian Mint has some advice for people who want to buy bullion, including shopping around among dealers and knowing the spot price. Just be careful of one thing, buy price and sale price are not the same. If you want to sell tomorrow, the dealer will give you a lot less. He can tell you a price now.

And some of us wait for our silver to do it. Save a few bucks. Easy. But a few huge bars is a different story. Silver is a pain to lug. You don’t want to be worried about theft and fire and if your insurance covers precious metals. A bank safe deposit box or professional storage facility can be an option, but these can add to the cost.

But that’s not the only real storage problem. If you are looking to sell you need to find a buyer that will give you a price you are comfortable selling your silver at. Depending on the buyer, this could be going to a dealer, arranging delivery or presenting paperwork.

Silver is especially important for industry, above all in electronics and solar technology. So it has a different demand profile from gold. Prices are not being pushed up by industrial demand.

Silver is fluid. It is subject to economic conditions, on the opinion of investors and on changes in demand. In Canada silver is usually priced in U.S. dollars, so Canadian buyers must take into account exchange rates. Someone who buys now may see his investment fall in the next month. You can lose money on the dealer margin and selling charges even if the market price does not change.

But then Sell It, it’s easy to focus on the buy

Which coin is more beautiful? Is the premium worth it? Now? Or after? But the more interesting question is: what then happens? If you needed the cash could you sell it in 6 months and not lose a tonne? Now what are you gonna do? And will your cash get commingled with your savings and investments?

Adding real silver to a more diversified investment portfolio. Don’t expect it to save you money either. And you need to think a little bit about what you’re paying for and what you’re going to get back.

#23. Trump administration orders ban on DeepSeek in federal agencies

The Department of Homeland Security has ordered artificial intelligence technology from the Chinese company DeepSeek Ltd. be removed from all federal civilian agencies.

The order, published on the Federal Register website today, warned that DeepSeek’s AI models present “multiple threat vectors,” that could give the Chinese Communist Party “extensive authority” to access American government infrastructure.

The new order from the DHS means all civilian agency information technology systems will now have to remove all any products affiliated with DeepSeek from their systems, which includes third-party services developed using the app. Going forward, all purchases of DeepSeek’s products and services are verboten in those agencies. The DHS justified the move by invoking the 2018 Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act following a review of the matter by the Federal Acquisition Security Council.

The DHS subsequently warned that the technology poses a danger to the U.S. in various forms. The agency explained that it could be used to “track or digitally fingerprint” users and may “transfer of sensitive data to the People’s Republic of China if used by U.S. government or vendors.”

The U.S. crackdown on DeepSeek had been brewing since last year, when the company stunned the tech industry with the release of its R1 model. Despite being trained using less powerful chips and at a fraction of the cost of some competing models, the open-source AI system outperformed models developed by American rivals OpenAI and Anthropic in several complex tests.

The Commerce Department last year banned DeepSeek from government devices, while the U.S. Navy directed all its members not to use the model because of potential security concerns. New York State banned DeepSeek from government devices and networks over “serious concerns” over potential data privacy and censorship risks posed by the app.

DeepSeek released its latest AI model, V4.1 Flash-1017 just recently. The upgraded model promised faster performance and improved reasoning and coding capabilities, with early reports suggesting it could compete with some of the most advanced American AI systems.

Portland's vegan athlete earns three gold medals at IPF World Masters Championships following a potentially career-ending setback

PORTLAND, Ore., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Two years after a shoulder replacement threatened to end his competitive lifting career, Vegan Strong PlantBuilt athlete Ryan Stills became a six-time world champion, winning the Classic Masters 2 men's 120-kilogram class at the International Powerlifting Federation World Masters Powerlifting Championships on Oct. 18 in Reno, Nevada. #26. Amazon challenges Nvidia’s software advantage with new tool for its own AI chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 19, 2026 at 6:25 amOctober 19, 2026 at 6:30 am

A new software tool from Amazon aims to make switching from Nvidia to the company’s own AI chips about as simple as changing a setting.

The software, dubbed TorchNeuron, runs code written in PyTorch, the open-source framework used by many AI developers, on Amazon’s Trainium chips. It has been in private beta since late last year, and Amazon said Monday that it’s opening the software to all developers as a public beta.

Until now, developers who wanted to run PyTorch code on Trainium had to modify it to call programming interfaces specific to Amazon’s chips, said Colin Brace, vice president of technology software at Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip-design unit. With TorchNeuron, the same code runs after a basic configuration change.

“If you know PyTorch, then you know Trainium,” Brace said in an interview.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI chips, partly because much of the industry’s AI software was built around its CUDA platform. Adapting that code to other hardware can take months of engineering work. That has made many companies reluctant to switch, even as Amazon, Google and others have developed their own chips.

TorchNeuron is part of a broader push by tech giants to loosen Nvidia’s grip on AI computing, even as they remain among its biggest customers.

Asked about Amazon’s relationship with Nvidia, Brace said the company has “always been about choice,” pointing to another high-profile example: AWS offers Intel processors alongside its own Graviton chips.

Amazon plans to release TorchNeuron as open-source software on Tuesday in conjunction with the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, Calif.

Trainium’s biggest users so far are AI labs with close financial ties to Amazon. Anthropic, in which Amazon has invested billions, uses the chips to train and run its Claude models. OpenAI agreed in February to use 2 gigawatts of Trainium capacity as part of a deal in which Amazon is investing $50 billion in the company.

Brace said Amazon’s goal has always been wide use of the chips, calling TorchNeuron “an accelerant” along those lines.

Amazon’s chip business traces back to its 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, an Israeli chipmaker, for a reported $350 million. The Annapurna team went on to design Trainium as well as Amazon’s Graviton processors.

In his annual shareholder letter in April, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy wrote that the company’s chip business, including Trainium and Graviton, had an annual revenue run rate of more than $20 billion. He estimated that figure would be about $50 billion if the chips were sold to AWS and other customers by a standalone chip business.

“There’s so much demand for our chips that it’s quite possible we’ll sell racks of them to third parties in the future,” he wrote.

More than 30 companies and internal Amazon teams have been using TorchNeuron during the private beta. Deepgram, a San Francisco startup that makes speech AI, says its benchmarks showed Trainium processing about 60% more audio per dollar than its existing GPU setup. The company now runs Trainium in production, Brace said.

Inside Amazon, the Prime Video team used TorchNeuron to build Prime 360, an AI system that reconstructs NBA plays in 3D so viewers can watch replays from angles a traditional camera can’t capture. The feature, which runs on Trainium, will appear on select Prime Video broadcasts this NBA season.

To make sure TorchNeuron works with the huge variety of AI models that developers build, Amazon tests it every night against more than 100,000 models from Hugging Face, the popular online hub for open-source AI, Brace said.

Brace said the timing of the project reflects changes in PyTorch itself. The framework has matured, and its maintainers have been working to make it less dependent on any one kind of hardware.

Amazon has contributed to that effort, removing code that tied PyTorch to specific chips. Newer versions of PyTorch can detect which hardware they’re running on, he said, so in some cases developers don’t need to change their code at all.

#28. Asia’s Startup Funding At Near Record High In Q3, Driven By AI

Asia’s startup funding held up at the second-highest level in years in the third quarter, even as investment fell slightly from Q2 totals.

Overall, investors put $38.5 billion into reported seed- through growth-stage financings for countries in the region in Q3, per Crunchbase data. Of that, a majority went to AI-focused companies, echoing the trends we’ve seen globally.

Deal counts, meanwhile, were relatively flat. That indicates concentration of capital into favored startups remains pronounced but is not intensifying.

Around 55% of investment — an estimated $21 billion — went to AI-focused companies. Total funding is down substantially from the prior quarter, which was boosted by a $7.4 billion financing for China’s DeepSeek, but still the second-highest tally on record.

For Q3, a couple of extra-large rounds bolstered the AI investment tally. The largest went to Beijing-based foundational model company Moonshot AI, which secured $3.5 billion in July at a reported $35 billion valuation.

Kling AI, the AI spinout of China-based short video platform Kuaishou Technology, was the second-biggest fundraiser. The generative video startup raised around $3 billion in a July financing that included Baidu and Tencent.

China was the leading Asian destination for venture investment by a very wide margin.

Per Crunchbase data, roughly $27 billion — or 70% of all Asian startup funding in Q3 — went to China-based companies. India was a distant second, with $2.9 billion, followed by Singapore, with $2.5 billion.

For perspective, below we charted third-quarter startup funding tallies for the six countries with the largest totals.

Most capital went to late- and growth-stage funding rounds.

Per Crunchbase data, investment at this stage totaled around $20 billion in Q3. That’s down a bit from the prior quarter but nearly double year-ago levels and the second-strongest showing in four years.

Multiple jumbo rounds kept the total high. The largest was Moonshot AI’s aforementioned $3.5 billion Series F.

Several others raised financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. Shenzhen-based D-Robotics, a provider of robotics hardware and software, for instance, picked up $400 million in a September Series C. And Hong Kong-based Qupital, an e-commerce fintech platform, secured $300 million in Series C funding as it eyes an IPO.

Early-stage investment drifted lower in Q3 but remained at historically high levels.

Per Crunchbase data, financing for startups at the Series A and Series B stages totaled $13.6 billion for the just-ended quarter. That’s a decline of 28% from the prior quarter but up 65% from year-ago levels.

Reported seed funding hit its highest level in years, boosted by investor enthusiasm around AI.

In total, investors poured $4.9 billion into reported seed and angel deals across Asia, per Crunchbase data. That’s up around 22% from the prior quarter and more than double year-ago levels.

Overall, Q3 was a robust period for venture funding to China-based companies, with far smaller sums going to other Asian startup hubs. Funding to startups based in India and Singapore was down significantly quarter over quarter, while Israel’s investment totals declined slightly.

We’ll keep an eye out in the coming months to see if this divergence of fortunes persists.

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026.

#29. Prediction markets are now ‘bespoke insurance’ for businesses, and a Los Angeles restaurant group’s $60,000 hedge on Kalshi is the latest example

One Los Angeles restaurant group traded $60,000 on Kalshi to hedge against the Dodgers’ abbreviated playoff run, and it’s just one example of how prediction markets are transforming how companies, particularly small businesses, are calculating and responding to risks.

Kalshi told Fortune that the hospitality group, which was unnamed but operates 25 bars, including several near Dodger Stadium, made the trade on the platform if the city’s MLB team did not advance to the World Series. The Dodgers lost in the NLCS to the Milwaukee Brewers last week, and the position returned almost twice the original bet. The stake helped the business make up for the revenue it would have gotten had the Dodgers played more playoff games.

The use of prediction markets as a financial hedge is likely to grow, a sign that these platforms are not just alternatives to online sportsbooks or prop bet forums, but a financial and decision-making tool.

“You could imagine that there are other risks that businesses face that if there were a market available which functions similarly to the insurance market, then those businesses might want to participate in that kind of a market,” Joshua Mitts, a law professor at Columbia University who studies prediction markets and securities law, told Fortune.

The example of the restaurant group making a trade as a hedge for the Dodgers’ playoff performance “is functionally quite similar to a form of bespoke insurance,” he added.

Prediction markets are surging in popularity: Trading volume on the platforms doubled between May and July of this year, according to Pew Research Center data, topping $58 billion on Kalshi and nearly $22 billion on Polymarket, driven primarily by sports. Some of the appeal of prediction markets lies in their looser regulations and fewer restrictions, a result of the sites being classified as financial exchanges, rather than gambling platforms.

Small businesses in search of an unconventional risk management tool appear to be among the markets’ growing usership. In June, a New York City bar, The Jeffrey, promised patrons that the bar would cover every person’s tab up to $100 if the Knicks won an NBA finals game. The bar then placed a $5,000 bet on Kalshi that the then-underdog Knicks would win, and a $13,500 payout meant the bar not only paid off its patrons’ tabs, but also reaped a $8,500 profit.

Last month, an unnamed third-party insurance company placed five trades on Kalshi that could pay out $3 million should Louisiana State University win this season’s national championship, matching what the college’s football program would owe coach Lane Kiffin in bonuses. Earlier this summer, a Los Angeles ice cream shop reported making nearly half its monthly rent, up to $1,500, betting on when cold fronts would roll into town, hedging against slow demand.

Platforms have caught on to their evolving purposes. In August, independent financial economist Lauris Zminsky launched his app Blanket in partnership with Kalshi, an AI engine that can suggest specific yes-or-no markets on the platform that could offset a risk for a specific business.

“It’s a reasoning tool. It’s a discovery tool that funnels you towards Kalshi,” Zminsky told Fortune at the time. “What if you actually can take this up a notch and build a tool that is not only probably useful for the Kalshi team and their endeavors—to scale their S&P insurance hedging initiative—but a self-service tool where anybody can come in if they own a small business?”

Prediction markets lend themselves well to risk management because they are able to incorporate such a large sample, especially for sports-related financial hedging, Dartmouth College economics professor Eric Zitzewitz explained.

“There’s so much data, there’s so much repetition, there’s so many games all the time that they can be very well-calibrated,” he told Fortune. “You’ll pay fees when you do that—so you’ll be paying something for the insurance you get from these markets—but you should be getting fair underlying prices.”

This use case is most effective for yes-or-no outcomes, such as weather or a game, Mitts noted, as opposed to a hedge based on the knowledge of certain information, which could make a business owner a “systematic loser” if a competitor has better intel. They will also likely work best in major metropolitan areas, where there is a large market for trading, while still serving an idiosyncratic purpose, such as one mom-and-pop shop’s risks.

The mass sampling and real-time information gathering on prediction markets can extend their utility to informing business decisions, according to Zitzewitz. For an e-commerce retailer, for example, looking at prediction market users’ trades on future Amazon credit card receipts could present an accurate forecast of consumer spending in the month to come.

“It’s probably a better signal for you than GDP growth,” he said. “And it’s certainly fresher.”

While the lack of regulation may be drawing users to prediction markets, the platform’s Wild West qualities may also prevent them from being reliable insurance proxies, Mitts argued.

Insurers have extensive resources to prevent insurance fraud and catch fraudsters. But the inherently decentralized structure of prediction markets and evolving regulatory environment mean these platforms do not have the same resources or guardrails to prevent abuse.

“We don’t have a small number of companies who are state-regulated and who are doing things in very organized ways,” Mitts said. “This is a bit of a free-for-all.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#30. Germany's Merck KGaA is buying U.K. gene-silencing biotech for $1.3 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The all-cash deal adds divesiran, an experimental rare-disease drug ready for late-stage trials, to Merck KGaA's pipeline

Merck KGaA agreed to acquire Silence Therapeutics, a U.K. biotech focused on gene silencing, for about $1.3 billion in cash, according to The Wall Street Journal. Silence stock was up 4% on Monday before the market opened, according to Reuters.

Merck KGaA will give shareholders $20 in cash per Nasdaq-listed unit of Silence, which is 130% above where the stock last closed, according to Reuters. The deal is slated to wrap up during the first three months of 2027.

Silence detailed the proposed acquisition in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The company said the transaction still needs shareholder approval, sanction from the High Court of Justice of England and Wales, regulatory approvals and the satisfaction of other closing conditions. Silence said it will file a proxy statement with the SEC.

Merck KGaA is separate from U.S.-based Merck & Co.

The purchase adds divesiran, an experimental medicine for the rare disease polycythemia vera, to Merck KGaA's pipeline, according to The Wall Street Journal. The drug is poised to begin later-stage studies in patients, according to The Wall Street Journal. Silence specializes in short interfering RNA, a gene-silencing technology.

Merck KGaA Chief Executive Kai Beckmann said the company continues to "transform our pipeline toward areas of high specialization and unmet medical need," according to The Wall Street Journal. “The planned acquisition of Silence Therapeutics will strengthen our capabilities to serve patients with targeted specialty and rare diseases,” Beckmann said, according to Reuters.

Iain Ross, Silence's chairman and interim principal executive officer, said Merck KGaA is well equipped, with its size, funding and commercial know-how, to hasten the drug's final-stage development, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The deal follows another acquisition by the Darmstadt, Germany-based company. Merck KGaA agreed in June to acquire Bio-Techne, a Minneapolis-based life-sciences tools supplier, in a transaction that values Bio-Techne at an enterprise value of about $11.3 billion. Beckmann became CEO in May, and the Bio-Techne agreement was his first significant deal in the role.

#34. AI work assistant startup Town secures unicorn status after raising $108M just weeks after launching

Town.com Inc., an artificial intelligence agent startup laser focused on getting work done by collaborating with other AI agents, revealed today that it has raised $108 million in a new funding at a $1 billion valuation.

The Series B round was led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures, and saw participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures and First Round Capital, bringing Town’s total amount raised to date to $160 million, following a $55 million Series A that closed in June.

The startup, co-founded by former Plaid Inc. Chief Technology Officer Jean-Denis Greze, has already achieved a revenue run rate in the millions of dollars just weeks after it launched its first assistants, known as “townies,” in June, according to a blog post by Menlo partners Shawn Carolan, Amy Wu Martin and Sam Borja.

Menlo’s partners explained that Greze was previously in charge of engineering at the financial services firm Plaid, while his co-founder Tony Vincent has been involved in two prior startups: Aspen Designs Inc., which was later acquired by Google LLC, and Sold Inc., which was bought by Dropbox Inc. in 2013. It was after joining Dropbox that Vincent met Greze for the first time, beginning a friendship that ultimately led to the founding of Town.

Town targets businesses, providing each employee with a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company.

In their blog post, Carolan, Martin and Borja wrote that Menlo’s entire team began using Town in June and, within a very short time, their Townies became their hardest working team members. “A few weeks after we put the firm on Town, our Slack was full of people posting screenshots of their ‘moments of magic,’” the partners wrote. “Townies that had caught commitments people had forgotten, pulled the right context into replies before anyone went looking for it, and held together days that were about to fall apart. More than once, one surfaced a contact or a founder that someone had spent weeks trying to find.”

Where Townies really stand out is through the extent of the business context they understand. In a blog post announcing today’s round, Greze and Vincent explained that Townies don’t just know their users, but also familiarize themselves with each of their colleagues.

As a result, they know how their CEO writes, who has the strongest relationships with each buyer, what each sales lead cares about most, and all of the processes that go into running the business. Because each of these people also has a Townie, they can work together, leveraging their deep understanding of how the company runs.

A crucial benefit for businesses is that Town ensures they own this context, which was previously trapped in the heads of their employees and buried inside their email inboxes. That context had a habit of disappearing whenever someone was too busy, or left the company. Townies ensure that no longer happens, transforming that context into a compounding asset that enables everyone to work faster and smarter.

“We believe that this context is a critical asset and should belong to the company that built it,” Greze and Vincent wrote. “That’s why if you ever leave Town, you can take it with you and use it anywhere.”

Going forward, the co-founders said they’ll use the money from today’s round to build more integrations to expand the usefulness of their Townies as they strive to become a permanent fixture in employees’ daily lives. While their capabilities are impressive, Townies still need to demonstrate longevity to justify the startup’s new unicorn valuation.

The article outlines how paper choices affect color, texture, and longevity in reproductions of artwork.

RUSTON, La., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What factors matter most when selecting materials for high-quality art reproduction? HelloNation has published the piece and provides the answer in an article exploring how to choose paper for fine art prints, with guidance from Henry McCoy of Fine Line Supply Co.

The HelloNation article explains how to choose paper for fine art prints by balancing visual goals with technical considerations. It describes how different types of paper influence the way artwork reproduction prints are perceived, from sharp detail to soft, expressive finishes. Smooth surfaces tend to highlight fine lines and clarity, while more textured options can create depth and a tactile feel that complements certain styles.

The HelloNation article explains how to choose paper for fine art prints by balancing visual goals with technical considerations. It describes how different types of paper influence the way artwork reproduction prints are perceived, from sharp detail to soft, expressive finishes. Smooth surfaces tend to highlight fine lines and clarity, while more textured options can create depth and a tactile feel that complements certain styles.

The article emphasizes that paper weight plays a key role in presentation. Heavier paper weight often gives artwork reproduction prints a more substantial, professional feel, while lighter paper can make them appear more casual. According to the article, choosing the best paper for fine art prints involves evaluating how the weight contributes to both durability and the overall impression of the piece.

Paper finish is another important factor discussed in the article. A glossy paper finish can enhance vibrancy and contrast, making colors stand out more prominently. Matte paper finish, on the other hand, reduces glare and softens tones, which may be better suited for certain display environments. The article notes that understanding paper finish helps artists maintain control over how their work is viewed under different lighting conditions.

Paper texture is also highlighted as a defining factor in choosing paper for fine art prints. The article describes how subtle or pronounced paper texture can change the personality of artwork reproduction prints. For example, a watercolor-style paper texture can introduce a painterly quality, while smooth photo paper delivers a crisp, precise appearance. Matching paper texture to the original artwork helps preserve the intended emotional impact.

Longevity is a key concern addressed in the article, particularly for artists creating pieces meant to last. Archival-quality paper is recommended to prevent yellowing and deterioration over time. The article explains that selecting archival-quality paper ensures that artwork reproduction prints maintain their integrity for years, making it an essential factor in determining the best paper for fine art prints.

Color accuracy is another critical topic covered in the article. It explains that different papers can subtly shift hues, making test prints an important step in the process. By evaluating color accuracy across various paper types, artists and printers can make adjustments that preserve the original vision. The article notes that attention to color accuracy is essential when choosing paper for fine art prints.

The article also discusses the importance of testing samples before making a final decision. Variables such as paper weight, paper texture, paper finish, and lighting conditions can all influence the final result. Taking time to compare options helps artists ensure the selected paper enhances both the visual quality and longevity of their work.

In summary, the HelloNation article presents a thoughtful process for choosing paper for fine art prints that combines technical knowledge with artistic judgment. By considering paper weight, texture, finish, archival-quality paper, and color accuracy, artists can produce reproduction prints that reflect their original intent while maintaining durability.

#36. Microsoft unveils tools to monitor and corral rogue AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Oct 19, 2026 at 6:05 amOctober 19, 2026 at 6:40 am

Microsoft is coming out with new security tools that treat AI agents as potential insider threats, continuously assessing their risk and restricting their access when something changes.

The features, announced Monday, are part of Microsoft 365 E7, the company’s top-tier bundle of workplace software and AI tools, and its Project Perception security system.

They escalate the company’s competition with rivals such as Google, Amazon Web Services, CrowdStrike and Okta to become the system businesses use to control their AI agents.

Microsoft’s new features come amid a steady stream of news about AI agents doing things they weren’t supposed to do, including high-profile reports from Anthropic about test agents taking unauthorized actions on government websites, and from OpenAI about agents escaping test environments and stealing credentials.

The move builds on Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s Oct. 10 blog post arguing that the controls on AI models need to come from outside the models themselves.

“The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most,” Nadella wrote. “It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

Microsoft’s tools include a continuously updated risk assessment for each agent, based on signals such as what data it can reach and whether its actions are starting to depart from the task it was given. When the risk level rises, the system can take away the agent’s ability to make changes while still letting it read data, require a person to approve a high-stakes step, or shut the agent down.

In addition, the company is expanding its ability to find AI agents running on employees’ computers, increasing the number of agent types it can detect to 60, up from 25. The list includes popular tools such as Anthropic’s Claude Code, OpenAI’s Codex and GitHub Copilot.

Microsoft is also adding “Guardian Agents” to Project Perception, an AI security system it unveiled in July that uses AI agents to find and fix security problems. The new agents can investigate why another agent’s risk changed and recommend or take steps to contain it.

The company’s new features are in private preview, with broader availability planned for Microsoft’s Ignite conference, Nov. 17-19 in San Francisco.

The E7 licensing level, which launched in May, costs $99 per user per month. It also includes the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant, the company’s E5 suite of productivity and security tools, its Entra Suite identity tools and Agent 365, a service for managing AI agents.

#38. The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker

The fourth quarter of 2026 has started out on a down note for more than 1,600 tech workers in sectors ranging from AI to blockchain to social media.

Leading this week’s tally is streaming media giant Netflix. According to a report from CNBC, the Los Gatos, California-based company said it will trim about 1,000 workers from its product, tech, legal and human resources teams. The reduction in force will affect global employees, so it is not clear how many U.S. workers will be affected.

Amazon also rejoins the tracker this week with a report that it has laid off a number of global workers in its customer service, marketplace and engineering divisions. While the total number of employees affected was not disclosed, Business Insider reported the count is fewer than 1,000.

And in a possible total shutdown, Redwood City, California-based chatbot platform startup Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in an effort to “facilitate a value-maximizing sale of all or substantially all of its assets.” A company statement about the proceedings says the platform will continue to operate, but adds: “To the extent the Sale Process does not result in a purchase that provides for a continuation of the Character.ai platform, the platform will be wound down.”

The following companies were added to the tracker this week:

Layoffs during the weeks ended Oct. 15, 2026: At least 1,635 U.S. tech sector employees were laid off or scheduled for layoffs, per a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2025: Around 127,000 workers were let go from U.S.-based tech companies according to our tally.

In 2024: At least 95,667 workers at U.S.-based tech companies lost their jobs in 2024, according to a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2023: More than 191,000 workers in U.S.-based tech companies (or tech companies with a large U.S. workforce) were laid off in mass job cuts.

In 2022: More than 93,000 jobs were slashed from public and private tech companies in the U.S.

This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs.

Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs.

We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers.

If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

A layoff can be either a permanent termination of someone’s employment — usually for cost-saving reasons — or a temporary one because there’s not enough work to justify a full workforce. Tech company layoffs generally fall into the permanent category.

A mass layoff is when a significant number of a company’s employees are cut in a short period of time, often as a result of economic conditions.

Tech layoffs started to surge in 2022 and continued in 2023 and 2024. Companies have given various reasons for conducting layoffs.

Some companies — especially those in the e-commerce sector — nearly doubled their employee headcount to meet consumer demand during the COVID-19 pandemic’s stay-at-home mandates, and later found that they were overstaffed as daily life returned to normal.

Large tech employers such as Salesforce and Google parent Alphabet noted that their post-pandemic layoffs followed several years of rapid hiring fueled by fast growth — between 2019 and 2022, some companies nearly doubled their employee headcount. Some large tech companies also cited slowing sales and fears of a recession as reasons for downsizing.

Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, also cut jobs as a way to cut costs and preserve their cash reserves, as venture funding fell significantly after the peak in 2021. Some startups that ran out of cash and couldn’t raise new funding found themselves filing for bankruptcy or shutting down.

Intel Corp. laid off the largest number of people among U.S. tech employers in 2024, by our count. The semiconductor giant laid off more than 15,000 employees last year.

It was followed closely by electric-car maker Tesla, which cut more than 14,000 roles, and networking company Cisco, with more than 10,000 total roles cut.

In 2023, Amazon layoffs led the numbers with 16,000 roles cut. Layoffs at Alphabet, the parent company of Google, totaled about 12,000, and Microsoft’s layoffs totaled about 10,000 workers in 2023, as did Facebook parent Meta’s layoffs.

Many venture-backed tech startups have also done layoffs as venture capital investment has fallen sharply since the peak in 2021, and falling startup valuations factor into their decisions to conduct layoffs.

Yes, more layoffs are likely coming. While there are signs that the volume of layoffs is tapering, experts we talked to expect job cuts in the tech sector to continue for the foreseeable future as large tech companies and startups continue to battle economic headwinds.

Seed and early-stage startups in particular may continue to conduct layoffs in an attempt to extend their cash runways in a difficult venture funding environment.

Tech layoffs noticeably increased at the start of 2022, ramped up in 2023, waned somewhat in 2024 and have continued in 2025.

Signs that may indicate a company is more likely to conduct layoffs include:

Layoffs declined in 2024 compared to the previous year, but are expected to continue into 2025, although likely not at the level seen in 2023. Startups that need to preserve cash to extend their runways are more likely to conduct layoffs.

Tech layoffs will likely slow when venture capital funding increases and the startup economy stabilizes, as well as when market conditions improve and more startups gain liquidity via IPOs.

Startups that raised capital during the venture funding heyday at inflated valuations in 2021 are more likely to need to conduct layoffs if they’re not able to sustain their previous valuations or growth projections.

Tech layoffs started surging in the 2022 market correction, with an estimated 93,000 U.S. tech workers laid off that year. That figure more than doubled in 2023, with around 200,000 U.S. tech employees laid off, according to our Tech Layoffs Tracker. Layoffs abated again in 2024, with around 95,000 reported tech layoffs.

Keep in mind, many companies don’t report detailed layoffs figures, and some companies continue hiring after cuts for positions deemed more beneficial to the business.

No, according to experts in the sector, who say a sale is unlikely to solve a tech company’s cash-flow issues.

This is especially true as fewer startup M&A deals are happening in the current downturn.

Tech layoffs have hit across departments at many companies.

Many layoffs from the large tech giants were software engineers. Startups tend to be more likely to retain engineers in favor of doing layoffs in their talent and recruiting, marketing and other departments.

Google cut roles in its sales, recruiting, product and engineering teams. Amazon layoffs included jobs in its AWS cloud unit, at its social video platform Twitch, and in its advertising department. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s recruiting department would be the first to see job cuts.

#39. Gen Z is chasing the American Dream in South Carolina, Missouri, and Tennessee—as California loses thousands of young adults and billionaires

As ultrawealthy tech founders like Larry Page, Peter Thiel, and Travis Kalanick flee California amid opposition to its proposed billionaire tax, a new report indicates Gen Z is also leaving the Golden State in droves.

California recorded the nation’s largest net loss of Gen Z adults in 2024, shedding roughly 58,109 young adults, according to a new LendingTree report analyzing the latest available Census data.

Texas was the biggest destination for young Californians on the move. Other states also recorded sizable net gains in nationwide Gen Z migration, including South Carolina, which gained 22,843; Missouri, with 14,063; and Tennessee, with 13,537. Several of these states offer a lower cost of living than many other parts of the country, potentially giving young adults more room to stretch their paychecks.

Washington, D.C., was a notable outlier. The nation’s capital recorded a net gain of 13,905 Gen Z adults despite ranking among the more expensive places to live. But the region’s concentration of high-paying jobs may help offset its steep housing and living costs for some young professionals.

Moving across state lines for school, a new job, or a change of scenery is nothing new for young adults. Still, the scale of the migration is striking: Nearly 11 million Gen Z adults—roughly one in four—moved in 2024.

“When you’re young, and you’re just getting started, you don’t have to worry about moving your kids to a new school or uprooting your entire family,” report author Matt Schulz told Realtor.com. “You can just kind of get up and go, and I think we’re certainly seeing some of that in this.”

Persistent inflation, stubborn housing costs, and higher energy prices continue to strain household budgets across the country. For young people, those pressures come on top of an unfriendly job market for entry-level workers and the restart of student loan payments, making it even harder to get their lives off the ground.

Some 42% of Gen Z are living paycheck to paycheck, according to a recent Bank of America study. Nearly half reported that the high cost of living is a top barrier to financial success.

Yet even as high living costs push some young adults to seek opportunities elsewhere, California in particular continues to attract some newcomers.

According to U-Haul’s 2026 Midyear Migration Trends report, which tracks the net gain of its one-way truck and trailer rentals, California ranked in the top three destinations for both Gen Z and millennial movers from July 2025 through June 2026. The San Francisco Bay Area specifically ranked among the generations’ top metro destinations.

The state’s role at the center of the AI boom may help explain its appeal. California is home to major AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, along with 56 Fortune 500 companies, ranging from Apple to Williams-Sonoma. For young workers hoping to break into technology or other high-paying industries, those opportunities may help offset the state’s steep living costs.

Still, California’s appeal to some newcomers hasn’t translated into stronger overall migration numbers. The state has ranked last in U-Haul’s annual growth rankings for six consecutive years, highlighting the challenge of attracting new residents while others continue to leave.

For Gen Z trying to decide where to put down roots, Scott Galloway, a podcaster and NYU Stern School of Business professor, has argued that big cities can offer a career advantage.

He said that two-thirds of global economic growth over the next 30 years will come from the world’s 20 “supercities” such as London, Milan, New York, and San Francisco, where wealth, talent, and innovation are concentrated.

“When you’re in a city, you’re playing against Serena Williams every day,” Galloway said on The Diary of a CEO podcast in 2024. “Everyone is smart, everyone is well-dressed, everyone is working hard, everyone is taking chances. And you are surrounded by people who are very successful, and you are gonna bump off professional and personal [opportunities] every day.”

But Barbara Corcoran, the self-made millionaire real estate mogul and Shark Tank investor, offers a different approach to building wealth: Look for affordable property in overlooked markets.

“Go anywhere that has a poor school district where prices are really low,” Corcoran said on the Elvis Duran radio show in 2023.

The South, she added, can be a particularly promising place to find deals—but not Florida, where housing costs in some markets have surged, and wealthy newcomers have helped fuel demand.

“Go anywhere in the South other than the hotspot,” Corcoran said. “There’s always a cheap house to buy, always. But not Florida, forget about Florida.”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

Pennsylvania kicked one fracking company out of the area for more than a decade. It just couldn't keep it out for good. It came back in late 2023, and by the next year, Texas-based company Coterra was running lines beneath dozens of homes in Dimock, Pa., including the one where local resident Victoria Switzer, a former schoolteacher, paints, according to Mother Jones. The noise from the construction and truck traffic have kept her up at night. "They are cutting up the valley like Swiss cheese," she said. "We came here to enjoy nature, and this has just torn our lives apart."

The gas-rich rock under Dimock, called the Marcellus shale, also runs under New York towns just over the state line, such as Dryden. New York spent years deciding whether to let fracking companies drill it the way Coterra drilled Dimock, but in December 2014 it said no. The state's ban has been in place since June 2015.

Now New York is freezing the construction of big data centers, and so is Texas. On July 14, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order telling the Department of Environmental Conservation to freeze state permit applications for data centers that use 50 megawatts or more. "As data center development threatens to hike up utility bills, deplete our natural resources, and create uncertainty for New Yorkers, it's my responsibility to take action and lead," Hochul said. In September, the Texas Tribune reported, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott $ABT ordered his state's environmental agency to stop issuing permits to data centers until the state finishes auditing them.

New York spent years deciding on fracking, and its ban has held ever since. Hochul and Abbott moved much faster on data centers, freezing permit applications while the studies they ordered were still underway. There is no defined end date, and the moratorium could be challenged in court.

While New York kept its shale closed, Pennsylvania drilled the same rock and produced more than twice as much gas in 2023 as it had in 2013, the year before New York announced its ban. Gas passed coal as Pennsylvania's biggest source of electricity in 2016, and by 2023 Pennsylvania was sending more electricity to other states than any other state did. New York's ban decided which side of the border the gas came out of, not whether anyone drilled for it.

Fracking brought money to Pennsylvania's side of the border. After New York's ban took effect, the economies of the seven Pennsylvania counties along the line grew larger than those of the New York counties across from them, according to a report from conservative think tank Heritage Foundation. Drilling for natural gas made all of the difference.

But the town of Dimock bore the cost. State regulators discovered that the fracking company had contaminated 19 of Dimock's private water wells, and a 2016 federal report confirmed harmful levels of lead and arsenic in the water of 27 homes, with enough methane in 17 of them to risk an explosion. When the case reached court in 2022, the company had been charged with eight felonies and ended up pleading no contest to one misdemeanor. It agreed to pay for a $16 million water line, and that same day, Pennsylvania let it drill near Dimock again. Two years later, the drilling was back and work on the water line hadn't started. Ray Kemble, Switzer's neighbor of 30 years, was moving away. "The water is still not fixed," he said.

Towns on the New York side of the same rock banned fracking too, and the studies they did first helped their bans survive in court. Hochul's data center freeze has no finished study behind it.

The gas companies were already there when the towns acted. They had been buying leases in Dryden and Middlefield for years. Both towns studied the question before voting, and Middlefield paid for a study of its own. When the companies sued, New York's highest court upheld both bans in 2014. "The Towns both studied the issue and acted within their home rule powers in determining that gas drilling would permanently alter and adversely affect the deliberately-cultivated, small-town character of their communities," Judge Victoria Graffeo wrote for the majority.

The state did the same kind of work before its own ban. Regulators spent seven years on their review and took in 260,000 public comments, and the state's health department finished a review of its own in December 2014. "I asked myself, 'Would I let my family live in a community with fracking?' The answer is no," Dr. Howard Zucker, then New York's acting health commissioner, said.

Data center developers are waiting the same way. They've rushed to get projects in line to plug into New York's power grid, and most of those requests came in just last year. If one of them sues over Hochul's freeze, the state won't have a finished study to point to, the way Dryden and Middlefield did.

That study is coming, but only after New York stopped issuing permits. Hochul's order hands the question to the state's Department of Public Service, which has to hold public hearings and take comments before it reports back, much as regulators did before the fracking ban. The permits stay on hold until the department finishes, and it's not clear when that will happen. Hochul's office has said the pause will last up to a year.

The longer the wait, the weaker New York's position if a developer sues. Vorys, the law firm that warned in April about moratoriums like these, argued that property owners have a stronger claim to compensation when a building pause keeps getting extended or starts to work like a permanent ban. Hochul's open-ended order invites that argument.

Texas's freeze is just as open-ended, and it comes from a governor who wanted data centers less than a year ago. Last November, Abbott said he wanted Texas to be an "epicenter of AI development," but by September, he said data centers "must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete" all the necessary audits. Until they do, permits are off the table.

New York studied fracking for seven years before it made its ban official. Hochul and Abbott halted data centers first and ordered the studies and audits afterward. Developers in New York and Texas who already have projects waiting are left holding plans that neither state has said yes or no to, and the families who live near those sites don't know when either state will decide.

#44. Amazon introduces toolkit for running PyTorch workloads on AWS Trainium chips

Amazon.com Inc. today introduced TorchNeuron, an open-source toolkit that enables developers to run PyTorch workloads on its AWS Trainium chips.

PyTorch is the industry’s most popular artificial intelligence development framework. Until now, running AI projects powered by the tool on Trainium-based Amazon Web Services instances involved a significant amount of manual work. That increased development costs and thereby created an entry barrier for users.

TorchNeuron makes it possible to run PyTorch projects on Trainium chips without extensive code changes. According to Amazon, developers only have to configure a setting that informs workloads which chip they should use. TorchNeuron supports Trainium2 and Trainium3, the two latest additions to the accelerator series. The chips support both training and inference use cases.

Trainium3, the more capable of the two processors, features eight computing cores. Each core comprises four modules that are each optimized for a different subset of the calculations with which AI models process data. The chip keeps model data in a 154-gigabyte pool of onboard memory.

AWS runs Trainium3 in custom servers that can each accommodate up to 144 accelerators. According to the Amazon unit, a single system can perform up to 362 quadrillion calculations per second when processing data in the MXFP8 format. The format is widely used by AI models.

The Trainium series features a custom programming language called NKI. The syntax, which comes with its own compiler, enables developers to make low-level optimizations to their AI models. Such customizations reduce AI models’ hardware usage and boost their speed.

TorchNeuron includes a set of pre-packaged NKI operators, software building blocks that customers can use to develop AI models. Some operators ease the task of implementing a mixture of experts architecture, while others are designed to reduce neural networks’ memory usage. They also speed up related tasks such as quantization.

TorchNeuron supports not only PyTorch but also the open-source tools that software teams often use alongside the framework. The list of supported tools includes TorchTitan, a popular AI training engine. It automates some of the work involved in distributing a training run across accelerators.

TorchTitan splits workloads across chips using a method called fully sharded data parallelism. It splits not only the model being trained but also optimizer states and gradients. An optimizer is a program that hones a model’s capabilities, while gradients are files that play an important role in that process. According to Amazon, TorchNeuron includes features that enable developers to further optimize the training workflow using Trainium chips.

The toolkit has already been adopted by several AWS customers. Cartesia AI Inc., a venture-backed voice agent startup, is using TorchNeuron to run inference workloads on Trainium chips. The Lieber Institute for Brain Development is exploring ways of optimizing its AI-powered medical research workflows.

Amazon plans to open-source TorchNeuron Tuesday, the first day of a two-day PyTorch Conference in San Jose.

#45. Tumor Ablation Market Set to Surge to US$ 1.8 Billion by 2031, Growing at 11.6% CAGR: Wissen Research

SHERIDAN, Wyo., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The global tumor ablation market is valued at USD 1.04 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 1.8 billion by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 11.6% over the forecast period (2026–2031), according to a new study by Wissen Research.

Tumor ablation destroys targeted tumor tissue with heat, cold, or other forms of energy while trying to spare the healthy tissue around it. In percutaneous procedures, a physician threads a probe through the skin and into the tumor under imaging guidance, which lowers the risks that come with standard surgery. For patients who are not candidates for surgery, or for whom preserving organ function matters, it is an increasingly important option.

The demand starts with patient numbers. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) counted about 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide in 2022, and expects the figure to rise significantly by 2050. A growing population of patients with solid tumors is driving demand for localized treatments that can work alongside surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy or, in specific cases, replace them.

Download Free Sample PDF — Explore Key Market Trends, CAGR & Patent Highlights: https://www.wissenresearch.com/request-a-sample/?report=tumor-ablation-market

The Probe Is Only Part of the System: Imaging and Planning Software Now Sit Beside the Energy Source

Tumor ablation is moving away from standalone energy delivery devices toward integrated systems. Modern platforms increasingly combine the energy source with CT, ultrasound, MRI, navigation, temperature sensors, and treatment planning software, so the physician can place the probe precisely, watch the treated zone, and plan how far the treatment should extend. CT and ultrasound help position the probe, MRI gives detailed images of the treated area, and software lets the physician define tumor borders before treatment begins. The report describes an industry that is becoming more technology- and software-oriented, with competition shifting toward more efficient image-guided tumor ablation, tighter control of the procedure, and larger, more predictable ablation zones.

Precision matters because physics can work against the treatment. The National Cancer Institute (NCI) notes that radiofrequency ablation, microwave ablation, and cryoablation are used for localized liver cancer, but tumor size and location can limit how well thermal ablation works. When a tumor sits close to a large blood vessel, flowing blood can carry heat away from the treatment area, a heat-sink effect that reduces effectiveness.

Beyond Heat: Freezing, Focused Ultrasound, and Electrical Pulses Widen the Toolkit

Radiofrequency ablation remained a leading technology in 2025 on the strength of its long clinical track record and wide availability, and the NCI lists it among the local treatment options for liver malignancies. Microwave ablation is gradually gaining ground because it can offer higher temperatures, larger ablation areas, and simultaneous treatment through multiple devices, while cryoablation, which destroys tissue by freezing and thawing, is getting stronger in kidney and prostate cancer.

Other approaches are broadening what can be treated. Irreversible electroporation (IRE) uses short electrical pulses instead of heat to disrupt cells, and is being explored where conventional heating is difficult, such as near sensitive structures. High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) delivers energy through concentrated ultrasound signals. Both remain more specialized than the established thermal methods, and the report notes that the state of the technology and the available evidence vary from one application to another, even as ablation spreads beyond the liver and kidney to other solid tumors.

What's Fueling Growth in the Tumor Ablation Market

Challenges Facing the Tumor Ablation Market

The central challenge is destroying the whole tumor while protecting what is next to it. Results depend on the tumor's size, shape, location, and tissue properties, and on how close it sits to vital structures. Tumors that are not fully destroyed can survive at the treatment margin, raising the risk of local recurrence and the need for repeat procedures or additional treatment. Tumors near bile ducts, airways, nerves, and intestines can force physicians to reduce the energy they deliver, and inconsistent probe placement can leave tumor tissue behind. That is why imaging, probe positioning, treatment planning, and monitoring have to be clear and dependable.

Adoption has its own hurdles. Using advanced imaging technology involves regulatory requirements, the availability of clinical evidence, and the level of physician training, and technologies such as irreversible electroporation, HIFU, and laser ablation are still developing.

Recent Strategic Developments in the Tumor Ablation Market

In August 2026, IceCure Medical Ltd. of Israel entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with Scovas Medical for its ProSense cryoablation systems in the Netherlands. The agreement expanded ProSense commercialization for breast cancer and interventional oncology, while the Netherlands-based THERMAC trial advanced to Phase III, supporting further clinical adoption of cryoablation.

In May 2026, AngioDynamics, Inc. of the United States announced that Palmetto GBA had issued a final Medicare coverage determination for irreversible electroporation using the NanoKnife System for selected prostate cancer cases and metastatic colorectal cancer to the liver. The coverage took effect July 5, 2026, supporting broader reimbursement and patient access to non-thermal tumor ablation.

One development opens a new market for cryoablation, and the other makes a non-thermal technique easier for patients to access.

Key Insights from Tumor Ablation Market Analysis

(Israel) as the top five players, with established positions across radiofrequency ablation, microwave ablation, cryoablation, and other interventional oncology technologies. Competition turns on energy-delivery performance, treatment precision, probe design, the predictability of the ablation zone, clinical evidence, regulatory approvals, imaging integration, procedural efficiency, and physician adoption.

(US), Siemens Healthineers AG (Germany), and Olympus Corporation (Japan). Regional Analysis and Growth Opportunities

North America leads the tumor ablation market, supported by advanced healthcare infrastructure, growing interventional radiology capacity, high spending on cancer treatment, wide adoption of minimally invasive procedures, and leading manufacturers. The U.S. has a well-structured regulatory framework for medical devices and interventional oncology technologies, in which regulators approve and clear many ablation systems for specific medical applications. The country is also a key center for clinical studies and procedure development in microwave ablation, cryoablation, radiofrequency ablation, HIFU, and electroporation.

Asia Pacific is the fastest-growing region, reflecting a growing number of cancer patients and rapid development of healthcare systems.
