#48. How To Build Your Team With Autonomous Humans, Not Just Autonomous Systems

How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity?

As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days.

It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company.

As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them.

“AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success.

The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up.

The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next.

Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative?

Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either.

In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly.

Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged.

Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold.

As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with.

The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing.

The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter.

Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment.

Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room.

#49. France is rioting over surging inflation, skyrocketing national debt, and crumbling schools. America is its sleeping twin

The fire that badly damaged Limoges’ 19th-century city hall was set on purpose, the local prefect said. By Sunday it was under control, and France was counting the damage: more than 2,400 arrests on Saturday alone, according to authorities, nearly 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, and hundreds of businesses looted in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other cities. Looting and fires continued Sunday night, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered localized curfews Monday. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police “lost control” and offered to resign. President Emmanuel Macron refused.

America has worse inflation, as Fortune’s Jason Ma reported Monday. U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, compared with France’s 3.4% on the EU-harmonized measure. What offsets it is growth. U.S. GDP rose 2.2% in the second quarter; unemployment is 4.2%; and wages are growing about 3.0% a year, below inflation. Meanwhile, France expects its economy to grow just 0.5% this year, and youth unemployment there is about 20%.

Set aside growth, and the two countries have a lot in common. And Americans aren’t thrilled about where the growth is coming from. Tech investment accounts for about a third of U.S. GDP growth, according to ING. Yet 39% of Americans now say AI does more harm than good, up from 31% a year ago, and 79% expect AI to cut U.S. jobs over the next decade, according to a Bentley-Gallup survey conducted in May. Among adults under 30, the harm figure is 47%. A Pew survey in June found 52% of Americans more concerned than excited about AI.

Start with the debt. French public debt sits at a record 119% of GDP, while U.S. debt held by the public reached 100.2% of GDP at the end of March. Lecornu’s budget, which would cut France’s deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%, faces its first critical vote in the National Assembly on Tuesday. Washington ran a $1.992 trillion deficit in fiscal 2026, about 6.2% of GDP based on CBO’s projections. Needless to say, that’s wider than the 5.4% deficit France is rioting over.

Bond traders are treating the two countries alike. Bank of America economists Claudio Irigoyen and Antonio Gabriel recently found that the French and U.S. 10-year yields have been moving on nearly the same track, and they say the cause is the same. “When interest rates are low, governments have incentives to run bigger deficits financed with cheap debt,” they wrote in a BofA Global Research report. “However, if that ‘cheap’ debt goes to finance a structural increase of the fiscal deficit, when interest rates increase it is politically difficult to implement the necessary fiscal consolidation to put the house in order.”

The riots are what “politically difficult” looks like. In the U.S., the warning has come through the bond market. On Sept. 8, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an audience at Southern Methodist University, “I am the house now.” The bond market disagreed. Over the next three weeks, the 30-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.69%, levels not seen since 2002, Johns Hopkins economist Steve Hanke and former Comptroller General David Walker wrote in Fortune.

France’s protests began in classrooms. In mid-September, high school students in the Paris suburbs walked out over missing teachers, overcrowded rooms, and buildings that can’t handle the heat. They blamed years of underinvestment. Teachers and unions joined, then people angry about fuel prices and the cost of living.

American schools show the same strain, and on some measures, it’s worse. Lost class time: In France, 9.8% of teaching hours in public middle and high schools went undelivered in 2024–25, mostly because absent teachers weren’t replaced, according to the Education Ministry’s statistics office. In the U.S., the GAO found that 19% of school districts canceled classes that year because of building problems, costing about 2 million students roughly 3.5 million days of learning.

Nearly half of districts had chronic facility problems that disrupted learning. Staffing: At the start of this school year, 53% of French middle and high schools were missing at least one teacher, according to a survey of 1,033 schools by SNES-FSU, France’s largest secondary teachers union. At the start of 2024–25, 74% of U.S. public schools had trouble filling at least one vacancy with a fully certified teacher, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. Qualifications: 11.1% of French secondary teachers aren’t fully qualified, according to the OECD. In the U.S., the Learning Policy Institute estimates 387,843 teachers aren’t fully certified for their assignments and calls that an undercount.

President Trump sees another cause. “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out-of-control mass migration,” he posted on Truth Social on Oct. 6, adding that it “isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” without addressing his own country’s fiscal similarities. Student demands have not mentioned immigration or religion. UBS Global Wealth Management chief economist Paul Donovan called the weekend’s violence “a different form of scapegoat economics” in a note to clients Monday.

The cushion holds as long as growth does. Market veteran Ed Yardeni argued last month that the U.S. economy is “less rate sensitive than it has ever been,” supported by wealthy retirees, large deficits, and “an extraordinary AI investment boom.”

Hanke and Walker end their column with a quote from the late MIT economist Rüdiger Dornbusch: “Crises take longer to arrive than you can possibly imagine, but when they do come, they happen faster than you can possibly imagine.”

#50. What science really says about 10 popular supplements

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A clear-eyed look at 10 popular supplements and what clinical evidence actually says about their benefits and limits

The distance between what a supplement label promises and what clinical trials have actually shown is wide, and it varies from product to product. Vitamin D for someone with a confirmed deficiency rests on decades of research into calcium absorption and bone density. A proprietary herbal blend sold for immunity or detox may rest on a few small studies and a persuasive label.

Part of what keeps that gap open is regulation. The Food and Drug Administration does not review dietary supplements for safety or effectiveness before they reach shelves, the way it reviews prescription drugs. Manufacturers vouch for their own products, and regulators typically act after a problem surfaces. That leaves the sorting to shoppers, in an aisle where a product backed by large randomized trials sits beside one backed mainly by a marketing budget.

This list covers 10 of the most popular supplements sold in the U.S. and what the evidence base behind each one looks like once the packaging language is set aside. Some have deep trial records: creatine for strength training, omega-3s for lowering triglycerides, melatonin for resetting a disrupted body clock. Others, including turmeric extracts and most multivitamins taken by healthy adults, have far less human data than their sales volume implies. Several sit in between, useful for a narrow group and unremarkable for everyone else.

It is not a buying guide. No brands are named, and no dosages are recommended, because those choices depend on blood work, diet, age and medical history. Anyone taking prescription medication should raise supplements with a doctor or pharmacist first. Interactions with blood thinners, antidepressants and thyroid drugs are documented and can be serious. A supplement that is harmless on its own is not automatically harmless alongside a prescription.

The useful question is rarely whether a supplement does anything at all. It is whether it does anything for a person who is not already deficient. The second question is whether the claim rests on large randomized trials or on a handful of small studies that no one has repeated.

Vitamin D has strong evidence behind one specific use: correcting a confirmed deficiency. In people with low blood levels, supplementation improves calcium absorption, supports bone mineral density and lowers fracture risk. For everyone else, the case thins out.

Deficiency is common. Skin makes vitamin D when ultraviolet light hits it, and that production falls with higher latitude, winter, darker skin pigmentation, age and an indoor routine. Conditions that impair fat absorption, including celiac disease and Crohn's disease, reduce how much of the vitamin the body takes up from food and capsules. Food supplies relatively little on its own — oily fish such as salmon and sardines, egg yolks, and fortified milk or cereal are the main dietary sources. A blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the only dependable way to establish where someone stands.

Broader claims are where the research stops cooperating. The VITAL trial, published in The New England Journal of Medicine, randomized more than 25,000 generally healthy U.S. adults to vitamin D or placebo and found no significant reduction in invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events. An ancillary analysis of the same trial found no reduction in fractures among participants, most of whom had adequate vitamin D levels at enrollment. Trial results for respiratory infection and mood have been inconsistent.

The Institute of Medicine set the recommended dietary allowance at 600 international units a day for adults up to age 70 and 800 IU after that. More does not translate into more benefit. Vitamin D is fat-soluble, so a surplus is stored in body tissue rather than cleared in urine the way extra water-soluble vitamins are. Sustained megadoses can push blood calcium high enough to damage the kidneys.

The practical case is narrow. If bloodwork shows a deficiency, or someone belongs to a group that reliably runs low, supplementation is well supported. For a healthy adult with normal levels and regular sun exposure, the evidence does not back vitamin D as a general-purpose health measure.

Fish oil lowers triglycerides. The effect is consistent enough that prescription-strength omega-3 formulations are approved in the U.S. for adults with severely elevated triglyceride levels. What the evidence does not support is the broader promise on most over-the-counter bottles — that a daily capsule protects an otherwise healthy adult from heart attack or stroke.

Two of the largest assessments point the same way. The VITAL trial, which followed more than 25,000 U.S. adults, found that marine omega-3 supplementation did not significantly reduce major cardiovascular events. A 2018 Cochrane review pooling dozens of randomized trials reached a similar conclusion, reporting little or no effect on cardiovascular death or events from increasing long-chain omega-3 intake.

One exception is often misread. REDUCE-IT tested icosapent ethyl, a purified prescription form of eicosapentaenoic acid, in high-risk patients already on statins whose triglycerides remained elevated, and found fewer cardiovascular events in the treatment group. That was a specific drug at a high dose, given to a narrow patient population under medical supervision. A drugstore softgel is a different product, and the trial result does not carry over to it.

Other claims remain unresolved. Trials in rheumatoid arthritis have shown modest improvement in joint tenderness and lower use of anti-inflammatory drugs. Research on depression and cognitive decline has produced inconsistent results, with no settled conclusion across trials. Oily fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel deliver the same fatty acids alongside protein and other nutrients, which is why dietary guidance generally points to fish before capsules.

Side effects are usually minor — fishy aftertaste, reflux, loose stools — and taking capsules with food or freezing them first can reduce the burping. Higher doses raise real interaction concerns for anyone on warfarin or another anticoagulant, because bleeding risk can compound. Several large omega-3 trials, REDUCE-IT among them, also recorded more atrial fibrillation in participants taking omega-3 than in those on placebo, which matters most for people already prone to arrhythmia.

Probiotic benefits attach to specific bacterial strains and specific conditions, not to the category as a whole. A label that reads only "probiotic" tells a shopper almost nothing about whether the capsule contains the organism actually studied for the problem they want to fix.

The firmest evidence sits with antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Randomized trials of Saccharomyces boulardii — a yeast rather than a bacterium — and of several Lactobacillus strains have found lower rates of diarrhea among patients taking a course of antibiotics. Evidence is weaker but still reasonable for certain strains used against irritable bowel syndrome symptoms such as bloating and abdominal pain. Response varies from person to person, and a strain that settles one patient's symptoms may do nothing for the next.

Marketing that stretches into general immunity and mood regulation through the gut-brain axis rests on much thinner ground. That research is active and biologically plausible, but it has not yet produced the large, replicated human trials that would support the language printed on many boxes.

Product quality is a separate variable. Supplements differ in colony-forming unit counts and in whether the organisms survive stomach acid to reach the intestine. They also differ in whether the bacteria remain viable at the expiration date rather than only on the day of manufacture. Some need refrigeration. Few companies publish data confirming what a capsule delivers at the point of use.

For healthy adults with no digestive diagnosis, fermented foods such as yogurt with live cultures, kefir, kimchi and sauerkraut supply live organisms at lower cost and with fewer unknowns. Anyone treating a specific condition should ask a doctor or pharmacist which strain carries trial data for that problem. Then check that the product names that exact strain, not just the genus.

Probiotics are also not uniformly harmless. People who are severely immunocompromised, critically ill or living with a central venous catheter face a real risk of infection from swallowing live organisms, and should not take them without medical supervision.

Magnesium delivers the most reliable results in two situations: correcting a documented deficiency and reducing migraine frequency. Outside those uses, the support thins quickly. The mineral acts as a cofactor in more than 300 enzyme systems that govern nerve signaling, muscle contraction and blood pressure regulation, which is why depleted levels produce symptoms that replacement genuinely resolves.

Low magnesium shows up most often in older adults, people with gastrointestinal conditions that impair absorption such as Crohn's disease or celiac disease, people with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, and people with chronic alcohol use. Restoring normal levels in those groups can quiet muscle cramps, eyelid twitching and unexplained fatigue.

Migraine prevention is the strongest claim that does not depend on deficiency. The American Academy of Neurology and the American Headache Society rated magnesium as probably effective for preventing migraine attacks, one of the few formal guideline endorsements any supplement has received for a defined medical condition. Trial evidence also points to some relief of premenstrual symptoms, though the measured effects are small.

Sleep is where the marketing has outpaced the research. A handful of small trials in older adults with insomnia reported better sleep quality, but studies in healthy, well-fed people are sparse. The mineral's standing as a bedtime aid rests largely on its role in nerve signaling rather than on large randomized trials.

The form on the label matters. Magnesium citrate and magnesium glycinate are absorbed more readily than magnesium oxide, the cheapest version and the one most likely to loosen stools, because unabsorbed oxide pulls water into the intestine.

Food covers the requirement for most people. Pumpkin seeds, almonds, spinach, black beans and whole grains all supply meaningful amounts, and a varied diet usually makes pills unnecessary. Excess from supplements causes diarrhea and abdominal cramping, and it carries real risk for anyone with reduced kidney function, since impaired kidneys cannot clear the surplus. A blood test ordered by a physician settles whether a deficiency exists.

Creatine monohydrate has the deepest evidence base of any sports supplement sold today. Decades of randomized trials show it raises muscular strength, power output and lean body mass when combined with resistance training, and the effect shows up across age groups and training backgrounds.

The mechanism is better understood than for most supplements. Creatine increases phosphocreatine stores inside muscle cells, and phosphocreatine helps regenerate adenosine triphosphate, the molecule cells spend for energy. That matters most during short, maximal efforts — a heavy set of squats, a 10-second sprint, a repeated jump. It does far less for steady endurance work such as marathon running, which draws on a different energy system.

Research on creatine and the brain is newer and far less settled. Neurons also draw on phosphocreatine, which is the rationale for testing creatine in cognition, and small trials have measured mental performance under sleep deprivation and other stressors. Some reported improvements. The trials are small, the designs differ, and the work should be treated as preliminary rather than established.

Safety data is reassuring by supplement standards. Studies tracking healthy adults for months, and in some cases years, have not found harm at the typical three to five grams a day. Early concern about kidney damage traced largely to the way creatine raises blood creatinine, a marker clinicians use to estimate kidney function. That rise reflects creatine metabolism rather than injury in people whose kidneys work normally. Anyone with existing kidney disease should clear the supplement with a doctor first.

Creatine draws water into muscle tissue, so people often gain a pound or two in the first weeks. That added weight is fluid rather than fat, and it is part of how the supplement works.

Monohydrate remains the cheapest and most heavily studied form. Newer versions sold at a premium — buffered, liquid or ester-based — have not beaten it in head-to-head comparisons.

Large randomized trials have not found that a daily multivitamin lowers the risk of heart disease or early death in healthy adults who already eat a reasonably varied diet. The Physicians' Health Study II, which tracked male doctors for more than a decade, found a modest drop in cancer incidence and no effect on cardiovascular outcomes.

That is a narrow finding from one specific population, and it is roughly where the case for general-purpose multivitamin use rests. The premise — close every nutrient gap at once, for pennies a day — is intuitive. Trial outcomes have not matched it.

The calculation changes for people with identifiable needs. Folic acid taken before conception and through early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects, which is why prenatal vitamins are standard medical advice rather than an optional wellness purchase. Older adults absorb less vitamin B12 from food as stomach acid production declines with age, so supplementation does real work. The same applies to people on restrictive diets, patients recovering from bariatric surgery and anyone with a malabsorption condition.

Dose is the quieter issue with broad-spectrum products. Many formulations deliver nutrients at several times the recommended daily amount, which adds nothing once diet has covered the requirement. Vitamins A, E and K are fat-soluble and accumulate in body tissue over months, unlike excess B and C vitamins, which are largely cleared in urine.

Food also delivers fiber, phytochemicals and nutrient combinations a pressed tablet cannot copy. Pulling one compound out of that context does not reliably carry the benefit with it. The Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta-Carotene Cancer Prevention Study found higher lung cancer rates among smokers given beta-carotene supplements — the reverse of what carotenoid-rich diets had suggested.

A multivitamin is defensible as cheap insurance for someone with a limited diet, a documented shortfall or elevated requirements. Sold as disease prevention or added years of life for a well-nourished adult, it promises more than the trial record supports.

Taking vitamin C every day does not stop healthy adults from catching colds. The Cochrane review by Harri Hemilä and Elizabeth Chalker, which pooled dozens of placebo-controlled trials, found no drop in how often people in the general population got sick.

The same review did identify a small effect on duration, limited to people already taking vitamin C before their symptoms began. Pooled across the trials, colds ran about eight percent shorter in adults and 14 percent shorter in children. On a week-long cold, that works out to hours rather than days.

Swallowing a high dose once the sniffles start — the way most cold-season products are sold — has not produced consistent benefit in trials. Vitamin C acts, to whatever degree it acts at all, as a steady background intake rather than a rescue treatment.

One group stands apart. In trials involving marathon runners, skiers and soldiers training in subarctic conditions, regular vitamin C roughly halved the incidence of colds. Those participants faced sustained physical exertion and cold exposure, and the finding does not carry over to an office worker in February.

The nutrient itself is essential, with jobs that have nothing to do with respiratory infections. The body needs it to synthesize collagen, to repair wounds and to absorb non-heme iron from plant foods. Severe long-term deficiency causes scurvy, now rare in countries with reliable access to fresh produce.

The recommended dietary allowance is modest: 90 milligrams a day for adult men and 75 for women, plus an extra 35 milligrams for smokers. A single orange, a cup of strawberries or half a red bell pepper covers most of that.

Supplements routinely sell doses in the hundreds or thousands of milligrams. Absorption efficiency falls as intake climbs, and the surplus leaves the body in urine. Very high intakes can trigger diarrhea and abdominal cramps, and may raise kidney stone risk in people already prone to them.

Melatonin works best as a timing signal, not a sedative. The clearest evidence supports its use for jet lag and shift work disorder, where it helps the internal clock realign with a new light-dark cycle faster than it would unaided.

The pineal gland releases melatonin as the evening darkens, telling the body that night has arrived. A supplement delivers that same message at an hour when the brain would not be sending it. A traveler flying east across several time zones, or a nurse rotating onto overnight shifts, has more to gain from it than someone who simply cannot settle down at 11 p.m.

For ordinary insomnia, the measured effect is small. Trials generally find that melatonin trims the time it takes to fall asleep by a matter of minutes. It does not produce the heavy sedation associated with prescription sleep medication, which is often what buyers in the sleep aisle are expecting.

Timing matters more than dose. A small amount — roughly half a milligram to three milligrams, taken a few hours before the intended bedtime — tracks the body's own evening release more closely than the 10 milligram tablets stocked widely in U.S. drugstores. Higher doses do not reliably work better, and they raise the odds of waking up groggy.

Label accuracy is a documented weak point. Analysis published in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine found that melatonin content in commercial products often departed from the amount printed on the bottle, in some cases by a wide margin in either direction, and some samples contained serotonin that the label did not disclose. Dietary supplements are not held to pharmaceutical manufacturing standards, so verifying what is actually in a capsule is difficult.

Short-term use in adults appears well tolerated, with headache, dizziness and next-day fogginess the most commonly reported complaints. Long-term safety data is thinner, particularly in children, and U.S. poison control centers have reported rising accidental ingestions among kids drawn to gummy formulations. Pediatricians typically look at bedtime routines, evening screen exposure and a consistent schedule before suggesting a supplement for a child.

Curcumin, the yellow compound that gives turmeric its color, blocks inflammatory pathways in cell cultures and animal models. Human trials have not reliably reproduced those results, and the ones that show benefit tend to be small, short and inconsistent with one another.

The obstacle is absorption. Curcumin dissolves poorly in water and breaks down quickly in the gut and liver. The body clears what remains fast, so little of an oral dose reaches tissue at the concentrations that produce effects in a laboratory dish. Supplement makers respond with piperine, an alkaloid from black pepper that slows curcumin's metabolism, or with phospholipid and nanoparticle formulations built to raise blood levels. Those methods do increase absorption. Raising a very low number is not the same as matching the exposure used in preclinical work.

Knee osteoarthritis is the application with the most human data. Several small randomized trials have reported improvements in pain and function with curcumin extracts, in some cases roughly comparable to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The trials differ in extract type, dose and duration, and many enroll fewer than 100 participants. Large independent replications remain scarce. That pattern supports further study rather than a settled conclusion.

Research on curcumin for depression, metabolic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease and cancer prevention sits at an early stage. Laboratory findings are plentiful. Clinical outcomes that would settle the question are not.

Turmeric used as a cooking spice is safe and has a long record in South Asian kitchens. Concentrated extracts are a different product. The National Institutes of Health's LiverTox database documents case reports of liver injury linked to turmeric and curcumin supplements — an uncommon outcome, but a documented one, and some reports involve high-absorption formulations.

Curcumin can also affect blood clotting and the liver enzymes that process many prescription drugs. Anyone taking anticoagulants, chemotherapy or a medication with a narrow therapeutic window should treat a concentrated turmeric supplement as a drug interaction question rather than a kitchen ingredient.

Hydrolyzed collagen peptides taken daily for roughly eight to 12 weeks have produced modest improvements in skin elasticity and hydration across several small and mid-sized randomized trials. The measured effect is small, and a sizable share of those trials were paid for by companies that sell collagen products.

Industry funding does not cancel out a result. It does warrant caution about reported effect sizes, since manufacturer-sponsored nutrition research tends to produce more favorable findings than independently funded work. The direction of the evidence is positive; the depth of it is shallow.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body and provides structure to skin, tendons, cartilage and bone. Production declines with age, which is the biological premise the whole category rests on. Whether swallowing collagen slows any part of that decline is a separate question from whether the decline happens at all.

Digestion sits at the center of that question. Proteins are broken into amino acids and short peptides before absorption, so ingested collagen does not arrive intact at skin tissue. Researchers have detected specific peptide fragments, including ones containing hydroxyproline, in the bloodstream after collagen is consumed. The proposed mechanism is that these fragments signal fibroblasts, the cells that build connective tissue, to increase collagen production. That pathway is still being characterized rather than settled.

Joint pain evidence is more divided. Some osteoarthritis trials report modest symptom relief; others find no meaningful separation from placebo. Differences in collagen type, dose and participant profile likely account for much of the inconsistency.

Products are sold as powders, capsules and ready-to-drink formulas, sourced from bovine, marine or porcine tissue. No source has been shown to outperform another for skin or joint outcomes.

The body also assembles its own collagen from ordinary dietary inputs — enough protein, plus the vitamin C and zinc that the synthesis process requires. For most healthy adults, these supplements carry little risk. The trial base behind them remains short in duration and limited in size.

#51. Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Elorian, the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The model, Glimpse, is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see.

Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.

For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night.

Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”

“Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said.

The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against.

Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.

But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.

Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.

The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test.

#56. Firmable launches Tech Intelligence, showing B2B sales teams what their prospects actually run and who to call about it

Firmable now detects 75,317 technologies across 19 million businesses, including the back-office infrastructure that website-based technographics miss. Every detection provides critical business context and comes with verified decision-maker contacts.

SAN FRANCISCO and MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Firmable, the AI-native B2B sales platform, today launched Tech Intelligence. It shows revenue teams the software, infrastructure, cloud and AI a company runs, and links it to the company and contact data Firmable already verifies. Name a technology and get back the companies running it and the people who own it, in one step. Tech Intelligence is now available as a paid add-on, in-product, and through the Firmable MCP in Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot.

Most B2B sales teams know who they want to sell to. Far fewer know what tech those companies already run. So reps open calls blind. They pitch accounts locked into a rival product and miss the migration and refresh moments that create pipeline. In a recent survey by Firmable of US sales teams, 71% ranked a lack of timing and context on a prospect as their biggest headache, ahead of bad contact data. Only 12% said they have a tool that solves it.

Most B2B sales teams know who they want to sell to. Far fewer know what tech those companies already run. So reps open calls blind. They pitch accounts locked into a rival product and miss the migration and refresh moments that create pipeline. In a recent survey by Firmable of US sales teams, 71% ranked a lack of timing and context on a prospect as their biggest headache, ahead of bad contact data. Only 12% said they have a tool that solves it.

Today's technographics tools weren't built to close that gap. Most read only a company's marketing website, and some look at job ads. That picks up analytics tags and the tools a company is hiring for. It misses the back-office systems that matter most to anyone selling into, alongside or against a tech stack: mail, hosting, identity, cloud and self-hosted services. And even when a team finds the right account, it still has to enrich the list in another tool to reach the right person.

"Being AI-native means we can build products that legacy data vendors can't bolt on," said Leigh Jasper, co-founder and co-CEO of Firmable. "Tech Intelligence is a good example. Our AI monitors 10 billion internet endpoints every week, reads four kinds of public signals, matches what it finds to 20 million businesses and joins it to verified people. It does that around the clock. You can't get there by patching an old database. We built our data layer for AI from day one, and that's why we can ship this depth fast. We launched our MCP in July. Now Tech Intelligence in October. Customers should expect that pace from Firmable."

Four ways of seeing a tech stack, in one platform

Tech Intelligence combines four detection methods, whereas most providers use one or two. Firmable reviewed 42 technographic and go-to-market data providers. None documented the same combination. Two of the methods, network and infrastructure observations, almost never show up in sales tools.

So sales teams see the back-office tech other tools miss: who hosts a company's email, which identity provider it uses, and whether it still runs aging on-premises infrastructure. Each detection is matched to Firmable's company records and verified contacts. The list a rep gets back already names the people to call and what to open with.

Built for teams that sell into the tech stack

Tech Intelligence is built for any B2B team whose next deal depends on what a prospect already runs. That includes software and technology vendors, managed service providers (MSPs), IT services firms and integrators, cybersecurity providers and MSSPs, and resellers and partner teams. It answers four questions those teams ask every day:

Every company in a territory on a rival email security product, plus the person who owns it

Who runs a tool that makes ours a natural add-on?

Companies with over 800 employees, running Shopify, for an e-commerce add-on vendor

Who needs services on the technology we support?

Accounts running VMware, for a migration partner

How big is the market for a technology, and where?

The number of companies using Claude, by size and location

Inside the Firmable platform, the package adds ready-made segments built around common buying moments. Teams can also pair a technology detection with Firmable's buying signals, such as a new Head of IT or a funding round. That surfaces accounts that are both a fit and in motion.

A rep can ask their AI assistant to "find companies in the US running a competitor's product, with more than 200 employees, and show me the IT decision-makers at each". They get a verified, ready-to-action list back in one step and can push it straight to a Firmable list or to their CRM.

Transparent confidence, from public-facing data only

Every Tech Intelligence detection carries a high, medium or low confidence score and a last-observed date. Detections are cross-checked across all four methods. Sales teams see how strong the evidence is and when it was last seen, so they don't have to trust a black-box tag that could be years old.

All of Tech Intelligence is built from public-facing information. Firmable never logs in, never uses credentials and never goes inside a company's network.

"Sales teams in the US and Canada have no shortage of data. What they're missing is the context that turns a list into a conversation," said Chester Thompson, VP, Americas at Firmable. "Tech Intelligence closes that gap. A rep in Chicago or Toronto can see which accounts still run VMware, which ones have switched email providers, and who owns the decision, all before they pick up the phone. For MSPs, IT services firms and channel teams across North America, that means getting to migration and refresh work before the RFP lands. We're growing fast, and this is exactly the kind of product that wins new logos."

The launch follows Firmable's MCP release in July 2026 and keeps up Firmable's fast product cadence as the company expands across the US and Canada, building on its base in Australia and APAC.

#57. Microsoft targets the ‘agentic insider’ with new controls for rogue AI agents

Microsoft Corp. today introduced security controls for rogue artificial intelligence agents that cut back what an agent may do as its assessed risk climbs.

The release takes on what Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, called the “agentic insider” in a blog post. Enterprise agents are often overprivileged, and their numbers are growing fast. Gallot argued that frontier models cannot be fully trusted because they are built to chase results. Some will reach a goal in ways nobody intended, she wrote, including by colluding with other agents.

Microsoft Chairman and Chief Executive Satya Nadella laid out the thinking behind the controls in an Oct. 10 essay that urged companies to treat models as insider risks, with safeguards kept outside the model itself. The most trustworthy system, he wrote, will be “the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

The controls start with finding agents. Microsoft’s discovery tools can now spot 60 types of local agents on employee machines after 35 were added. The list includes Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex, as well as GitHub Copilot from Microsoft’s own GitHub unit. The company is also extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID to give those agents, and unknown ones its sensors find, identities of their own.

Once found, each agent carries a continuously updated risk score under a feature Microsoft calls Dynamic Agent Risk. The score draws on signals from Microsoft’s identity, endpoint, cloud and network tools, and it climbs when an agent’s behavior drifts from what its user or organization intended.

Microsoft has extended Microsoft Entra Conditional Access to agents, and the resulting Dynamic Conditional Access feature decides what happens as the score rises. An agent might first lose the ability to change anything while keeping read access. Higher-impact actions can be held for verified human approval, and at the top of the scale the runtime is isolated or stopped entirely.

Access itself becomes temporary under Dynamic Permissions. An agent gets what a single task needs for as long as the job lasts, inside companywide limits that stop it from ever holding more authority than the person it works for. Microsoft Execution Container is one sandbox an agent can run inside. Because the monitoring sits outside the container, a compromised agent has no way to switch it off.

Project Perception, which Microsoft introduced in July as an agentic security system, gets new tools of its own. Playbooks added today let security staff set the outcome they want, and a new team of Guardian Agents carries out the work. A shift in an agent’s risk score sets the Guardian Agents investigating, and they can recommend containment or apply it on their own. People keep control of policy and approval rules.

In her post, Gallot also wrote that future controls should explain why an agent acts, and getting there means seeing a model’s reasoning tokens. “Model transparency will not replace containment,” she added. Microsoft said it is bringing chain-of-thought and other model-level signals into Dynamic Agent Risk.

Microsoft did not give availability dates or pricing for the new controls, which it is positioning as part of Project Perception and Microsoft 365 E7. That suite bundles Agent 365 with Microsoft 365 Copilot. Microsoft Ignite opens Nov. 17, and the company is pointing customers there for more detail.

#58. Cybersecurity Investors Put $6.8B To Work In The Third Quarter, Mostly In Larger Rounds

It’s an insecure world out there, and investors are responding by scaling up their cybersecurity spending.

For the third quarter of 2026, global cybersecurity- and privacy-focused startups pulled in a total of $6.8 billion, per Crunchbase data. That’s up about 50% from the prior quarter and tied for the highest quarterly tally in years, as charted below.

The funding bump was due to larger rounds, not more of them. Round counts actually declined sequentially across all stages last quarter, Crunchbase data shows.

AI startups accounted for the overwhelming majority of cybersecurity funding, with a particular focus on identity security. Overall, at least 18 companies at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity closed rounds of $100 million or more this past quarter.

Of those, the largest funding recipient by far was enterprise identity security provider  Keyfactor, which picked up $1 billion in a July growth round led by Summit Partners. Founded in 2001, the Ohio company isn’t exactly a startup, but it has attracted the bulk of its venture funding in the past 10 years and its pivot to AI is also of a more recent vintage.

Dallas-based Island tied for second place with a $400 million September Series F led by Evolution Equity Partners. The startup, which offers tools for enterprises to see and govern how people and AI agents interact with applications and data, also secured a post-money valuation of $6.4 billion.

Cyera, operator of an enterprise data security platform focused on AI agents, also announced a fresh $400 million Goldman Sachs Growth Equity-led investment in September, just three months after raising $600 million. The latest infusion set a $12 billion valuation for the New York startup.

For a bigger-picture view of leading fundraisers, below we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 largest round recipients.

We also saw some good-sized acquisitions of cybersecurity startups this past quarter, even as the IPO market was fairly sluggish.

Visa led the M&A pack with its $2.4 billion purchase of anti-fraud technology provider BioCatch in August. The acquisition is part of a broader effort by Visa to beef up its fraud detection and prevention capabilities for the AI age.

Among private unicorns, meanwhile, Cyera proved it can find a way to spend a good chunk of the capital it raised. It acquired Oasis Security, an enterprise access management platform built for AI agents, in a deal reportedly valued around $1 billion.

As for public offerings, Aura, which offers digital security services to consumers, was the lone sizable venture-backed market debut. The Boston-based startup completed an acquisition of an Australian public company, Qoria, in July, and then renamed the combined company Aura.

Overall, Crunchbase funding data points to an upbeat environment for cybersecurity startup funding. This doesn’t seem particularly surprising given the steady drumbeat of worrisome news about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI technology.

It’s not an especially reassuring time for most of us. But for cybersecurity founders, there’s certainly an ever-expanding array of hazards to keep at bay. We’ll keep watching in the current quarter to see if investment momentum continues to build.

#60. 10 supplement categories independent labs keep flagging

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A review of supplement categories independent testing has repeatedly flagged for contamination, mislabeling or hidden ingredients

Dietary supplements reach U.S. store shelves without FDA approval. The agency can act only after a product is already being sold and linked to harm. That gap makes independent testing one of the few real checks on an industry that largely polices itself. Groups such as ConsumerLab, NSF International, USP and the nonprofit Clean Label Project buy products at retail, send them to laboratories and publish the results.

What those results show varies by category. Some failures are a matter of potency — a vitamin dosed far below its label claim, or a probiotic carrying a fraction of the live bacteria it promises. Others carry direct health risk. Heavy metals turn up above safety thresholds. Prescription drugs turn up inside capsules marketed as herbal remedies. In 2015, the New York Attorney General's office used DNA barcoding on store-brand herbal supplements from four large retailers. Most of the products contained no detectable DNA from the plant named on the bottle, the office reported. Industry groups disputed the method, but the investigation pulled products off shelves and reopened a long argument about quality control.

Supplements sit in an odd legal middle ground. They are regulated closer to food than to medicine, yet many people take them expecting the purity and potency assurances that come with a prescription. Independent testing does not catch every bad product, and it covers only a fraction of what is sold. A passing result is not permanent either, because formulations change, suppliers change and contamination can vary from batch to batch within a single brand.

The categories that keep turning up in failed results are worth knowing before the next purchase. The 10 below have each drawn repeated, documented scrutiny — for contamination, for mislabeling, or for ingredients that were never disclosed. Understanding why each one fails also points to the questions worth asking about any supplement on the shelf.

Store-brand herbal supplements failed DNA testing badly enough in 2015 to trigger a formal state investigation. The New York Attorney General's office applied DNA barcoding — a method that identifies plant species from genetic material — to products sold at GNC, Target $TGT, Walmart $WMT and Walgreens $WBA, and reported that about four in five contained no detectable DNA from the herb named on the label.

Many of the tested bottles showed material from rice, wheat or common houseplants instead. The products were familiar single-herb sellers: echinacea, ginkgo biloba, St. John's wort, ginseng, saw palmetto and valerian root, sold as capsules and tablets rather than whole dried plant.

The methodology drew immediate objections. Trade groups argued that barcoding suits raw botanicals better than herbal extracts, since the heat, solvents and concentration steps used to produce an extract can degrade the genetic material the test looks for. That dispute limits what the results prove about any individual bottle.

The structural issue the episode exposed remains. Herbal ingredients travel through global supply chains, and a finished-product company often sits several steps removed from the farm or processor that handled the plant. Confirming that a capsule holds the right species at the right concentration, with no undisclosed filler, requires analytical work that no company must complete before shipping.

Retailers pulled products from shelves after the findings, and the industry spent the following years defending its quality controls. For a shopper, the lesson is narrower. Single-herb botanical products carry more identity risk than categories where the active compound can be measured by a straightforward chemical assay, because verifying that a powder is ginkgo rather than rice flour is a harder analytical question.

Products carrying a USP Verified or NSF certification mark have passed independent checks on identity and purity. That is a different proposition from an uncertified store brand, where the printed label is the only assurance a buyer has.

Fish oil has failed independent testing for oxidation, the chemical breakdown that happens when omega-3 fatty acids degrade and turn rancid. ConsumerLab has reported fish oil products exceeding voluntary industry limits for oxidation across multiple rounds of testing, including capsules that smell and taste normal.

Oxidation is measured through a value called TOTOX, which combines peroxide and anisidine readings of how far the fats have broken down. That standard is voluntary, set by the industry rather than enforced by the FDA, and no rule requires a bottle on a U.S. shelf to meet it.

This is a different kind of failure from heavy metal contamination. The concern is lost value rather than acute poisoning: the EPA and DHA a buyer is paying for have partly broken down, taking some biological activity with them. Long-term effects of regularly consuming oxidized fish oil are not well established, which is part of why the limits remain voluntary.

Oxidation depends on time and handling, not just formulation. Heat, light and oxygen all drive it, and they act on a product through manufacturing, shipping, warehousing and months in a cabinet at home. A batch made correctly can still be rancid by the time anyone swallows it, especially after a stretch in a warm distribution center or under store lighting. A clean result at the factory means less here than it would for a stable vitamin tablet.

Label accuracy has been a second problem in this category. Testing has turned up products containing less EPA and DHA than the panel claims. A partly oxidized capsule that also underdelivers on active ingredients shortchanges the buyer twice over.

Smaller bottles rather than bulk jars, refrigeration after opening and products carrying NSF International certification or an International Fish Oil Standards rating all reduce exposure. None of that removes the risk. Checking the expiration date and discarding a bottle that smells strongly fishy on opening remains the most practical check available without a laboratory.

Protein powders have shown some of the highest heavy metal readings in supplement testing, and plant-based versions test worse than whey. The nonprofit Clean Label Project tested more than 130 protein powders in a 2018 study and reported detectable lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury in many of them, with rice, pea and hemp products generally higher than dairy-derived powders.

The cause is agricultural rather than industrial. Plants draw cadmium and arsenic out of soil and irrigation water as they grow, and rice absorbs both efficiently. Concentrating that plant matter into an isolate concentrates whatever came with it. Whey is separated from milk during cheesemaking and skips that pathway, which is why dairy-based powders tend to come out cleaner on the same panels. Soil chemistry, local water and a region's mining or industrial history all feed into what ends up in a harvest. Contamination tracks where and how a crop was grown, not what the finished tub costs.

A single serving is not the concern. Heavy metal exposure is assessed as cumulative intake across months and years, and regulatory thresholds are built around long-term consumption rather than one shake. The use pattern matters more: someone drinking a shake every day as part of a training routine, for years, treating it as a staple food. Cadmium accumulates in the kidneys and clears slowly, which is why daily intake matters more than any single measurement. U.S. supplement labels are not required to disclose heavy metal content at all.

Certification programs built for this category offer the clearest filter. NSF Certified for Sport and Informed Choice both screen finished products for contaminants and banned substances, and their marks appear on a wide range of powders sold to athletes. Companies that publish batch-level test results, rather than pointing to a logo, give buyers something checkable. Rotating protein sources limits reliance on any single crop supply.

Weight loss products are the category the FDA most often flags for hidden prescription drugs rather than for a simple purity or potency failure. Its tainted products database lists hundreds of slimming and fat-burning supplements found to contain undeclared drugs, most often sibutramine, an appetite suppressant withdrawn from the U.S. market in 2010 over cardiovascular risk.

Phenolphthalein appears in the same listings. The laxative compound lost its over-the-counter status in the U.S. in 1999 after animal research raised cancer concerns, and it has no legitimate role in a dietary supplement.

These are not trace contaminants from a sloppy supply chain. Regulators treat them as deliberate adulteration, because the drugs produce the fast results the marketing promises and botanical blends cannot deliver on their own. A bottle labeled natural can still carry a pharmaceutical dose high enough to interact dangerously with medication for blood pressure, depression or a heart condition.

Enforcement is reactive. Testing usually follows reports of adverse events, so a product can sell for months through online marketplaces and small retailers before enough harm accumulates to prompt a warning or a recall. Once a brand name reaches a federal list, the same formula is often repackaged and sold under a new one, which makes the warnings hard to keep current.

The FDA's tainted products database is searchable by product name and by the drug detected, which gives a buyer a way to check a specific brand before purchase. Its limits matter as well. A product absent from the list has not necessarily been tested and cleared; it may simply never have been reported. The marketing language on these products tends to run the same way: rapid fat loss with no change to diet or exercise. The ingredient list beneath it is usually plant extracts that would not produce that effect alone.

Products sold for male sexual enhancement are among the categories the FDA most often identifies as containing undisclosed prescription drugs. Laboratory analysis has repeatedly found sildenafil, the active ingredient in Viagra, or tadalafil, the active ingredient in Cialis, inside capsules whose labels list only herbs and amino acids.

Sildenafil and tadalafil interact with nitrates, a class of medication prescribed for chest pain and other heart conditions. The combination can cause a sharp drop in blood pressure. A man managing angina with a nitrate has no way to know an herbal capsule contains the ingredient his cardiologist told him to avoid. The label does not disclose it, so no clinician gets the chance to screen for the interaction.

Dosing is the second problem. Prescription sildenafil comes in measured strengths, dispensed after a clinician reviews a patient's other medications. A drug added covertly to a supplement passes through no such control. FDA warnings have described products carrying undeclared amounts of these ingredients that bear no relationship to any approved dose. Amounts can also vary between capsules in the same package, because the ingredient is not added under pharmaceutical manufacturing controls. Some products have been found to contain chemical analogues of sildenafil — modified versions of the molecule that have never been studied in people.

Marketing language is part of the pattern. Words like natural, herbal and safe alternative appear on packaging that testing has shown to be an unreliable description of the contents. Distribution follows the same logic. These products circulate heavily through gas stations, convenience stores and third-party online marketplaces rather than pharmacy chains that vet suppliers.

Enforcement has not closed the gap. The FDA has issued consumer alerts on individual sexual enhancement products for well over a decade. New ones with the same hidden ingredients keep appearing, often under a fresh brand name once the previous one draws a warning.

Probiotic supplements have repeatedly fallen short on the one number that defines them: the count of live organisms in the capsule, measured in colony-forming units, or CFUs. ConsumerLab testing has found products delivering a fraction of the CFU count printed on the label by the time a shopper buys them.

The cause is usually biological rather than fraudulent. Probiotics are living bacteria, not stable chemical compounds, and their numbers fall from the moment they leave the production line. Heat, moisture and elapsed time all kill live organisms, so a product accurate at manufacture can still fail a lab test months later after sitting in a warm warehouse or a sunlit retail display. The expiration date on a probiotic marks a declining population, not a fixed dose.

Some manufacturers handle this through overfilling — adding more live organisms than the label states so the count still holds at the expiration date. Companies that skip that step, or that use strains more sensitive to degradation, are the ones most likely to underdeliver at the point of use. Refrigerated probiotics generally hold potency better than shelf-stable formulations, though shelf-stable versions have spread because they cost less to ship and are easier to stock.

Potency is not the only labeling gap testing has raised. Strains within the same bacterial species can produce different effects, and clinical research is normally run on one named strain rather than the species as a whole. A bottle listing only Lactobacillus acidophilus, without the strain designation that follows the species name, gives a buyer no way to confirm the product contains the organism used in the research cited to sell it.

Checking the label for a strain code and a CFU count guaranteed through the expiration date, rather than at manufacture, separates products that have accounted for die-off from those quoting a number true only on the packing day.

Turmeric supplements have failed independent testing on two separate fronts: lead contamination and adulteration with synthetic yellow dyes. Both problems originate in the raw spice rather than in capsule manufacturing, so a product's quality depends largely on where the root was grown and who handled it first.

Lead is the better-documented of the two. Turmeric roots can absorb lead from contaminated soil, and lead chromate, a bright yellow industrial pigment, has been used in parts of South Asia to brighten dull or low-grade turmeric before sale. Public health agencies treat lead as having no known safe level of exposure, and a capsule swallowed every morning is a different exposure pattern from a spoonful of spice in a weekly curry.

Dye adulteration is a separate form of cheating. Metanil yellow, a colorant not approved for food use in the U.S. or the European Union, has turned up in adulterated turmeric, where it makes diluted or inferior powder look richer than it is.

Potency is the third weak point. Curcumin, the compound most studied for anti-inflammatory activity, accounts for only a small fraction of the dried root and absorbs poorly in the gut on its own. Manufacturers commonly add piperine, a black pepper compound, to improve uptake. Others use lipid or phospholipid formulations for the same purpose.

A label reading only "turmeric extract," with no standardized curcuminoid percentage, leaves a buyer unable to judge whether the dose resembles anything used in published trials. Two products with nearly identical front-label claims can deliver very different amounts of curcuminoids.

Certification carries more weight here than in most categories. A USP Verified mark, or test results published by an organization such as ConsumerLab covering both heavy metals and curcuminoid content, tells a buyer more than packaging that leans on the word turmeric and the deep color of the powder inside.

Multivitamins fail independent testing mostly on dosing accuracy rather than contamination. ConsumerLab's recurring multivitamin reviews have found products whose vitamin D, vitamin A or mineral content sits well outside the range the label implies. The number on the bottle is not always a reliable guide to what one tablet delivers.

Underdosing is the quieter problem. Someone taking a multivitamin to close a documented shortfall — vitamin D is the common case — may assume the gap has been filled. The deficiency only shows up again at the next blood test. The product does no harm; it simply fails at the job it was bought for.

Overdosing runs the opposite risk, and it concentrates in the fat-soluble vitamins. Vitamins A, D, E and K are stored in body tissue rather than flushed out in urine. Sustained intake above what the body needs can build toward toxicity. Water-soluble nutrients such as vitamin C and the B vitamins are far more forgiving of an inflated dose. An overage in vitamin A therefore matters more than an overage in B6 at typical supplement levels.

Minerals bring their own margin problem. Iron and zinc leave a narrower gap between a useful dose and an excessive one than most vitamins do. Iron is also the ingredient behind the accidental-poisoning warning printed on iron-containing supplement labels, a risk tied specifically to young children in the household. A mislabeled iron figure matters more when someone is also taking a separate iron tablet or eating fortified cereal.

Dosing accuracy is not the only failure mode. A tablet can contain the correct amount of a nutrient and still pass through the digestive tract largely intact if it never disintegrates. USP's verification program tests disintegration alongside identity and potency. The USP Verified mark therefore signals something in this category beyond label math alone.

Pre-workout powders have repeatedly turned up in laboratory analyses containing stimulants that appear nowhere on the label, DMAA chief among them. The FDA has stated that DMAA does not qualify as a legal dietary ingredient and has issued warning letters to companies selling it, yet the compound kept surfacing in tested products for years afterward.

DMAA appears under names that disguise it — 1,3-dimethylamylamine, methylhexanamine, or the misleading "geranium extract." The FDA has tied it to reports of elevated blood pressure, heart attack and stroke. The U.S. military pulled DMAA products from base exchange shelves in 2011 and opened a review of the ingredient after two soldiers died during physical training. Several other countries restricted or banned its sale. Products containing it kept reaching American buyers through online sellers and small distributors that sit outside the supplier vetting large retail chains apply.

Caffeine is the more routine labeling problem in this category. U.S. rules let a manufacturer declare a proprietary blend as one combined weight without itemizing each ingredient, so a buyer often cannot tell how much caffeine a scoop delivers. These formulas rarely stop at caffeine anyway. Many pair caffeine anhydrous with synephrine, yohimbine or other stimulants, which makes the total stimulant load unlike that of a plain caffeine tablet. Someone who handles 200 milligrams from coffee without trouble has no reliable way to judge what a multi-stimulant blend is doing.

Competitive athletes face a separate exposure. Sports supplements, pre-workouts included, are a recognized source of inadvertent anti-doping violations, since a banned substance missing from the ingredient panel will still register in a urine sample. NSF Certified for Sport and Informed Choice screen finished sports products against banned-substance lists, a narrower and stricter check than general purity verification. For an athlete subject to drug testing, that mark is the baseline worth looking for.

CBD products have produced some of the least reliable label accuracy in any supplement category. A 2017 study published in JAMA tested 84 CBD extracts bought online and found that only about 30% carried the amount of cannabidiol listed on the label.

The mismatch runs in both directions. A product that underdelivers wastes money and makes it impossible to judge whether a given dose does anything. One that overdelivers hands a buyer a quantity they never chose, which matters for anyone taking CBD alongside prescription medication, since cannabidiol changes how the liver metabolizes certain drugs.

The same analysis detected THC, the psychoactive compound in cannabis, in about one in five of the samples. Because cannabidiol is extracted from a plant that also produces THC, trace amounts can survive processing and end up in a bottle sold as THC-free. That matters for workers subject to employer drug screening and for anyone choosing CBD specifically to avoid intoxication. A zero-THC claim is only as good as the laboratory work behind it.

The regulatory gap is wider here than in most supplement aisles. The 2018 Farm Bill legalized hemp containing less than 0.3% THC, but the FDA has maintained that CBD cannot legally be marketed as a dietary supplement. Day-to-day quality control falls to state rules, which differ sharply, and to testing companies choose to run on themselves. The inconsistency shows up across tinctures, capsules, gummies, beverages and topical creams.

The practical safeguard is a certificate of analysis, a document from an independent laboratory confirming cannabinoid content and screening for pesticides, residual solvents and heavy metals. Established brands publish one for every production batch, often reachable through a QR code on the carton. A seller who cannot produce it has given the buyer no way to verify what is inside.

#61. Ukraine’s drones lose their Starlink link above 100 mph. Musk, Rubio, and Trump all say it wasn’t them

Speed of communication has been essential on the battlefield for as long as humans have waged war. From the legendary roughly 25-mile messenger’s run to announce an Athenian victory at Marathon, to war drums and carrier pigeons, to the telegraph, and right up to today’s militaries’ reliance on high-speed digital links, rapid information transmission is imperative for military success.

The speed of a weapons system is essential, too.

That’s why a sudden loss of satellite connectivity for Ukrainian drones and vehicles moving faster than 100 miles per hour earlier this month represented a major blow to the country’s fight against Russia.

Overnight from Oct. 13 to Oct. 14, Ukrainian military users found that satellite-connected hardware traveling faster than 100 mph (160 km/h) lost its connection, according to Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor to Ukraine’s president. Some units even reported problems at lower speeds: Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps said connections dropped for 10 to 20 seconds at 110 to 120 km/h, and Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko, citing military reports, claimed drops at speeds as low as 60 to 70 km/h—roughly 37 to 43 mph.

Beskrestnov said the restriction applied to Starshield’s military service package, the government- and defense-focused version of the satellite internet network run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. (SpaceX’s civilian service, Starlink, has more than 12 million customers.) Exactly which service Ukraine’s forces rely on has itself become a point of dispute: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Ukraine does not currently have access to Starshield and that its request for it is “under conversation.”

Whatever the label, the effect on the battlefield was immediate. Ukraine uses domestically built interceptor drones to hunt Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drones, known in Russia as the Geran-3, which can fly as fast as 370 km/h, or about 230 mph. An interceptor that loses its link above 100 mph—or, by some accounts, above 43 mph—is badly outmatched. Ukrainian sources have said terminals need to work at speeds of at least 450 km/h to counter the jet drones.

“The maximum speed today is 161 km/h; after exceeding it, Starlink shuts down, and we lose the drone,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 17, adding that Ukrainian specialists had tested terminals at 180 km/h inside the European Union without losing connection. “The restrictions operate on the territory of Ukraine and do not operate on the territory of EU countries.” Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said service had partially stabilized for terminals moving below about 160 km/h, but as of the weekend, Zelensky said the cap remained in place.

Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation, told Fortune in an interview that the interference hurt Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, not just its offensive capabilities. It greatly hindered “Ukraine’s ability to defend against very high-speed drones,” she said. That happened at the same time Ukraine stopped getting early warning notifications from the U.S. about incoming Russian missiles. “Those things going hand in hand, it seems like there was a deliberate effort to try and impede Ukraine’s ability to defend itself,” Samson said.

Much of the initial blame fell on Musk and SpaceX. Radosław Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, posted on X: “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you.” Poland has paid for tens of thousands of the terminals Ukraine uses. (The two men have clashed before: In 2025, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man” in a dispute over Starlink in Ukraine.)

Condemnation also came from both sides of the U.S. political aisle. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) asked Musk on X to confirm the “overnight disruptions to Starlink terminals in Ukraine were unintended” and to clarify SpaceX’s position, warning that “intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer.” He later called for a Pentagon inspector general investigation. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) wrote that “these restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately.” (Fortune reached out to both senators’ offices for comment but did not hear back before publication.)

Musk disavowed responsibility, posting on X, which he owns: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

Two U.S. officials and a Western official later told Reuters that the order to slow Starshield service for Ukraine came from inside the White House, though they did not say who made the decision. A senior Ukrainian official told the news agency that Kyiv had called the White House, State Department, and Pentagon and was told it was a White House decision. Separately, the Telegraph, citing four sources, reported that Musk himself proposed the caps to Trump, who approved them.

Appearing on NBC’s Meet the Press on Oct. 18, Zelensky said Ukraine’s generals, its government, and he himself believe the throttling was “a message from [the] American government to limit the speed.” He added: “Technically, SpaceX did it,” but “it’s limited because it’s a decision,” and said service would be restored “if President Trump will decide tomorrow—or better, today—if he will personally decide to lift this decision,” according to Yahoo Finance.

The Trump administration denies any involvement. Rubio, who serves as both secretary of state and national security advisor, told reporters that “no one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” calling such reports “categorically false,” according to Al Jazeera. He also said the slowdown “sort of happened” but that service had been restored to where it was before—a claim Kyiv disputes. Trump himself told reporters, “It wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” per CBS News.

The throttling comes amid a series of administration moves that have eased pressure on Russia as Trump pushes Kyiv to halt drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for rising energy prices ahead of the midterms. On Oct. 9, after Trump announced a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin, the Treasury Department issued General License 135, allowing the sale and import of Russian-origin diesel—blocked by sanctions since 2022, the year Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine—through April 7, 2027. The deal drew bipartisan backlash in Congress.

Then, late on Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order waiving nearly all of the substantive sanctions, tariffs, and restrictions in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026—a law he signed just a month earlier—before they took effect on Oct. 18. The administration has also threatened to cut arms supplies to Ukraine, and Trump has called for Ukraine to get a new president.

A White House spokeswoman has said the sanctions authorities give the president tools to pursue peace. But critics argue that renewed fuel sales and suspended sanctions and tariffs put more money in Vladimir Putin’s pocket to fund the war.

Those economic measures may weaken Ukraine’s position over months. Losing the ability to fly fast drones, by contrast, hurts Ukraine right now—and hands Russia an immediate advantage in the skies.
