Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own.

“Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns.

At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream.

Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding.

“It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.”

Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies.

She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday, she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said.

#65. Amazon’s new Bee AI devices have a bystander problem, says former AWS security engineer

by Todd Bishop on Oct 16, 2026 at 4:02 pmOctober 19, 2026 at 6:42 am

Amazon’s new Bee AI devices ask the wrong person for consent, according to a privacy and security veteran who previously worked as a senior principal security engineer at Amazon Web Services.

In a LinkedIn article, Jeff Williams writes that Bee’s consent safeguards are aimed at the wearer, while the people being recorded have no practical way to say no.

Amazon unveiled the devices Thursday, the first new Bee hardware since it acquired the San Francisco startup last year. The $74.99 Bee Frontier goes on the wrist or clips to clothing, and the $99.99 Bee Eclipse snaps onto the back of a phone.

How Bee handles consent: Amazon says users are prompted to get permission from call participants each time they start a recording, and the devices show an indicator light while in use.

The problem, Williams says, is that neither one reliably tells the other people in a conversation that they’re being recorded. He writes that the prompt appears only on the wearer’s phone, and nothing enforces it.

“A prompt instructing the user to obtain permission is a liability allocation,” he wrote, arguing that Amazon is shifting responsibility for obtaining consent onto the wearer.

The light is easy to hide under a sleeve or in a pocket, he notes, and a device on the wrist or phone sits outside the frame on a video call.

Williams points to Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses as an example. In September, the data protection authority in Hamburg, Germany, found the glasses’ recording light hard to see outdoors and concluded that a recording indicator alone doesn’t establish informed consent under Europe’s GDPR.

In the U.S., about a dozen states, including Washington state and California, generally require consent from everyone before a private conversation can be recorded.

Whose data is protected: Williams gives Amazon credit for Bee Private Compute, which processes audio in an isolated, encrypted environment built on AWS Nitro and then deletes it. Amazon says only the customer can access the resulting data, not Amazon or Bee.

But that protects the wearer. The words of the people around the wearer still end up in transcripts and summaries they can’t see or remove. Amazon says those speakers aren’t identified by name unless they complete a voice training exercise with the device’s owner.

Williams notes that Amazon has changed comparable privacy commitments before, such as ending the “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” option on some Echo devices last year.

Williams also advises companies to keep the devices out of client meetings and privileged discussions, since the transcripts end up in an employee’s personal account, where the company can’t see or manage them.

A proposed fix: Williams says Bee should leave other people’s voices out of transcripts by default, unless they’ve enrolled their voices and agreed to be recorded. Before the acquisition, Bee indicated plans to record only the voices of people who had verbally consented, according to TechCrunch.

“I know first-hand that Amazon has the engineering talent to ship it,” he wrote.

Amazon’s response: The company didn’t comment directly on the critique but pointed to safeguards built into the devices.

One is an automatic shutoff: the devices turn off if they don’t detect the owner’s voice for 5, 15, 30 or 60 minutes, depending on the user’s setting. Amazon says that reinforces that Bee is “a personal AI assistant, not a device designed to passively pick up audio throughout the day.”

The company says it educates customers about responsible use in the Bee app, and that Eclipse will send push notifications encouraging users to let people around them know they’re using Bee and to ask for permission.

Williams, now chief information security officer at Sigma360, worked at AWS from 2023 to 2025 and spent more than 12 years at Microsoft before that, including as a privacy officer for its services business. Read his full article on LinkedIn. Read his full article on LinkedIn.

#68. Exclusive: Chariot Raises $10M To Help Consumers Fight Back Against Hidden Fees And Hard-To-Cancel Subscriptions

While helping another founder build an app that collected information about class-action settlements, Zim Hang came to learn how challenging it can be for consumers to seek compensation from companies they believe wronged them.

He also discovered mass arbitration, a way to pursue individual claims when companies’ contracts prevent customers from joining class actions. At the same time, he also realized that relatively few law firms were set up to manage thousands of those claims at once.

That gap became the basis for Chariot Claims, which has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Silverton Partners to help consumers pursue claims over alleged privacy violations, hidden fees and subscriptions that are difficult to cancel. Indicator Ventures, Lightbank, Neon Fund, ZVC, Rosecliff Ventures, Alumni Ventures, FJ Labs, Graph Ventures and Vermilion Ventures also participated in the financing.

The New York-based startup works with law firms to identify potential cases, find affected consumers and gather information needed to pursue compensation. The round brings its total funding to $15.7 million, which includes a $3.6 million seed investment in April 2025 and an earlier pre-seed round.

Chariot’s latest round comes amid a surge in investment across legal tech. Funding to the legal tech space hit a record high last year, with $4.6 billion invested, per Crunchbase data. So far this year, legal tech startups have pulled in more than $3 billion, putting the sector on pace to match or exceed the 2025 total.

The Chariot process works like this: For each case, consumers complete an intake questionnaire that assesses preliminary eligibility in real time. Chariot’s team then reviews these pre-qualified claims through a multi-layered system of technology and human oversight before sending it to the partner law firm handling the case. Hang, the company’s CEO, told Crunchbase News that Chariot typically receives more than 200,000 claim submissions per month and that it has taken on roughly 80 cases since shifting to its current business model just over a year ago.

The company has about 15 employees and is currently breaking even, he said. It plans to spend the new funding primarily on hiring and product development, including AI tools to review cases and help determine whether consumers qualify to participate.

Chariot is Hang’s third startup. His first company grew out of sleep research he conducted while studying psychology and neuroscience at Washington University. He turned that research into a smart-pillow business and later sold its intellectual property to a medical-device operator. He later worked in healthcare technology and fintech, founded a startup in the Web3 space, and then moved into legal technology.

Across those industries, he said, he encountered complicated systems in which the interests of businesses and their customers did not always align. His experience helping the class-action settlement startup brought those concerns into focus.

He described being “frustrated and mystified and horrified by how our justice system works.”

Chariot started about three years ago, adopting its current model after Hang saw an opportunity to help law firms handle mass arbitration. Firms accustomed to class actions could struggle with the work required to manage large numbers of individual claimants, he said.

“It’s just really inefficient for them to try to build workflows around 10,000 claimants or 100,000 claimants,” Hang said.

Chariot handles parts of that administrative work, while its partner firms handle the legal claims. The startup charges the firms flat service fees, and they work on a contingency basis. Hang emphasizes that since it’s not a law firm, Chariot itself doesn’t file claims.

It helps consumers pursue a variety of claims. Those claims include allegations that websites or apps tracked their information without consent, that companies added fees during checkout, or that businesses made subscriptions easy to start but difficult to cancel, for example.

Chariot starts by looking for potential cases involving privacy violations, hidden fees and other consumer complaints. Its software scans public records, including federal court filings, and uses AI to analyze the allegations and prepare research for its partner law firms.

That research includes legal memos based on publicly filed complaints. Chariot is also developing tools to track changes in laws and court decisions that could affect whether a case can proceed. The work remains in the early stages, with the goal of automating more of the research that associates and paralegals would otherwise do, according to Hang.

Chariot reviews a few hundred potential cases each month, he said. It tests ads for about 30 potential cases to gauge whether it can find consumers who may have a claim, then selects roughly 10 to pursue more extensively with its partner law firms. Each case can involve many individual consumers, whom Chariot reaches through advertising and partnerships with consumer financial technology companies.

To determine whether they have a claim, consumers must provide information to help assess it. For example, in the case of a data breach, that could be a notice from the company saying their information was exposed. For a hidden-fee complaint, it could include what they purchased, when they bought it, and how much they paid.

Chariot is building AI tools to help review that supporting information and determine whether a consumer has a claim, according to Hang. The required evidence, and the difficulty of verifying it, varies by the type of alleged violation.

The startup plans to make that step easier by allowing users to connect their email accounts so its software can look for relevant documents, rather than asking consumers to fill out forms.  Hang estimates that such improvements could help the company handle 10x to 100x its current claim volume.

Not everyone welcomes Chariot’s approach. Advertising for potential claimants has brought strong objections from some of the companies involved. In fact, Chariot has received cease-and-desist letters challenging, among other things, its use of company names and trademarks in ads, noted Hang.

But he asserts that identifying those businesses is necessary to reach people who used their products or services.

“As a part of our business, we need to mention the name of the company that has this alleged violation,” he said.

Chariot reviews the letters with legal counsel and complies with demands it considers valid, Hang said. He declined to name specific companies for this article.

His broader goal is to make alleged consumer abuses more costly for businesses. If more affected customers pursue compensation, he reasons, companies will have a stronger financial incentive to change those practices.

“We want to make unethical unprofitable,” he said.

Mike Dodd, general partner at Silverton, told Crunchbase News via email that his firm was attracted to Chariot’s vertical AI approach to working with law firms, which he called “exciting and defensible.”

“It’s a greenfield market with space to expand horizontally and eventually into a generalized consumer legal AI solution,” he wrote. The firm was also drawn to what Dodd described as “a business model that aligns capitalistic incentives with access to justice.”

“When a company breaks the law and breaks what it promises to its consumers, the consumer rarely seeks justice,” he added. “Chariot has built the technology to make individual consumer claims work at scale, and the team to operate it in a category where execution is genuinely hard.”

#69. Nvidia, Dell back $200M round for AI model developer doubleAI

Artificial intelligence developer doubleAI today announced that it has raised $200 million in funding.

Lightspeed and Bessemer co-led the Series A round. They were joined by Nvidia Corp., Dell Technologies Inc. and several others. CTech reported that the investment values doubleAI at more than $1 billion.

Tel Aviv-based doubleAI, officially AA-I Technologies Ltd., has created an AI model called Maxwell that can automatically make software code more efficient. It also lends itself to a variety of other tasks. Maxwell broke a long-standing chess challenge earlier this month, while a doubleAI-developed agent made a new mathematical discovery around the same time.

Nvidia offers an open-source library called cuGraph that enables customers to harness its graphics cards for graph analytics. That’s a data science approach used in fields such as supply chain management. In March, doubleAI revealed that Maxwell had rewritten cuGraph to lower its hardware usage. The company says that the model sped up 55% of the algorithms in the library by a factor of two or more.

Maxwell went on to create an optimized version of pandas, a popular open-source data science toolkit. The AI improved the library’s performance on PDS-H, a query speed benchmark, by a factor of 38. A more recent project saw doubleAI use Maxwell to double the video generation speed of a world model called LTX-2.5.

The company plans to sell the model to enterprises interested in lowering their AI workloads’ hardware usage. According to doubleAI, Maxwell finds optimization opportunities by analyzing how a program interacts with the data that it processes and the underlying chips. The model supports both graphics processing units and central processing units.

Processors don’t run applications’ source code directly. Instead, they run a version of the source code called a binary. It’s a machine-generated translation that represents a program as a series of simple computing operations.

When developers find a way to make an application more efficient, they usually implement the optimization by modifying the program’s source code. Maxwell, by contrast, applies optimizations to a program’s binary. That removes the need for developers to manually make source code changes. Furthermore, doubleAI’s approach makes it possible to modify applications while they’re running in production.

The company’s technology also lends itself to other use cases. Earlier this month, doubleAI used an internal AI agent to make a new discovery about graphs, mathematical structures with an important role in software development. The agent paired its proof with a Lean file, a code snippet that makes it relatively simple to verify the finding.

In conjunction with today’s funding announcement, doubleAI revealed that Maxwell recently broke a nearly 50-year chess record. The model found a chess position, or arrangement of chess pieces, in which 63 moves give check. The previous record was 60 moves.

The Wall Street Journal reported that doubleAI will use half its funding round to buy 1,000 of Nvidia’s B300 Blackwell graphics cards. The chips should make it easier for the company to compete with OpenAI Group PBC and Anthropic PBC, whose latest AI models are also capable of automating research tasks.

A few days ago, the ChatGPT developer released 722 AI-generated math papers. A month earlier, an Anthropic model created a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The file comprises 13 million lines of code that would have taken a team of human mathematicians several years to write.

#70. Melinda French Gates has a 48-hour rule for criticizing employees. The billionaire philanthropist says it’s because ‘being clear is kind’

Melinda French Gates shared her secret formula for handling conflict at work.

“If I’m unhappy with work you have done, you will hear from me within 48 hours,” French Gates told Bloomberg’s Leaders With Francine Lacqua podcast in March. “I’m not going to tell you right away, because I need time to think it through.

“If I’m angry about something [I do this] to calm down,” she added. “That’s on me.”

This practice, she explained, is less about withholding criticism and more about delivering it with honesty, integrity, and grace. The flip side of the 48-hour clock is just as deliberate. If the window closes without any feedback, that means employees are in the clear.

“If they pass the 48-hour mark, they can be confident that the job they did was a good job,” she said. “You’re not going to get to your performance review and have a surprise.”

This is a practice the billionaire philanthropist has been honing for decades. She cochaired the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the world’s largest private charitable organization, from 2000 until she stepped down in 2024, about three years after the couple’s divorce.

Today, French Gates runs her own organization, Pivotal Ventures, an investment and incubation company she founded in 2015 to advance opportunities for women and families in the U.S. As part of her divorce settlement from the Microsoft founder, French Gates received $12.5 billion to direct toward philanthropic work through Pivotal. She committed an additional $1 billion each year through 2026 to advance women’s power globally.

Bloomberg’s Lacqua framed French Gates’ approach to feedback as her “leadership superpower,” one that requires emotional discipline and candor.

“Being clear is kind,” French Gates responded, “because I’m giving them feedback so they can actually grow and become better.”

French Gates also described her 48-hour feedback mantra as maintaining personal integrity while keeping the other person’s dignity intact: “gracious, thoughtful, before you go into it.”

Her philosophy conflicts with some of the more aggressive feedback cultures from other executives. Ray Dalio, for example, built his firm’s culture around what he calls “radical transparency,” a system in which employees at every level are expected to deliver unfiltered, real-time criticism, and nearly every meeting is recorded for postmortem analysis.

“If you start to realize, intellectually, that being really truthful with each other is something that is to be treasured,” Dalio told Business Insider, “it’ll build trust.

“There’s a lot of trust that’s going on,” added Dalio, who founded Bridgewater Associates, the world’s largest hedge fund firm. He even recalled to Business Insider a time in which a junior staffer sent him an email grading his performance in a meeting as a “D-” for being disorganized.

So while Dalio prefers immediacy and unvarnished feedback, French Gates opts for more reflection time and a respectful tone.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella takes a slightly different approach. When he took the helm of Microsoft, he pushed to transform a “know-it-all” culture into a “learn-it-all” culture—one grounded in humility, curiosity, and psychological safety. It’s a mantra inspired by American psychologist Carol Dweck, who is best known for her research on motivation and mindset.

“If you take two people—one of them is a learn-it-all and the other one is a know-it-all—the learn-it-all will always trump the know-it-all in the long run, even if they start with less innate capability,” Nadella told Bloomberg in a 2016 interview.

Still, French Gates is clear she doesn’t shy away from difficult conversations.

“I don’t mind conflict,” she told Bloomberg. “I learned to do it in a way for me that maintained my integrity.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 27, 2026.

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#71. From focaccia to injera: TasteAtlas's top 10 breads in the world

Free daily briefing on global business news.

TasteAtlas ranks global breads by taste, and these 10 traditional loaves consistently top the list for flavor and craft

TasteAtlas catalogs traditional dishes, ingredients and restaurants from around the world, and ranks them using ratings submitted by its users. Its bread category is one of the busiest. The entries that climb it are rarely novelties. They are the loaves, flatbreads and rolls that hold up entire cuisines, eaten daily in the places that made them. For home bakers and travelers, a list of the best breads in the world according to TasteAtlas doubles as a shopping list. These are the breads worth seeking out at a neighborhood bakery, a market stall or a table abroad.

The ranking is useful because it insists on origin. Rather than lumping everything under labels like white bread or whole wheat, it names specific regional breads with their own methods, histories and rules. The range runs from Ethiopia's sour injera to the baguette sold in bakeries across France. That precision matters more for bread than for almost any other food. Local wheat, water, climate and generations of inherited technique all leave a mark on the finished loaf. In France, what a bakery may legally call a traditional baguette is set out in national regulation. Naan needs the heat of a tandoor, which few home kitchens can match.

The 10 entries below are the breads that sit near the top of the category. Each is also treated in culinary literature as a defining example of its type. What sets them apart is rarely one thing. Sometimes it is fermentation, as with sourdough. Sometimes it is the grain, as with teff. Sometimes it is the cooking method, as with the boiled bagel or the lye-dipped pretzel. Some are staples eaten several times a day. Others belong to a particular meal, holiday or region.

Taken together, they show how far flour, water and heat can be pushed in different hands. Each entry covers where the bread comes from, how it is made and what separates it from everything else on the counter.

Focaccia is a flat Italian bread built around olive oil, with a crisp base, a dimpled top and a soft, oil-saturated interior. The oil goes into the dough and over it. That is what separates focaccia from leaner oven breads made from the same flour, water, yeast and salt.

Liguria, the coastal strip running from the French border to Tuscany, is the bread's home region, and Genoa is its commercial center. The basic idea — a flat dough baked with oil and salt — predates the Roman Empire. Focaccia Genovese is the everyday version sold there, relatively thin, salted on top and often brushed with a mix of water and oil before baking.

The dimples are not decorative. Bakers press their fingertips deep into the proofed dough so the depressions hold oil and salt through the bake. The surface stays moist while the base crisps against the pan.

Focaccia di Recco works differently despite the shared name. It contains no yeast. Two paper-thin sheets of unleavened dough are stretched over a filling of soft, tangy stracchino cheese and sealed at the edges. The bread bakes at high heat until the top blisters and browns in patches. Recco, a town east of Genoa along the coast, is where it belongs.

Toppings on the leavened style shift with the season and the baker. Cherry tomatoes, pitted olives, thinly sliced onion and sprigs of rosemary all turn up pressed into the surface. In Liguria the bread is eaten plain as a mid-morning snack, dunked in cappuccino in Genoa, served alongside antipasti or split open for sandwiches.

The fermentation shows in the crumb. A well-made focaccia carries large, uneven bubbles from a slow rise, often an overnight rest in the refrigerator, and reads as moist rather than greasy. Bakeries across Europe and North America now sell versions seasoned with sun-dried tomatoes or flaky sea salt. The Ligurian method still sets the standard for how much oil a dough can absorb and still bake well.

The baguette is a long, thin French loaf with a brittle crust and an open, chewy interior. In France, the term "baguette de tradition française" is defined by law. That designation requires the loaf to be mixed, shaped and baked on the premises, never frozen, and made from nothing but flour, water, salt and yeast or leaven.

An ordinary supermarket baguette falls outside that definition. It can be baked from frozen dough or made with additives permitted in standard bread, which is why bakery counters list the two separately.

The shape most people picture — roughly 26 inches long and a few inches across — settled into place in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Labor rules that barred bakers from working before 4 a.m. played a part. A slender loaf proofed and baked faster than a thick round country loaf, which let bakers get bread on the shelf by the morning rush.

A well-made baguette crackles when squeezed and reveals a crumb full of irregular holes. Those pockets come from a slow fermentation that lets gas form unevenly through the dough. The interior should smell faintly of wheat and carry a mild tang rather than a pronounced sourness.

Paris holds an annual contest, the Grand Prix de la Baguette, with judges scoring entries on baking, crumb, aroma, taste and appearance. Entries must be baguettes de tradition française, and the competition sets limits on length and weight. The winning baker supplies bread to the Élysée Palace, the French presidential residence, for the following year.

Freshness is the loaf's weak point. With almost no fat and a thin crust, a baguette dries out within hours of leaving the oven. French bakeries bake in batches through the day for that reason. A second trip to the counter before dinner is routine in households that eat bread at every meal.

Day-old baguette rarely goes to waste. It becomes croutons, bread pudding or the sliced base for tartines spread with butter and jam at breakfast. The short shelf life follows from the ingredient list rather than any failure in the baking.

Naan is a leavened flatbread baked against the inner wall of a clay tandoor, where extreme heat produces charred blisters and a soft, pillowy chew. It is a daily staple across India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and parts of Central Asia, and preparation shifts from region to region.

The dough usually includes yogurt or milk alongside flour, water and yeast. That dairy content makes naan tender rather than brittle, and it adds a faint tang that plain flatbread dough lacks. Bakers shape the dough by hand into a teardrop or an oval rather than a perfect circle, which is why the finished bread often has one tapered end.

Cooking is fast. Tandoor temperatures can exceed 900 degrees Fahrenheit, and a naan slapped onto the clay wall is done in under two minutes. The dough clings to the hot surface, puffs as its moisture turns to steam, and picks up dark spots where it touches the clay directly. A long metal hook or skewer lifts it off.

The plain version is the baseline, but the variations show regional preference. Garlic naan is brushed with garlic butter once it leaves the oven. Peshawari naan is stuffed with a sweet mixture of nuts and dried fruit before baking. Butter naan gets an additional coat of ghee or butter for richness.

Home kitchens rarely have a tandoor, so cooks substitute a very hot cast-iron skillet or a preheated pizza stone. Those methods get close, though the radiant heat thrown off by clay walls is hard to match on a stovetop. The bread is meant to be torn by hand and used to pick up curries, dals and other sauced dishes rather than eaten on its own.

Naan now appears on menus far outside South and Central Asia, and the word often gets applied loosely to any Indian-style flatbread. The term specifically describes a leavened, oven-baked bread. That distinguishes it from roti and chapati, which are unleavened and cooked on a flat griddle rather than inside a tandoor.

Pita is a round, lightly leavened flatbread that inflates in the oven and leaves behind a hollow center. That pocket is what makes it the standard vessel for falafel, shawarma and grilled meats. It is eaten daily across the Levant, Greece, Turkey and North Africa, and each region bakes its own version.

Steam does the work. A thin disc of dough meets a very hot oven floor. The water inside turns to vapor almost at once, and the bread balloons before settling back as it cools. The split left in the middle becomes the pocket. High heat is essential, usually above 475 degrees Fahrenheit, along with dough rolled thin and evenly.

Not every pita is built to open. Greek pita runs thicker and softer, folded around gyro meat or souvlaki rather than split and stuffed. Lebanese and Syrian styles are rolled thinner and separate more reliably, which suits sandwiches and tearing by hand to scoop hummus or labneh. In Arabic the bread is usually called khubz, a general word for bread rather than a term for the pocketed version alone.

Leavening varies by tradition. Some pita is made with yeast, which yields a softer crumb and a faint tang. Other versions use little or no leavening, turning denser and closer to a cracker if the bake runs long. Each reflects local practice rather than a single standard recipe.

Stale pita rarely goes to waste. Torn and toasted or fried, it forms the base of Lebanese fattoush salad and of fattah dishes across the Levant, where crisp pieces sit beneath yogurt, chickpeas or meat.

Supermarket pita sold far from the Eastern Mediterranean often fails to pocket at all. Industrial lines run cooler ovens and thicker dough, producing a flat, foldable bread rather than a hollow one. A fresh round from a bakery behaves differently, as does one baked at home on a preheated stone or steel. It stays pliable and holds a wet filling without splitting down the side, and the crumb keeps a soft chew instead of drying into something that cracks when bent.

Injera is a large, spongy flatbread made from teff flour and soured through several days of fermentation. In Ethiopia and Eritrea it works as plate, utensil and staple at once. Stews are ladled straight onto its surface, and diners tear off pieces to scoop up the food.

Teff is a tiny gluten-free grain native to the Horn of Africa. Its seeds are small enough that the whole grain gets milled together, which keeps the bran and germ in the flour. The ground teff is mixed with water and left to ferment, drawing on wild yeasts and bacteria in the grain and the air rather than a maintained culture. The rest takes several days and produces a pronounced sour note. That acidity balances the heat and richness of the dishes served on top.

Fermentation also shapes the texture. Gas released during the long rest creates small, evenly spaced holes across the bread's surface. Cooks call them eyes. They catch sauce and show that the batter soured properly before it reached the griddle.

Injera cooks on a wide, flat griddle called a mitad, traditionally made of clay. The thin batter is poured in a spiral, starting at the outer edge and working inward. A lid goes on so steam sets the top. The bread is never browned, flipped or crisped, which leaves one side smooth and the other pitted.

A full meal arranges several wats, or stews, across a single round of injera. Those stews are built from lentils, split peas, greens or meat. Extra injera arrives rolled at the side for scooping.

Teff grows best in East Africa's highland conditions, so injera made elsewhere is often cut with wheat or barley flour. That substitution softens both the sourness and the sponge. Ethiopian and Eritrean kitchens abroad have kept the method largely unchanged, and injera remains one of the few breads that anchors a meal rather than accompanying it.

A bagel is a dense, chewy ring of bread that gets boiled before it ever reaches the oven. That brief bath in hot water gelatinizes the starch on the dough's surface, which produces the glossy, taut skin and the pull that separates a bagel from an ordinary roll.

The bread took shape among Jewish communities in Poland, where it was being made as early as the 17th century, and the name comes from the Yiddish beygl. Immigrants carried the practice to the U.S. in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and New York City became the place most associated with it. The city's water is often credited for the result, though the boiling step and the use of high-gluten flour likely matter more.

Bagel dough is stiffer and lower in hydration than most bread doughs. Less water means less steam and less oven spring, so the crumb stays tight and heavy instead of opening up. The hole is not decorative — it adds surface area and helps the dense ring cook through evenly. After roughly a minute of boiling per side, the rings go into a hot oven and bake until deeply browned. Many are rolled through sesame seeds, poppy seeds, coarse salt or an everything blend first.

Montreal-style bagels follow a different path. The water is sweetened with honey, and the baking happens in a wood-fired oven. The result is sweeter, thinner and denser than the New York version. People from either city tend to treat the two as separate foods rather than regional variants of the same bread.

Most bagels are halved, toasted and served with cream cheese, lox or sandwich fillings. Industrial production has introduced softer versions that shorten the boil or skip it altogether, which speeds output but gives up the chew. Bakers working in the older method treat that as a different product, since the boil is the step that defines the bread.

A German pretzel gets its deep mahogany sheen and its particular flavor from a dip in an alkaline solution before baking, not from the oven alone. Bakers use food-grade lye, sodium hydroxide dissolved in water, which reacts with the dough's surface in the oven and delivers a color and taste plain water cannot.

The Laugenbrezel is the standard version sold across German bakeries. The name comes from Lauge, the German word for the alkaline bath itself. It is eaten plain, split lengthwise and spread with butter, or served next to mustard and sausage. Bavaria holds the strongest claim to the tradition, and the bread turns up constantly at beer gardens and at Oktoberfest.

Where the knot shape came from is not settled. One common account credits medieval monks who folded strips of dough to suggest arms crossed in prayer, but that story has never been confirmed. Better documented is the pretzel's long presence in southern Germany and in Alsace, where bakers have made versions of it for centuries.

Size and bake time change the result considerably. A fresh bakery pretzel has a chewy, slightly dense interior and a crust firm enough to resist the first bite. The soft pretzels sold at stadiums and mall kiosks tend toward a fluffier, milder product. Large operations usually swap in a baking soda solution, since lye is caustic and demands careful handling at volume.

Coarse salt is the usual topping, and the crystals are large enough to brush off for anyone who wants less. Sweet versions circulate too, particularly in the U.S., where cinnamon-sugar pretzels are sold at bakeries and amusement parks.

The hard pretzel sitting in American grocery aisles is a separate food with a separate history. It is baked far longer and dried out to stay shelf-stable, built for months in a cupboard rather than for eating warm. The soft bakery version depends on freshness in a way the packaged snack never does.

Ciabatta is an Italian white bread with an open, irregular crumb and a thin, flour-dusted crust, and it dates only to 1982. Baker Arnaldo Cavallari developed it that year in Adria, in the Veneto region, as an Italian answer to the French baguette's commercial reach.

The dough is unusually wet, with hydration often above 70% of the flour's weight. That water content makes conventional kneading impractical. Bakers handle the slack mass with floured hands, scrapers or a mixer. Rather than working it into a tight ball, they fold it at intervals during the rise to build strength.

All that water is what builds the crumb. Steam escapes unevenly through the loose gluten structure during the bake, leaving pockets that range from pinhole size to large enough to see through a slice. A tight, uniform interior usually points to a dough that was too dry or handled too much. The loaves are cut from a single slab and dusted with flour rather than rounded and scored, which is why no two come out quite alike. The name describes the result: ciabatta means slipper in Italian, a nod to the flat, elongated shape the loaf takes in the oven.

Sandwich makers favor ciabatta for structural reasons. The crust holds up to wet fillings without turning to paste. The porous interior soaks up olive oil, vinegar or pan juices and still keeps its shape under pressure from a grill press. It also arrives at Italian tables in place of a dinner roll, torn and dipped in oil.

Ciabatta moved quickly for a bread invented in the 1980s. It spread across Italy, then into bakeries worldwide, and now appears in versions enriched with olive oil, scattered with herbs or made with whole wheat flour. What stays constant is the high-hydration dough and the airy, uneven crumb that separates it from dense Italian loaves such as pane di Altamura.

Sourdough rises on wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria living in a flour-and-water starter, with no commercial yeast involved. That slow fermentation produces the bread's acidity, its chewy crumb and a shelf life longer than most loaves leavened with packaged yeast.

A starter is a maintained culture rather than an ingredient bought off a shelf. Flour and water are combined, left to attract microbes from the grain and the surrounding air, then fed on a schedule to keep the population active. Establishing one from scratch usually takes days or weeks. Bakers who keep a culture going for years are common, and some starters are handed down within a family or a single bakery.

San Francisco carries the strongest sourdough association in the U.S. A wild yeast strain found widely in the city's bakeries was identified and named Fructilactobacillus sanfranciscensis after it. The technique itself is far older and far more dispersed. Rye sourdoughs form the backbone of traditional baking across Germany, Poland and Scandinavia, where rye's low gluten content makes acidic fermentation necessary for a workable loaf.

Before commercial yeast arrived in the 19th century, nearly all leavened bread in Europe depended on some version of this process. What changed was not the method but the convenience of the alternative.

The bacteria in a starter generate both lactic and acetic acid, and the balance between them shapes the flavor. Cooler, stiffer, slower fermentations push the dough toward a sharper edge. Warmer, wetter ones stay milder and closer to yogurt than vinegar.

The finished loaf tends to have a thick crust, scored with a blade before baking so the bread expands along a controlled line rather than splitting at random. Crumb structure shifts with hydration and timing. Wetter dough and longer fermentation open the interior. A shorter-fermented loaf stays denser.

Home sourdough baking surged in 2020, when people stuck indoors took up starter feeding as a daily routine. The learning curve is steeper than that of most yeasted bread. Judging when a starter has peaked, timing the bulk rise and scoring a wet dough cleanly all take repetition.

Brioche is a French bread enriched with eggs and a large proportion of butter, which gives it a tender, cake-like crumb and a deep golden color. It sits closer to pastry than to everyday bread in both composition and use.

The butter can account for as much as half the weight of the flour, and the dough also carries several eggs. That richness makes the finished bread soft, but it complicates the mixing. Bakers add the butter gradually and keep it cool so it stays emulsified into the dough rather than greasing it. A long, cold fermentation, often overnight in the refrigerator, firms the dough enough to shape. It deepens the flavor at the same time.

Several traditional shapes exist. Brioche à tête is baked in a fluted mold, with a small ball of dough set on a larger base, producing the topknot that gives the form its name. Brioche Nanterre is built from balls of dough lined up in a rectangular pan, which bake together into a pull-apart loaf. Sliced brioche is a standard base for French toast and bread pudding, since the crumb soaks up custard without disintegrating.

Brioche has been part of French baking since at least the 15th century, and it carries cultural weight beyond the bakery. The phrase usually rendered in English as "let them eat cake" referred to brioche in the original French. It is routinely attributed to Marie Antoinette, though no historical evidence shows she said it.

Contemporary bakeries and restaurants have pushed the dough into new uses. Brioche buns are a common choice for burgers, where the faint sweetness and soft texture work against salt and fat. Brioche feuilletée laminates sheets of butter into the dough for a flakier, layered result. The high butter and egg content shortens the bread's life. Brioche is best eaten within a couple of days of baking.

#72. Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “superfakes,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.

Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.

Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link.

“Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.

The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass.

“The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.”

This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.

The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.

The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.

Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.

Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon.

#74. Prism Data Tecnologies Raises $20M in Series A Funding

Prism Data Tecnologies, a New York City-based developer of cash flow analytics and automated credit risk underwriting software, raised $20m in Series A funding.

The round, which brought total capitalization to over $25m, was led by Story Ventures, with participation from FINTOP Capital, Core Innovation Capital (Core VC), Obvious Ventures, 1st & Main Growth Partners, and Mana Ventures.

The company intends to use the funds to accelerate its next phase of enterprise platform growth, expand its computational data infrastructure, invest in its newly launched REFRACT™ artificial intelligence engine, and scale its commercial implementation teams to support mainstream bank deployments.

Led by CEO Jason Rosen, Prism Data provides open-banking transaction analytics software that develops proprietary risk scoring infrastructure—specifically its flagship CashScore® model—to analyze real-time consumer bank statements and generate explainable creditworthiness metrics for regulated lenders.

The startup has scaled its system to achieve a 100x increase in monthly API transaction volume over the past two years, serving six of the top ten digital banks and three of the five largest fintech lenders in the United States, while powering consumer credit approval integrations for financial data distributors like Equifax, Plaid, LexisNexis, and Synchrony Financial.

#75. Etzioni on AI: The colorful and cranky language of the AI era, from slop to slap

by Oren Etzioni & Daniel S. Weld on Oct 16, 2026 at 1:01 pmOctober 17, 2026 at 8:20 am

We’ve all encountered the phrase AI slop, but what’s an AI slap? A meat proxy? Chatfishing? Or agentsomnia? Following up on my glossary of AI, which demystified AI jargon, Prof. Dan Weld is joining me to shine a light on the nontechnical lingo of the AI era. We also sneak in a few phrases that should exist to capture the AI zeitgeist, circa 2026.

We introduce more than 35 phrases, so we’ve divided them into sections to keep the broligarchy from crowding enshittification.

“Digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence,” which is how Merriam-Webster defined slop, its 2025 word of the year. Shrimp Jesus is the specimen, Christ fused with crustaceans, posted to Facebook by the thousands.

AI cream is our name for the rare opposite, superb writing authored with the help of AI. We hope that over time the cream will rise to the top and the slop will sink.

Until that happens, we have the meat proxy, “a person who forwards AI-generated text, code, or other output without reading, understanding, or validating it.” We call the action of sending AI-generated text blindly an AI slap. It stings.

Your AI Slop Bores Me is a website where you type a prompt and a randomly chosen human answers it while pretending to be a chatbot. Fifty million views in a week, which tells you how badly people wanted to say something back.

AI suspicion is our name for the nagging feeling that what you’re reading was AI generated. You could also call it Turing tingle or AI-dar.

AI shaming is the accusation that follows, attacking someone’s work by insinuating a machine wrote it. The paper that named it is subtitled “Birth of a Classist Slur in Knowledge Work,” and it argues that the accusations fall hardest on racial minorities and on writers whose first language isn’t English.

See also: tasteslop, workslop, slopaganda.

A video or recording altered by machine learning so that a real person appears to say or do something they never said or did. Named in late 2017 for the Reddit user who called himself deepfakes. The word we all use for AI deception descends from one anonymous pornographer’s handle.

The liar’s dividend is the payoff a real wrongdoer collects once any authentic recording can be waved off as a fake. The damage isn’t the fake video. It’s that real video stops counting.

Counterfeit people was Daniel Dennett’s last argument, that machines able to pass as human are “the most dangerous artifacts in human history, capable of destroying not just economies but human freedom itself.” He wanted them outlawed and watermarked like banknotes.

Tilly Norwood is one of them, an AI actress unveiled at the Zurich Film Festival in September 2025. Her makers said talent agents wanted to sign her. Emily Blunt, shown a picture, said “Good Lord, we’re screwed” and told the agencies to stop.

Most of the damage doesn’t need AI at all. A cheapfake is manipulation made with cheap software or none at all. Chatfishing is using AI to write your messages on a dating app, where the con used to be a fake photo and is now a rented personality.

A name for the Silicon Valley billionaires and venture capitalists who think democracy is finished and want corporate rule in its place. Gil Durán’s book, subtitled Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, traces the idea to a 1997 book, The Sovereign Individual, and to Peter Thiel’s circle, which Durán says believes “technology means democracy is an obsolete software system.”

Durán didn’t coin the phrase. Someone in the crypto world told him they’d been using it for years.

Durán’s target is the broligarchy, “a small group of extremely wealthy men, particularly those in technology, who wield significant political and economic power.” The word sat on Twitter from 2009 and went nowhere until Carole Cadwalladr wrote about “a new super-class of broligarchs” in July 2024.

The mental deterioration that comes from consuming too much junk online, chosen by Oxford University Press as its 2024 word of the year. Thoreau got there first, in Walden in 1854, complaining that England was busy curing the potato-rot while nobody was curing the brain-rot.

Dead internet theory is the supply side, “a theory that a lot of the internet is no longer created by real people but rather by bots and other AI tools.” It started as a forum post in January 2021 and is quietly turning into a description.

Enshittification is Cory Doctorow’s three-stage decay: “first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves.”

AI fatigue is what’s left over, “the exhaustion or the sense of being overwhelmed by the rapid proliferation and constant engagement with artificial intelligence technologies.” The phrase has been drifting through the trade press since 2023 with no author attached; the definition above comes from Route Fifty, a trade publication for state and local government.

Andrej Karpathy’s February 2025 coinage, crowned Collins Dictionary’s word of the year for 2025, is “fully giving in to the vibes, embrac[ing] exponentials, and forget[ting] that the code even exists”—accepting whatever diff the AI hands you without reading it.

Promptatory is our word, styled on “purgatory,” for the state of being trapped in an unending edit-and-re-prompt loop with an AI system. You fix the bug the AI introduced, and in fixing it, the AI introduces two more, each smaller and more absurd than the last. Progress is hard earned: you close in on “done” like the runner in Zeno’s paradox, forever eating the remaining distance in half. Promptatory is vibe coding’s hangover: the vibe wears off, and the rereading begins.

A related condition we dub agentsomnia is the chronic inability to rest or disconnect from work, driven by the haunting feeling that your autonomous software or AI agents are stalled without your feedback. The Wall Street Journal calls it agent FOMO.

An OpenAI rallying cry. AGI is the point where a machine can do any intellectual task a person can, and the phrase became a general exclamation for the moment a model does something that rearranges your sense of what’s coming. Ilya Sutskever used it inside the company and posted it publicly in 2022. It works as celebration and as diagnosis.

P(doom) runs in the other direction: “your personal probability that AI ends the world, stated as a number so the vibe feels like math.” It started as shorthand among a small online community in 2022 and now gets asked at dinner parties.

Talk that outruns the technology comes in other flavors too.

Bragawatts, a unit of measurement for boasting, is “the practice of AI companies boasting about very large projects to create excitement and attract investment, even though many of these projects are never completed,” as Britain’s Cambridge Dictionary put it in January 2026.

Vibe revenue does the same thing to the income statement, “money or funding that an AI company is given because people are excited about the potential of AI, rather than because the company’s products are already successful.”

A one-sided relationship with someone who doesn’t know you exist. Donald Horton and Richard Wohl coined it in 1956 about television viewers, and Britain’s Cambridge Dictionary made it the 2025 word of the year, citing celebrities, influencers, and chatbots. A seventy-year-old term about Ed Sullivan turns out to describe your relationship with ChatGPT.

AI addiction is what happens when the one-sided relationship takes over. A 2026 study sorted it into three kinds: escapist roleplay, where people come to prefer the world the chatbot builds; pseudosocial companionship, where it replaces the relationships; and the epistemic rabbit hole, compulsive question-asking that crowds out everything else.

The researchers blame the design and call the chatbot an AI genie, a thing that gives you exactly anything you want with minimal effort.

AI psychosis is the far end, “a phenomenon wherein individuals reportedly develop or experience worsening psychosis, such as paranoia and delusions, in connection with their use of chatbots.” The Danish psychiatrist Søren Dinesen Østergaard suggested the term in a 2023 editorial in the journal Schizophrenia Bulletin. It isn’t a recognized clinical diagnosis, and we should say so.

Nearly every phrase above names a problem. Slop, shaming, deepfakes, brain rot, psychosis: what the AI era has added to English so far is a vocabulary of complaint. There’s still no common word for AI doing something well. We’ve offered AI cream. If you have a candidate for a phrase we’re missing, please send it to us.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#77. HelloNation Article Explains Roof Inspection Importance With Insights From Roofing Expert Seth Brown

The article outlines how annual inspections help prevent damage and extend the life of a residential roof in the Greater Richmond area.

ASHLAND, Va., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What role does a roof inspection play in protecting a home from long-term damage? HelloNation has published an article providing clear guidance for homeowners in the Greater Richmond area.

The article features insights from Roofing Expert Seth Brown of BNH Roofing and explains why routine roof inspections are essential for maintaining a residential roof. According to a HelloNation article, most homes in Greater Richmond receive at least one roof inspection each year. Regular evaluations help identify small issues early, reducing the likelihood of costly roof repair and preventing long-term structural problems.

The article features insights from Roofing Expert Seth Brown of BNH Roofing and explains why routine roof inspections are essential for maintaining a residential roof. According to a HelloNation article, most homes in Greater Richmond receive at least one roof inspection each year. Regular evaluations help identify small issues early, reducing the likelihood of costly roof repair and preventing long-term structural problems.

The article explains that seasonal weather patterns in Greater Richmond can put a residential roof under stress. Heavy rains, temperature shifts, and winter freezes can weaken shingles and other roofing materials over time. A consistent roof inspection schedule allows homeowners to monitor these effects and take action before minor wear develops into significant damage.

Storm activity is another major concern addressed in the article. Wind, hail, and debris can cause storm damage that is not always visible from the ground. The article notes that a prompt roof inspection after severe weather is critical for detecting hidden issues. Even small areas of damage to shingles or flashing can lead to leaks if left untreated, increasing the need for more extensive roof repair later.

The HelloNation article also details what homeowners can expect during a professional roof inspection. A qualified roofing contractor will assess shingles for signs of wear or displacement, check for water damage, and inspect vulnerable areas such as vents, chimneys, and flashing. The article emphasizes that proper home maintenance includes clearing debris and ensuring gutters remain functional, as clogged drainage systems can contribute to roof deterioration.

In addition, the article highlights that homeowners often underestimate the importance of routine roof inspection services. A residential roof may appear to be in good condition, but underlying issues can go unnoticed without a trained evaluation. A roofing contractor in Greater Richmond can identify subtle warning signs that, if ignored, may lead to expensive roof repairs.

Timing is another key factor discussed in the article. Annual roof inspection appointments should be scheduled during dry periods to allow for a thorough review. The article also recommends scheduling an inspection within a few days of a storm to assess damage quickly. Acting early helps prevent moisture intrusion and protect the home's structural integrity.

The article further explains that consistent home maintenance, including regular roof inspections, can extend a residential roof's lifespan by several years. By addressing issues with shingles and other materials early, homeowners reduce the likelihood of emergency repairs and maintain their property's overall value. This proactive approach is especially important in Greater Richmond, where weather conditions can accelerate roof wear.

BNH Builders and Roofing's Roofing Expert perspective reinforces the importance of staying ahead of potential problems through routine care. The HelloNation article presents roof inspection as a fundamental part of responsible home maintenance, helping homeowners avoid unnecessary costs and preserve their roofing system's performance.

In conclusion, the article emphasizes that combining annual roof inspections with post-storm evaluations provides the best protection against storm damage and unexpected roof repairs. #78. Exclusive: Stella & Dot Founder Raises $5M For Her Next Act, AI Marketing Startup Marklo

Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot, a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers.

Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.

Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders.

Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks.

While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away, Clare V., Monica + Andy, Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers.

The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support.

To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems.

Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive, Meta and Google, then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign.

Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run.

From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email.

Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it.

“Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking.

In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before.

Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin.

In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models.

As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free.

“I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.”

The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future.

That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said.

“For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News.

When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores.

She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.”

Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo.

She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again.

“As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said.

She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign.

“The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said.

For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot.

She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com, but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability.

“Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?”

With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience.

“Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.”

Kirsten Green, founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo.

“Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added.

While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations.

The opportunity comes as AI is taking a larger share of investment in the broader sales and marketing sector. Startups in sales, marketing and customer relationship management raised $7.5 billion across 830 rounds globally this year through mid-September, with most of that investment going to companies in Crunchbase’s AI-related categories. Funding is on pace to finish below 2025’s $11.1 billion, while deal volume could fall for a fourth straight year — a sign that investors are concentrating their bets in fewer companies.

“It’s one thing to collect the information; it’s another thing to understand how to present it and how to recommend an action against it,” Green added.

The investor also pointed to Marklo’s ability to serve businesses at different stages, noting that coordination becomes more complex and information harder to share as brands grow. As such, the prospect of software that can grow alongside its customers was another draw.

Green said she also valued Herrin’s decision to develop Marklo alongside brands already using it, giving the company customer feedback before its broader launch.

“I like the fact that she built this product while it was being used,” she said.

#79. MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash model, says it cuts AI agent costs by 70%

Chinese artificial intelligence developer MiniMax Group Inc. today released M3.1 Flash, a faster and cheaper update to the M3 large language model it launched in June.

The release takes aim at the cost of running AI agents, which often need dozens of model calls to finish a single job. MiniMax said Flash represents its “ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability.” Agentic tasks cost 70% less to run than on its previous model, the company said, and inference is close to three times as fast, with output at everyday peak topping 200 tokens per second.

Size has barely changed from M3. MiniMax’s developer guide for the preview release lists 428 billion parameters in all, and the launch post credits the extra speed to more aggressive sparsity at inference time. Reasoning stays on for every request, with developers choosing one of five effort levels from Low to Max. The model accepts text, image and video input, and prompts can run to 1 million tokens.

In MiniMax’s own testing, M3.1 Flash scored 61.7 on OSWorld V2, which tests how well a model can operate a computer, and the company said no Chinese model has done better. BankerToolBench, a banking workflow test, gave it 76.2.

For security work, MiniMax pointed to an 82% score on CyberGym. University of California at Berkeley researchers built that benchmark to test whether AI agents can reproduce real software vulnerabilities, and the company listed code auditing, penetration testing and malware analysis among the jobs M3.1 Flash can take on.

At a flat 15 cents per million input tokens, M3.1 Flash lines up directly against the V4.1-Flash model from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd., which charges the same rate off-peak. DeepSeek said over the weekend that its updated V4.1-Flash resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering test. M3.1 Flash managed 73.7%, and neither result has been checked independently.

MiniMax, which has traded in Hong Kong since a $619 million initial public offering in January, saw its shares fall after the original V4.1-Flash launched in September, Bloomberg reported.

The launch also settles who was behind Space Bunny, an anonymous model that turned up on OpenRouter Inc.’s model routing service in late September. Community testers soon linked it to MiniMax by probing its tokenizer, and the company confirmed today that Space Bunny was an early M3.1 Flash build. More than 200 trillion tokens went through it while its maker stayed unnamed, according to the launch post.

M3.1 Flash is available now through the MiniMax API, the company’s M Plan subscription and its MiniMax Code desktop app. Output costs 60 cents per million tokens and cached input 1.5 cents. The company said it will release the Flash weights later, and a more capable Pro model is also coming.

#80. Morgan Stanley’s favorite AI stock is 92% exposed to the $1.6 trillion build-out it’s bullish on

By Morgan Stanley’s count, 91.7% of Nvidia’s 2027 revenue is exposed to one thing: AI infrastructure demand. No company on the bank’s list scores higher. Not Vertiv, at 90%. Not Broadcom, at 81%.

The same report, published Oct. 15, calls Nvidia the best risk/reward in the sector.

The bull case for the world’s most valuable company and the bull case for the build-out are now essentially the same case, and Morgan Stanley’s North America Insight, led by Nicholas Lentini, makes both. The note, titled Following AI’s $1.6 Trillion Money Trail: Mapping the Revenue Generated by the Capex Boom, includes a section that runs under the heading “We Are Bullish This Spend.” The 65-page note also spends a good part of its length explaining how the spending could break.

Nvidia’s defenders would say that exposure describes the company. Its data center business has supplied the large majority of its revenue for years, but the report adds a closer look on how few buyers that exposure runs through.

The firm estimates hyperscalers and AI cloud providers will spend $1.58 trillion in 2027, up roughly 60% from about $980 billion this year, and will spend $1.8 trillion in 2028. About $195 billion of the 2027 figure is data center leases, which never show up as capital spending on a cash flow statement. The report calls leases “synthetic capex.” Hyperscalers have disclosed more than $1.1 trillion in lease commitments that haven’t started yet.

About $1 trillion of the 2027 spending lands as S&P 500 revenue, by Morgan Stanley’s estimate. Nearly $700 billion of it goes to Nvidia. Revenue from hyperscaler and neocloud customers makes up 5% of total S&P 500 revenue in 2027 but drives about 25% of the index’s revenue growth.

Nvidia’s own customer list is even narrower. In the bank’s model, SpaceX and Amazon Web Services together account for about 54% of Nvidia’s hyperscaler revenue in 2027 and 72% of its growth.

Morgan Stanley’s argument is that Nvidia is cheap for what it is. The stock trades at 15 times fiscal 2028 earnings, and the bank says multiple expansion “is also not required for the stock to work as numbers continue to go higher.” It expects the spending to earn 25% to 50% on invested capital. It also argues Wall Street has underestimated compute cycles by 38%, on average, based on four past cycles: PCs, the internet, mobile, and cloud.

The bank even says its own Nvidia numbers may be low. It calls its SpaceX and Amazon estimates conservative, creating “a low bar for remaining hyperscalers.” Its model has Nvidia’s share of the other hyperscalers’ spending slipping from 18% in 2026 to 16% in 2027. Nvidia expects to gain share.

Other parts of the company have sounded less certain. In March, Morgan Stanley’s global investment committee said the bull market “rests, more than anything, on the durability of AI capital expenditures.”

The report’s risk section reads like a list of everything the 91.7% depends on.

Money comes first. Morgan Stanley expects 2027 to bring the largest cash flow deficit of its forecast period, and with it more debt. Hyperscalers have already sold about $255 billion of unsecured bonds this year, roughly 30% of estimated 2026 spending. In what the bank calls a theoretical exercise, it models the cost of borrowing more. Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft, rated AA or higher, see combined interest coverage fall from about 31x to 12x. Oracle and SpaceX fall from 4x to 1.8x.

Some of the spending growth is inflation. A meaningful part of recent capex increases reflects higher component prices, according to the report. It cites Amazon’s finance chief attributing most of an increase in Amazon’s spending plan, from $200 billion to about $220 billion, to rising memory costs, with no change to the build plan.

Then there’s power. The $1.6 trillion assumes every chip ordered gets switched on. Morgan Stanley’s own power model projects a 32-gigawatt U.S. shortfall for data centers through 2028, about one-third of the 97 gigawatts needed. The report notes that hyperscalers can keep buying scarce GPUs ahead of power, which would hold up chip revenue for a while and “could produce hoarding and stranded inventory.”

“But buying power-dependent equipment that cannot be turned on is hard to sustain,” it says.

Politics is last. The firm calls data center restrictions a wedge issue in the midterms. It doesn’t expect a federal pause, but it sees tax breaks as “the consensus target regardless of who wins.”

Morgan Stanley’s downside case is a timing problem. If spending plateaus, it argues, volumes can hold up while prices fall, and suppliers’ margins disappear first. The bank points to the late-2022 memory downturn, when NAND shipments fell only about 5% while prices fell 20% to 30%.

The bank argues Nvidia would be spared the worst. In a pause, it writes, “we’re likely to see the most disruption at the tail of the bullwhip,” in memory, optics, and other small-dollar parts most likely to be over-ordered.

By the report’s own map, Nvidia sits at the other end of the whip as the single largest supplier in the chain.

The same report that says Wall Street underestimates compute cycles by 38% also says Wall Street “is underprepared for the depth of cuts to the downside.” The risk of volume and price falling together, it says, is underappreciated.

“It’s the standard capital-cycle playbook,” the report says, “just compressed by how concentrated the hyperscaler customer base is.”

#81. When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
