Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.

Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.

Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.

“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”

The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.

Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.

“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.

Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million.

Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.

#83. From mole to birria: Mexico's best-rated dishes on TasteAtlas

Free daily briefing on global business news.

TasteAtlas users consistently rank these 10 Mexican dishes among the country's most beloved, from mole to birria

TasteAtlas is a crowd-rated food encyclopedia rather than a panel of judges, and its Mexican rankings should be read that way. Entries are scored by diners worldwide, so the dishes that rise highest tend to be the ones that travel well. They are plates that make sense to someone who did not grow up eating them. Mexican cuisine joined UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. The best-rated Mexican dishes on the site reflect much of what earned it that recognition: specific technique, strong regional identity and a history documented over centuries.

Ranking Mexican food runs into the problem of range. A mole negro from Oaxaca and a cochinita pibil from the Yucatan Peninsula share almost no ingredients, no cooking method and no common ancestor. A trompo of al pastor turning in Mexico City has little to do with barbacoa pit-cooked in Hidalgo beyond the tortilla it lands on. Each region built its kitchen around what grew, grazed or swam nearby. Outside technique arrived later — Spanish pork and dairy layered onto Indigenous corn traditions that predate contact by thousands of years. Al pastor adds one more layer: a vertical spit brought to central Mexico by Lebanese immigrants in the early 20th century.

The 10 dishes below sit near the top of Mexico's entries on TasteAtlas and in most serious conversations about the country's cooking. Treat the order as a guide rather than a scoreboard. Crowd ratings shift as new reviews come in, and a dish's exact position in a given month matters less than the fact that it keeps appearing. Several entries are meats cooked slowly enough to occupy most of a day. Two are chile sauces assembled from 20 or more ingredients. Several are corn, handled in ways a plain flour tortilla never suggests. Each entry stands on its own, naming the region it comes from, how it is built and where to order it. Travelers $TRV, menu planners and anyone arguing about what to eat next will find the familiar and the overlooked side by side.

Mole poblano is the dish most often held up as Mexico's culinary showpiece, and it ranks near the top of the Mexican entries on TasteAtlas. The sauce blends dried chiles — usually ancho, mulato and pasilla — with nuts, seeds, spices and a small amount of chocolate, simmered slowly until it turns dark, thick and glossy.

Puebla claims the dish, and the familiar origin story sets it in a convent kitchen in the 17th or 18th century. One account credits nuns at the Convent of Santa Rosa with improvising it for a visiting archbishop. The chronology is disputed. Mole comes from the Nahuatl word for sauce, and cooks were grinding chiles and seeds on metates long before Spanish ingredients reached Mexico, which points to a gradual evolution rather than a single invention.

Chocolate is not in the sauce to sweeten it. Used in small quantity against a dozen or more chiles, it softens bitterness and binds the separate elements into one flavor. A full version can run to 20 ingredients or more, with each chile toasted, each nut and seed fried, and everything ground and then cooked down in stages. Many households keep a recipe that has passed through several generations with small edits along the way.

The standard service is over turkey or chicken with rice alongside, usually for significant occasions: weddings, baptisms, Día de Muertos, Independence Day. The labor explains the timing. Cooks commonly start a batch the day before the meal.

Quality varies because the shortcuts are hard to detect before the first bite. Jarred pastes and powdered mixes sold in supermarkets across Mexico produce a flatter, sweeter sauce than one built from whole dried chiles. In Puebla itself, a fonda or a market stall that grinds its own sauce is a more reliable option than a restaurant positioned for visitors.

Tacos al pastor are pork marinated in dried chiles and achiote, stacked on a vertical rotisserie called a trompo, and shaved onto small corn tortillas as the outer layer crisps. The technique arrived with Lebanese immigrants who settled in Mexico, principally in Puebla, during the first decades of the 20th century and brought the spit-roasting method used for shawarma.

Tacos árabes are the intermediate step, and they are still sold in Puebla today. They come on a flatbread closer to pita than to a tortilla, seasoned lightly rather than with chile. Mexican cooks later traded that flatbread for corn and built a marinade around guajillo and ancho chiles plus achiote, which supplies the orange-red color more than it supplies heat. The name translates roughly as "shepherd style," a nod to the lamb cooked on the Levantine original.

Pineapple is the element cooks disagree about. A whole or halved fruit usually sits at the top of the trompo, and a slice gets flicked onto the taco as the meat is carved. Its acidity cuts the fat of the pork, and bromelain, the enzyme in raw pineapple, breaks down protein, which is why marinades containing it tenderize meat. Plenty of stands leave it out.

The standard build is minimal: two or three ounces of meat on a small tortilla, chopped white onion, cilantro, lime and a salsa of the vendor's own making. A gringa swaps in a flour tortilla with melted cheese.

Mexico City is the dish's best-known home, with taquerias running trompos from early evening past midnight. Turnover is the clearest quality marker. A spit sitting half-finished under a low flame yields leathery meat, while a busy one keeps the exterior rendering and crisping without pause. Tortillas warmed on the plancha to order, rather than held in a steamer for an hour, matter nearly as much as the pork.

Chiles en nogada is a roasted poblano pepper stuffed with picadillo, covered in a cold walnut cream sauce and scattered with pomegranate seeds and parsley. The green chile, white sauce and red seeds match the colors of the Mexican flag. That visual tie binds the dish to national identity more directly than most plates in the Mexican repertoire.

The season is short. Chiles en nogada appears in late August and September, timed to the walnut and pomegranate harvests in Puebla and to Independence Day on September 16. Fresh walnuts, known as nuez de Castilla and peeled of their papery skins by hand, give the nogada its pale color and mild flavor. Dried walnuts darken the sauce and push it toward bitterness, so versions sold outside the harvest window rarely match the original.

The filling carries the dish's history. Picadillo here usually means ground pork, sometimes blended with beef, cooked with apple, pear and peach alongside almonds, raisins and warm spices such as cinnamon and clove. That sweet-savory balance reflects Spanish colonial cooking built on Indigenous ingredients, a pattern that runs through much of central Mexican food. The poblano is charred and peeled before stuffing, and in Puebla it is often served without a batter coating, which keeps the plate lighter than a fried chile relleno.

The best-known origin story credits nuns in Puebla with creating the dish in 1821 to honor Agustín de Iturbide after independence. Documentation is thin, and the account is better understood as folklore that shaped the dish's meaning than as settled history.

Temperature is part of the design. The nogada goes on cold or at room temperature against a warm pepper, and the contrast is deliberate rather than a sign the plate sat too long. Restaurants in Puebla City build limited menus around the dish for a few weeks each year, and the town of San Andrés Calpan, near the slopes of Popocatépetl, holds an annual festival devoted to it. Travelers $TRV who want a faithful version should plan around that window.

Cochinita pibil is pork marinated in achiote and sour orange, wrapped in banana leaves and roasted slowly until it shreds under a fork. It comes from the Yucatan Peninsula, and its name points to its origins: "pib" is the Mayan word for the earth oven the dish was traditionally cooked in.

The technique predates the pig. Mayan cooks buried wrapped meat over hot stones in a pit, sealed it with earth and left it to cook for hours, a method used for game and fowl long before Spanish ships arrived. Pigs came with colonization, and the pib method was applied to a new animal. The order matters: Indigenous technique first, imported meat second.

Achiote does most of the visual work. The paste is made from annatto seeds ground with spices, and it stains the meat the deep brick red that makes cochinita recognizable on sight. It adds an earthy, faintly peppery flavor rather than heat. Sour orange, naranja agria, supplies the acid that tenderizes the pork and cuts the richness.

Most kitchens now use a conventional oven or a slow cooker rather than a pit. The banana leaf is the part that stays. It traps steam, keeps the pork from drying out over a long cook and leaves behind a green, grassy aroma that foil cannot produce.

The standard accompaniment is pickled red onion, sliced thin and steeped in more sour orange or vinegar, served with habanero salsa. Habaneros are native to the Yucatan and give the peninsula's cooking a sharper, more floral heat than the smoky dried chiles common in central Mexico. The pork turns up in tacos, packed into tortas, or plated with rice and black beans.

Merida, the Yucatan's capital, is where the dish is most firmly rooted, sold at market stalls and family-run loncherias through the morning. It appears on menus across the U.S. and Europe, though versions built without achiote paste or a banana leaf wrap lose the two elements that define it.

Birria is a slow-cooked, chile-braised stew from Jalisco, traditionally made with goat and served with its own broth. The dish is centuries older than the cheese-filled taco version that carried its name abroad. The meat cooks until it pulls apart under light pressure, then reaches the table with warm tortillas and a cup of the braising liquid.

Goats arrived in Mexico with Spanish colonizers, and cooks in western Mexico folded them into slow-cooking methods already in use rather than copying European preparations. The marinade starts with dried chiles, usually guajillo and ancho. They are ground with garlic, vinegar, cumin, cloves and cinnamon into a paste that coats the meat before a long braise. One common account traces the name to a Spanish word for something worthless or badly made — a dismissive label for goat meat that the dish outlasted.

The broth matters as much as the meat in the Jalisco version. Known as consomé, it holds the rendered fat and chile sediment from the braise, and it arrives in a cup for sipping or dunking. A plate of birria there is usually meat and broth together, finished at the table with chopped onion, cilantro, dried oregano and lime. Tortillas come on the side.

Beef birria, typically chuck or shank, is now at least as common as goat. Beef costs less, is easier to source and holds its shape better on a griddle. That last point matters for quesabirria — a tortilla dipped in the red fat from the consomé, griddled with cheese and packed with shredded meat. It took shape at taco stands in Tijuana and spread through Los Angeles and the rest of the U.S. during the 2010s.

Guadalajara remains the reference point for the older form. Its birrierias open early and sell out by afternoon, and they treat the stew as weekend and holiday food rather than a late-night order. Asking for birria de chivo there gets a plate much closer to what the name originally described.

Elote is grilled corn on the cob dressed with mayonnaise, crema, crumbled cotija cheese, chile powder and lime, sold from carts and market stalls across Mexico for small change. Esquites is the same idea served loose: kernels cut from the cob, spooned into a cup with the same toppings and eaten on the move.

Corn underpins the entire cuisine. It was domesticated in Mexico from the wild grass teosinte roughly 9,000 years ago and bred steadily since. Elote is the least elaborate use of it: no nixtamalization, no masa, no grinding. A cob is held over coals until the kernels char in spots. The vendor smears and dusts it at the counter while the buyer waits.

Toppings are where regional habit shows. Some vendors reach for bottled hot sauce, others stay with mayonnaise and ground chile alone, and a few finish with chamoy or Tajín. Cotija, named for the Michoacan town where it originated, is the traditional cheese because of how it holds up. It is hard and salty, it does not melt into the mayonnaise, and its salt cuts the richness underneath. Queso fresco is the usual substitute, though it is milder and wetter.

The corn itself matters more than any of that. Mexican field corn tends toward starchy, chewy kernels rather than the sweet varieties favored in the U.S., which is why a well-made elote tastes savory rather than sugary.

Eloteros work neighborhoods in the late afternoon and evening, pushing carts fitted with a steamer or a small grill and announcing themselves with a bell or a shouted call. In Mexico City and Guadalajara, that sound carries the same signal an ice cream truck's jingle does elsewhere.

Cost keeps it everyday food. It is cheap, needs no utensils on the cob and travels in one hand — part of why it ranks alongside dishes that take a full day to cook.

Tamales oaxaqueños differ from the rest of Mexico's tamales in two specific ways: they are steamed in banana leaves rather than corn husks, and the masa is paired with mole negro, the darkest and most labor-intensive of Oaxaca's sauces. The leaf changes both the shape and the result — a wider, flatter, softer tamale with a faint vegetal aroma a dried husk cannot supply.

Tamales are older than the empires usually credited with them. Masa steamed inside a wrapper was eaten in Mesoamerica long before the Mexica or the Maya built their capitals, valued because it kept well, traveled easily and needed no plate. The method changed little over the centuries while fillings split along regional lines, which is why the wrapper still signals where a tamale comes from.

Mole negro sets the Oaxacan version apart. The sauce is built from several dried chiles, including the chilhuacle, along with seeds, nuts, spices, bread or tortilla for body, and a measured amount of chocolate. Cooks char some of the chiles on purpose, and that controlled burn gives the sauce its color and its bitter edge. Masa worked through a sauce that complex turns dense and deeply seasoned, rather than mild with a topping added at the end.

Chicken is the standard protein, pork is common, and vegetarian versions are widely available. Vendors sell them straight from large covered steamers and unwrap them at the counter. They are eaten as often at breakfast as at dinner, frequently with hot chocolate or atole alongside.

The dish sits inside a broader Oaxacan kitchen shaped by Zapotec and Mixtec cooking that remains visible in everyday meals across the state's valleys. Mercado Benito Juárez and Mercado 20 de Noviembre in Oaxaca City both keep tamales oaxaqueños moving through the day. Stalls serving the same mole negro over chicken or rice usually sit a few steps away, so the sauce can be tasted in two forms in one stop.

Pozole rojo is a pork and hominy stew simmered in a broth of rehydrated dried red chiles, usually guajillo and ancho, and it is the version of pozole most often named among Mexico's top-rated dishes. The corn, not the meat, defines it.

Hominy comes from nixtamalization, in which dried field corn is cooked and steeped in an alkaline solution, usually slaked lime. The treatment loosens the hull, shifts the corn's aroma and makes some of its nutrients easier for the body to absorb. Kernels prepared this way swell during the long simmer into large, chewy pieces that split under a spoon. Sweet corn cannot stand in for them.

The stew has pre-Hispanic roots among the Mexica, who served it in a ceremonial context tied to religious observance. Its ingredients and customs changed after the Spanish conquest, and pork became the standard meat.

Three main styles exist. Rojo draws its color and smoky depth from red chiles. Verde, associated with Guerrero, is built on tomatillos, pumpkin seeds and fresh herbs. Blanco, common in Jalisco and Nayarit, leaves the broth unseasoned by chile so the hominy and pork carry it, with heat added at the table. Regional cooks adjust the chile blend and the garnishes, which is why a bowl in Guadalajara and one in Mexico City rarely taste the same.

Assembly happens in front of the diner. Bowls arrive with shredded cabbage or lettuce, sliced radish, diced white onion, dried oregano, lime wedges and crushed chile de arbol set out alongside, plus tostadas to eat between spoonfuls. The raw garnishes supply crunch and acidity the stew lacks on its own.

Pozole belongs to the calendar as much as the kitchen. It turns up on Independence Day tables in September, on Christmas Eve, at christenings and at birthdays, cooked in quantities that assume a crowd. Pork and hominy both need hours to soften, so families start early and let the pot run through the afternoon.

Carnitas is pork simmered slowly in its own fat until it falls apart, then crisped at the end so each portion carries both soft interior meat and browned edges. The dish belongs to Michoacan, where cooks still work over wide copper pots called cazos, holding large cuts in lard for hours.

The method took shape after Spanish settlers brought pigs to the region. Cooking meat in fat and keeping it submerged served a practical purpose before refrigeration, because the fat sealed the pork and extended how long it stayed edible. The flavor outlived the preservation logic, and the technique became a regional specialty rather than a storage trick.

A full traditional preparation draws on several cuts from the same animal. Shoulder and belly do most of the work. Some vendors also fold in skin or offal such as liver, which produces a more varied plate. Many kitchens now stick to shoulder and other lean cuts, a milder version that suits a broader audience but gives up some of the textural range the older style is known for.

Seasoning stays minimal. Salt is the foundation, with orange or a splash of milk sometimes added to the pot. The richness comes from the fat and the length of the cook rather than a spice blend. That is the clearest line between carnitas and cochinita pibil, the Yucatan's slow-roasted pork, which leans on achiote and sour orange for a tangy, brick-red finish. One dish is built on acid and aroma, the other on rendered fat and time.

Once cooked, the meat is chopped or shredded and piled into corn tortillas with white onion, cilantro and salsa verde or salsa roja.

Quiroga, a town in Michoacan, is closely associated with the most traditional version, with cazos set up along its main street and pork sold by weight. Mexico City and Guadalajara have strong carnitas scenes of their own. Many of them trace back to Michoacan families who carried the method with them and kept the copper pot at the center of it.

Enchiladas are corn tortillas dipped in chile sauce, then filled, rolled and topped with more sauce, cheese and garnishes. The name comes from the Spanish verb "enchilar," meaning to season with chile, and the dish descends from a much simpler pre-Hispanic habit of dipping a tortilla in chile sauce and eating it on the spot.

That earlier form had no filling and no roll. Mexica cooks and other Indigenous groups used chile sauce as a seasoning for the tortilla itself. The stuffed, sauced, oven-finished plate now sold across the U.S. and Europe is a later elaboration on that idea.

Regional versions diverge sharply. Enchiladas suizas arrive under a green tomatillo sauce and melted cheese, a style developed in Mexico City in the mid-20th century and named for the dairy-heavy cooking associated with Switzerland rather than for any Swiss origin. Enchiladas potosinas, from San Luis Potosi, take a different route: the chile is worked into the masa before the tortilla is pressed, giving the dough itself a reddish color and some heat. Enchiladas rojas rely on a guajillo-based red sauce. Enchiladas verdes lean on tomatillo and green chile.

Fillings run from shredded chicken to cheese to beans. In parts of Oaxaca and Puebla, mole stands in as the sauce, a variant often called enmoladas. The finish is usually crema, crumbled cotija or queso fresco, sliced white onion and sometimes avocado.

Speed is what sets enchiladas apart from Mexico's long-braised classics. A cook who already has sauce and cooked filling on hand can assemble a tray in minutes, which is why the dish turns up on weeknight tables and in formal restaurant kitchens alike.

Travelers $TRV will find enchiladas nearly everywhere in the country, but the version on the plate shifts by state, and what arrives in San Luis Potosi looks little like what arrives in Mexico City. That range, paired with a lineage reaching back centuries, keeps enchiladas among the Mexican dishes diners rate consistently well worldwide.

#85. Traffic data pioneer Inrix to be acquired by Allstate’s Arity after more than two decades

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 16, 2026 at 12:58 pmOctober 19, 2026 at 2:53 pm

Inrix, the Bellevue, Wash.-based traffic data company that spun out of Microsoft in 2004 and became one of the Seattle region’s longest-running independent tech companies, has agreed to sell substantially all of its assets to Arity, the mobility data subsidiary of insurance giant Allstate.

The deal, announced Friday, would end Inrix‘s 22-year run as a standalone company. Inrix has raised more than $288 million and flirted with an IPO multiple times over its lifetime. Terms were not disclosed. The companies expect the acquisition to close later this year.

Founded in 2016, Chicago-based Arity analyzes driving behavior for insurers, marketers and public-sector customers. It says it has amassed more than 3 trillion miles of driving data. The acquisition would pair that information with Inrix’s analytics on traffic, road conditions and transportation networks.

“By combining Arity’s predictive insights on driving behavior and risk with Inrix’s transportation intelligence and mobility analytics, we will be uniquely positioned to deliver more robust intelligence and insights into how people, vehicles, goods, and roads interact,” Gary Hallgren, president of Arity, said in a statement.

While the companies are touting the benefits of combining their data and analytics, Arity’s data practices have faced legal scrutiny. In January 2025, Texas sued Allstate and Arity, alleging they collected and sold consumers’ driving and location data without adequate consent.

“We are confident in our compliance with all laws and regulations and are committed to ensuring consumers are informed when their data is used for personalized insurance rates,” an Arity spokesperson told GeekWire via email.

The proposed acquisition charts an alternate course to Inrix’s earlier plans for going public. In 2012, Inrix hired Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase with an eye toward a 2013 IPO that was expected to raise up to $100 million. The company looked to go public again in 2022 but backed out amid economic uncertainty stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and other factors.

“We were about two weeks away from filing our documents with the SEC,” Inrix CEO Bryan Mistele said in an August 2022 GeekWire story. “We’re on standby right now, waiting to see when the markets and economy improve, in which case we’ll take another run at it.”

Inrix declined via email to comment on the reason why it chose to sell at this time.

“By leveraging the complementary strengths of both organizations, we see an opportunity to turn transportation data into actionable intelligence that helps organizations make better decisions and create safer, more efficient, and more connected transportation systems,” an Inrix spokesperson said.

Inrix serves corporate, automotive, technology and public-sector customers including Amazon, IBM, General Motors, Windermere Real Estate and state departments of transportation.

The company got its start selling traffic and transportation-related data. In recent years, it moved beyond supplying raw traffic data into subscription software that helps customers interpret it, including tools for traffic-signal timing, road safety and retail site selection.

Recent public releases include its first Parking Scorecard, which ranks the availability and cost of parking in major cities in the U.S. and Europe.

Inrix has about 277 employees, based on LinkedIn data. A spokesperson said that “all eligible” employees will receive job offers from Arity, and there are no planned changes to the company’s Bellevue headquarters.

Editor’s note: Comments from Arity and Inrix spokespeople were added 10/19.

CORAL SPRINGS, Fla., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cruise Planners is once again setting the pace for artificial intelligence (AI) and technology innovation in the travel industry, unveiling a powerful new generation of AI-driven solutions at its annual CP World conference. With 23 innovations introduced in 2026, Cruise Planners continues to push the boundaries of what's possible, delivering sophisticated, proprietary technology designed to give its franchise owners a distinct competitive advantage.

While much of the travel industry continues to explore the possibilities of artificial intelligence, Cruise Planners is putting AI into action across nearly every aspect of an advisor's business. From conversational vacation research and predictive sales intelligence to automated digital marketing and connected itinerary management, the company's expanding technology ecosystem helps advisors work smarter, sell more and deliver exceptional personalized service.

The five featured innovations—Maxx Assist, Maxx Reach, Genius Agents, enhanced Trip Summary and Maxx SharePlace—represent the next evolution of Cruise Planners' commitment to technology leadership. Unveiled before more than 1,300 travel advisors and suppliers at CP World 2026, these innovations build on an extensive suite of proprietary tools designed to keep Cruise Planners advisors ahead of the competition.

"At Cruise Planners, we don't wait for the future of travel technology. We build it," said Michelle Fee, CEO and Founder of Cruise Planners. "We've always believed that technology should be one of the greatest competitive advantages we give our franchise owners, and AI is taking that commitment to an entirely new level. While others are still talking about what AI can do, we're delivering powerful, practical solutions that are transforming how our advisors run their businesses. From identifying the next sales opportunity to researching an entire vacation in minutes, we're putting AI to work in ways that drive real results. Our mission is simple: to give Cruise Planners advisors the most innovative technology and the strongest competitive advantage possible."

Maxx Assist: Revolutionizing Vacation Research with Conversational AI.Built directly into Cruise Planners' technology ecosystem, the AI-powered tool helps advisors research flights, transfers, pre- and post-cruise hotels, excursions, insurance quotes and more through a single conversational, natural language interface. For an existing cruise booking, Maxx Assist understands where clients are traveling and when, giving advisors a contextual starting point for building the complete trip faster, smarter and easier.

Maxx Reach: Transforming Predictive AI into Revenue Opportunities.Each week, the AI-powered sales tool matches promotions, offers and sailings with clients based on a myriad of signals including past travel, marketing behaviors, supplier loyalty and predictive analysis. Recommendations include a Maxx Reach Score indicating the strength of the opportunity, a suggested brand, offer or sailing, and talking points to help start the conversation. Within CP Maxx, advisors can act on recommendations by sending an eCard, creating a flyer and tracking outreach.

Genius Agents: An AI-Powered Digital Marketing Workforce.Three specialized AI-powered agents help advisors get found, build trust and stay visible. The Reputation Agent creates on-brand responses to online reviews and flags sensitive feedback for personal attention. The Search Agent optimizes local business listings to improve search visibility. The Social Agent creates and publishes on-brand content tailored to individual businesses, routing sensitive content for human review. The agents learn from advisor feedback and actions over time to refine their responses and recommendations.

Trip Summary: Redefining the Itinerary Experience.The upgraded itinerary builder within CP Maxx introduces a refreshed interface, flexible free-form proposal sections, expanded supplier lookups, integrated hotel imagery and client-view tracking. Two-way synchronization between Trip Summary and advisor bookings reduces duplicate entry and helps keep trip information current. Advisors can also import details from any supplier confirmation for tours, hotels and flights, reducing manual entry while creating polished, comprehensive itineraries. With sophisticated new capabilities and seamless integration within CP Maxx, Trip Summary delivers a powerful itinerary-building experience that rivals standalone solutions while remaining included at no additional cost for Cruise Planners advisors.

Maxx SharePlace: Powering Collaboration Across the Cruise Planners Network.The new resource-sharing space allows advisors to contribute and access templates, text snippets, Maxx Creator flyers, newsletter assets, information buckets and other materials created by their peers. Inspired by collaboration already taking place across the Cruise Planners network, Maxx SharePlace makes practical advisor expertise easier to share and reuse throughout the network.

Beyond AI Tools: Building the Future of the Travel Advisor BusinessCruise Planners' technology leadership goes beyond the number of innovations it introduces. The company's greatest differentiator is how its proprietary tools, AI-powered intelligence and marketing capabilities work together to create a smarter, more connected business environment for its franchise owners.

Through its proprietary CP Maxx platform, Cruise Planners continues to integrate artificial intelligence, predictive sales intelligence, marketing automation, booking capabilities, itinerary management and business analytics into a comprehensive technology ecosystem designed specifically for travel advisors.

From identifying the next sales opportunity with Maxx Reach and simplifying vacation research through Maxx Assist to creating seamless itineraries with Trip Summary, automating digital marketing with Genius Agents and sharing resources through Maxx SharePlace, each innovation contributes to a more efficient and connected advisor experience.

Together, these advancements represent a fundamental shift from technology that simply helps advisors complete tasks to intelligent solutions that proactively uncover opportunities, automate processes and support business growth.

Cruise Planners isn't simply adding AI to its technology platform. It's building an AI-powered business ecosystem designed to give its advisors a competitive advantage at every stage of their business.

An Unmatched Commitment to Technology Innovation.The CP World announcements extend a year of innovations across consumer discovery, advisor operations and client engagement. Redesigned corporate and franchise websites support visibility and connections with travelers, while the CP Mobile redesign makes it easier for clients to find inspiration, book vacations, manage trips and reach their advisor. Direct hotel consumer booking adds another way for travelers to book through advisor digital channels.

"Every year, I think Cruise Planners can't possibly top what they've already created, and then they introduce innovations like these," said Alena Einfeldt, Cruise Planners franchise owner based in Hollywood, Florida. "What's most exciting is how much time these AI-powered tools are going to give back to us. Between simplifying vacation research, automating marketing, and identifying new sales opportunities, we're eliminating hours of work that used to be done manually. That means more time to connect with clients, close sales and focus on growing our businesses. It's another example of why Cruise Planners continues to lead the industry in technology and innovation."

Additional innovations include Flight Tracker enhancements, Ask Maxx V2, the Maxx Intelligence redesign, AI Cruise Import, AI Cruise Search, Hotel Sheets, Additional Rates, Maxx Media, the My Settings redesign and the Maxx Adventures Game. These tools expand research and selling capabilities, simplify access to business insights and marketing assets, and make training more interactive.

Cruise Planners' specialty marketing magazines—including the River & Expedition Guide, Romance Guide and Luxury Look Book—give advisors evergreen content to inspire travelers and showcase specialized experiences. Digital editions are available at no cost through advisor websites, extending their value beyond the initial launch.

CP World Brings the "Game On" Theme to LifeCP World 2026 brings together more than 1,300 Cruise Planners advisors and suppliers in Fort Lauderdale for education, training, networking and a first look at the company's latest innovations. With a "Game On" theme, the conference reinforces Cruise Planners' commitment to equipping franchise owners with the technology, marketing resources and business development opportunities they need to stay ahead of the competition.

Held at the Broward County Convention Center, CP World features travel industry partners, breakout sessions, a trade show, and presentations, panels and fireside chats with senior executives from leading cruise, tour and resort brands. The experience extends beyond the convention center with ship tours, professional headshots and networking, followed by a four-night conference sailing aboard Princess Cruises' Star Princess to Grand Turk, featuring additional educational sessions at sea.

Beyond the announcements and experiences, CP World reflects Cruise Planners' larger vision for the future of travel—one where cutting-edge technology, AI-powered innovation and the expertise of professional travel advisors come together to create an extraordinary competitive advantage.

"Technology innovation has always been part of our DNA, and we're accelerating that investment like never before," said Fee. "Our advisors deserve more than tools that help them keep up. They deserve technology that puts them ahead. That's why we continue to push boundaries, challenge what's possible and deliver solutions that give our franchise owners an extraordinary competitive advantage. AI is transforming our industry, and Cruise Planners is committed to leading that transformation."

With 23 innovations introduced in 2026, Cruise Planners is demonstrating that its commitment to technology leadership goes far beyond announcements. By combining powerful AI capabilities, proprietary technology, industry-leading marketing programs and comprehensive advisor education, Cruise Planners is equipping its franchise owners to work smarter, grow their businesses and deliver exceptional client experiences.

For Cruise Planners, "Game On" is more than a conference theme. It's a commitment to staying ahead of the competition, redefining what's possible and leading the next era of travel technology and AI innovation.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

#88. How I Learned That Some Startup Problems Are Too Big For A Minimum Viable Product

A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary.

Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause.

For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on.

After selling my first venture, Tink, to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing.

Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours.

Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another.

Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget.

“Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one.

In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder.

The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you.

Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it.

Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink.

We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs.

You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet.

Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda, the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022.

#89. ‘An army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention’: Anthropic calls human attention the bottleneck in the botsitting world to come

Anthropic just released a study of its own workforce that offers one of the earliest looks at what an AI-dominated company of the future might look like—and spoiler alert, it includes babysitting a whole lot of bots.

AI agents are now moving so fast that 80% of the elapsed time in Claude sessions was the result of agents waiting on a human’s input, Anthropic’s report found. “This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output,” the report read.

Instead of actively doing the work themselves, even non-supervisor employees are increasingly acting like managers to multiple AI agents that complete tasks but also require direct attention at times.

One employee described the experience of bot management as “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.”

That bottleneck is the flip side of a big jump in output. Employees are producing more and moving faster, the company found. AI agents collectively surpassed human working hours for the first time in March, and by August AI agent hours worked outnumbered the hours worked by humans six to one.

Software engineers’ code commits have also increased fivefold over the past six months. And even nontechnical employees have personal agents monitoring their email and calendars, sending to-do lists compiled from messages, and briefing them on the purpose of their upcoming meetings.

These changes have taken some manual labor off employees’ plates, but they’ve also transformed what the workday looks like.

Managing agents is becoming a job in itself. The share of employees’ interactive Claude sessions devoted to this kind of “meta-work” rose from 10% to 22%, according to the report. Even for nontechnical employees, reading everything their Claude agents produce would take up about half their workweek. And private work, done in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is “invisible, confusing, and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace,” the report said.

The median employee now spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Part of that is a result of the company’s growth (Anthropic now has more than 3,500 employees), and part is owing to an emphasis on hiring in nontechnical roles. But meeting time is up 16% even among technical individual contributors, a sign that humans are spending more of their time on coordination and decision-making, while agents handle tasks like repetitive coding on their own.

And the pace keeps ratcheting up. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems, the report found. One employee described the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.”

In some cases, employees using AI have streamlined their own responsibilities away. The report mentions a product design team—previously responsible for writing short pieces of copy for the company’s website, including greetings displayed on Claude.ai—that started using AI to write the copy this spring.

“The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude,” the report read.

This phenomenon is increasingly common at Anthropic as AI takes over tasks. The company claimed in the report that employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than in 2025. Still, the company said in the report it has made an effort to identify at-risk jobs and reassign employees to other positions.

The hiring process is changing, too. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise, the report said.

And there are fewer entry-level people being hired. The share of junior-level employees in technical departments fell to 14% from 21% in early 2025, and the share of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Open positions for those junior roles also plummeted since December, the report found.

That’s likely to add to anxiety about AI job displacement, which is running especially high among young people. A survey from recruiter platform iCIMS published earlier this year found that 51% of Gen Z respondents considered AI the greatest threat to their job security.

A Deutsche Bank Research survey from last year also found that nearly one in five Gen Z workers is worried AI will cost them their job over the next two years, compared with just one in 10 baby boomers who said the same.

In the future, employees at Anthropic see AI taking up more and more of their daily responsibilities. As of August, employees at Anthropic said they expect AI to be able to complete three-quarters of their work by 2030, compared with a less optimistic 28% predicted by other U.S. workers, according to another study by Anthropic.

It’s unclear whether the changes at Anthropic are an accurate reflection of how the average workplace might look in the future. To be clear, the AI company has massive resources and is nearing a potential $2 trillion IPO that could break records. The company is also implementing AI deeply in its workflows to an extent other companies may not be.

Still, the report paints a picture of transformative change that could reflect how companies and corporate roles change as AI adoption takes root.

As tasks like writing code, identifying bugs, or writing emails get automated away by AI, employees at Anthropic have now found that the big picture tasks are increasingly what count.

As one employee in the report put it, “That 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job.”

For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield, and all of them presented a live demo in front of VCs and tech leaders who served as judges.

After hours of deliberation, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.

The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.

We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:

Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.

Read more about Intero Biosystems in our separate post here.

Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.

Read more about Apate in our separate post here.

These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. #91. Elon Musk, Anthropic pledge to give away billions of dollars in shares

SpaceX Corp. Chief Executive Elon Musk today pledged to gift a single share of the spaceflight company to every child in America.

“This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in the brief X post that revealed the move today. The announcement came a few hours after Anthropic PBC pledged to donate at least 5% of its equity to a public benefit fund.

There were 72 million children in the U.S. as of last July, which suggests that Musk intends to give away 72 million SpaceX shares. That’s the equivalent of $10.5 billion at the company’s last closing price.

Musk didn’t specify how he plans to disburse the shares. However, he disclosed in an X post responding to Anthropic’s donation that he plans to give “shares directly to the public.” In another post, Musk wrote “thanks for helping enable this” to tech investor Brad Gerstner, who played a central role in the creation of Trump Accounts. Those are investment accounts that the White House opened for U.S. children earlier this year.

In July, SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell pledged more than $320 million of her shares in the company to the Trump Accounts program.

Musk’s charitable activities have drawn scrutiny in recent months. He maintains a charity that had more than $14 billion in assets as of December, but reportedly failed to meet minimum donation requirements over the past four years. The funds that it did disburse reportedly went to nonprofits aligned with Musk and his companies.

Musk pledged $1 billion to OpenAI Group PBC shortly after its 2015 launch. He only donated $38 million and later proposed to take majority control of the artificial intelligence provider, which at the time operated as a traditional nonprofit. OpenAI changed its organizational structure a few years later to accommodate its commercialization efforts.

The ChatGPT developer’s top competitor, Anthropic, announced a major charitable initiative of its own shortly before Musk’s announcement. The company plans to donate 5% of its equity to a new public benefit fund. Anthropic intends to add another 2% every time its valuation increases by 50% “above a set baseline.”

The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will operate as a subsidiary of the AI provider rather than as a standalone nonprofit. The company indicated that one of the unit’s priorities will be addressing the impact of AI on the labor market. Earlier this year, Anthropic committed $200 million to external research initiatives focused on that topic.

The shares earmarked for the fund will come on top of the significant amount of equity the company’s employees have pledged to give away. Put together, the two initiatives will commit about 20% of Anthropic’s stock to charitable causes. That stock could be worth $400 billion if the company achieves the $2 billion valuation it reportedly hopes to reach in its upcoming public offering.

#92. Retro tech meets modern AI: Inside an Amazon developer’s garage turned working computer museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 16, 2026 at 7:06 amOctober 16, 2026 at 7:24 am

Darko Mesaros used to park a car in the garage of his Maple Valley, Wash., home. These days, it’s wall-to-wall computers.

A towering server rack glows with red LEDs. CRT monitors are stacked beside vintage workstations, and a workbench overflows with tools, cables, and half-repaired components.

“I started getting stuff, and then … it just kind of snowballed to a point I actually had to slow down because I legitimately don’t have space for it anymore,” Mesaros told GeekWire during a recent tour of his retro hardware labyrinth.

The lore of tech innovation is full of suburban garages where visionary founders tinkered their way to world-changing companies. Mesaros, a distinguished developer advocate at Amazon Web Services, isn’t launching a startup out of his. Instead, he’s using it as a living museum to rescue, repair, and resurrect the discarded digital ghosts of computing history — and then daring them to run modern artificial intelligence.

The collection has spilled into an upstairs office and now spans more than 100 full computers, from an early-1970s minicomputer to Silicon Graphics workstations from the ’90s and HP workstations from the 2000s. Add roughly 25 vintage video game consoles, rescued software, peripherals, a leather-bound TRS-80 owner’s manual, and nearly a decade of 1980s Byte magazines, and the total tops 1,000 items.

Most of it arrives broken, and that’s the point.

“Buying a mint old system is not fun,” he said. “Buying something that’s broken and then having that excitement of fixing it is just fantastic.”

He finds gear at Goodwill, through local Facebook Marketplace groups, and through Seattle’s large retro computing community. Sometimes it takes a rescue mission: when a man in Washington, D.C., was about to throw away a pallet of 1980s computers, Mesaros had a friend there grab it, then paid to ship the whole load to Seattle.

At one point, he had seven Commodore 64s. He gives extras to other collectors, and he’s never sold a single piece.

Mesaros’ fascination with vintage hardware goes beyond nostalgia; it’s the foundation of a lifelong obsession with how things work under the hood.

Growing up in Serbia, he faced an economic reality where cutting-edge tech was out of reach. From 1991 to 2003, his only computer was a Commodore 64 — a machine released in 1982. While the rest of the computing world sped through the 1990s and early 2000s, Mesaros skipped straight to modern PCs.

“I feel like I missed that whole thing,” he said. “I missed the whole, you know, Sun workstation, Silicon Graphics, HP 9000, all of those things … and I just wanted to explore how that was.”

So he bought a couple of Sun workstations to see what he’d missed. Then he kept going.

“It’s a hobby, but it’s also a problem,” he said with a laugh.

If the garage caught fire, the one machine he’d grab? A bright blue Silicon Graphics Indy, the 1990s workstation from the very era he missed growing up. It was the first SGI he bought.

“It showed me how this amazing workstation worked!” he said. He still fires it up from time to time just to enjoy its IRIX operating system.

Still on his wish list: a DEC VT520 terminal with an amber screen. Working units only seem to turn up on the East Coast, and he won’t risk shipping a fragile CRT across the country.

Before joining Amazon nearly a decade ago, he held system administration and engineering roles at companies including AT&T and Tipico. Now at AWS, his day job involves leveraging his experience to help developers and customers adopt and use AWS services via blogs, webinars, code, and technical advocacy. The garage doubles as his set: he records AWS videos and live streams there.

Mesaros moved to the Seattle area around the start of the pandemic, arriving with a couple of workstations, a monitor, and a handful of laptops before his collection expanded. He soon realized gear was far cheaper here than in Europe.

“Most of these things are older than me. Especially older than my tech career,” the 38-year-old noted. “Actually, all of these things are older than my career. However, again, I find it fascinating how computer history has evolved.”

His arrival timing meant he narrowly missed the chance to visit Seattle’s beloved Living Computers: Museum + Labs before it permanently closed its doors. But in his own home, he’s essentially built a private version of the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen’s former institution.

Beyond the vintage hardware, Mesaros’ appreciation for computing history is permanently etched onto his body.

He sports a collection of retro tech tattoos on his arms, including symmetrical DOS and Linux terminal prompts (C:\WINDOWS> and root@localhost), a classic Windows 95 logo, MS-DOS branding, a shebang and a quit command that mark the start and end of a script, and detailed microprocessors like the Zilog Z80 and MOS 6502 paired with assembly code — a setup he jokingly calls his literal “ARM CPUs.” He’s still waiting, he said, on his check from Microsoft.

“I only tattoo ancient technology on myself,” Mesaros said, noting that people frequently stop him at airports to take pictures. “Old technology will stay with me … I feel like this is an investment in my career.”

He has plans for more ink during his next trip home to Serbia.

For Mesaros, collecting vintage computers is about more than admiring silent plastic shells on a shelf; it’s about making them talk across the digital chasm. In his garage and upstairs office, he routinely bends ancient hardware to modern purposes — proving that an 8-bit machine or a mechanical teletype can still interface with the cutting-edge cloud.

Mesaros has chatted with an AI coding agent from a Commodore 64 and deployed Kubernetes via a 1986 Tandy 102 portable computer. He wired a 1984 DEC DECwriter IV teletype to Amazon’s Kiro coding agent, explaining in a blog post how he talks to Kiro through the clacking machine — and he’s even deployed AWS infrastructure from it.

“Should this be done? Probably not,” he said. “But is it fun? Absolutely.”

In a demo for GeekWire, we watched the teletype clatter out the agent’s answer to his query, “What is GeekWire?” After a few seconds of hammering, it printed: “Seattle-based tech news site covering Pacific Northwest startups, Amazon, Microsoft and the broader tech industry.”

Not bad for a machine older than its operator.

Mesaros also spent a weekend trying to get stuck in 1999, using a Windows 98 machine as his only computer and documenting it on a VHS camcorder.

“The only window into the future was Kiro,” he said.

While these stunts might sound like elaborate practical jokes, Mesaros believes they serve a vital purpose in the age of AI. In a modern development landscape where tools let programmers “build a to-do app and walk away,” he argues that developers are losing the art of paying attention.

He likes to point out that a 2017 Google paper titled “Attention Is All You Need” helped kick off today’s LLM boom. “Now in 2026, to be a really successful developer,” he said, “attention is all you need.”

“I think being curious and paying attention are the two most important skills for a developer these days because it is so easy not to do those things,” Mesaros said. “And if you want to be relevant, if you want to be good at your job, especially with AI, I think those are the two important things that are critical.”

When he isn’t troubleshooting an obscure serial card data-ready pin or attempting to hook up a military field phone from his native Serbia to an LLM, he balances his digital obsession with analog pursuits. He wrenches on an old Jeep TJ — parked in the driveway because there’s no room in the garage.

He’s not the only tinkerer in the house. His wife is a fashion designer who 3D prints clothing and purses on a farm of printers in one of the upstairs rooms.

“She’s more creative than I am,” he said. “I get to tinker with old things that don’t want to work, and she uses technology to actually make new things.”

When it comes to the tech he lets into his own life, Mesaros is choosy. He wears a classic analog Timex and bought Meta’s smart glasses when they came out — then sold them within a month. “I don’t like the camera on my face,” he said. (He does use a camera-free pair that can display real-time translated subtitles when he travels abroad.)

That same instinct is why he doesn’t see screens going away, even as AI agents take on more work. “We still have the need for control,” he said. “Being able to observe and see, visualize what’s happening is still important.”

Old tech offers something else modern tech rarely does: a slower pace. Computer manuals once took months to produce because they’d stay accurate for years. “Today, if you create a manual that’s printed, it’s going to be valid for a week,” he said.

That’s what makes his garage an antidote to the endless scroll, a place anchored to the glowing screens and clacking keys of computing’s past. The hobby is his “computer away from a computer.”

“I spend my days in the email factory … and then in the afternoon, I just come here and tinker with something ancient that shouldn’t work anymore,” Mesaros said.

#95. CorePower Yoga Announces Two New Studio Openings in Miami

The nation's largest yoga studio brand expands its Florida footprint with a new studio in Midtown Miami, opening October 19, followed by a flagship location in Coral Gables

MIAMI, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CorePower Yoga, the nation's largest yoga studio brand, announced the opening of two new studios in Miami, reinforcing its growing presence and continued investment in the Miami market as part of its national expansion across high-growth wellness markets. The new Midtown Miami studio opens Monday, October 19, with a flagship studio in Coral Gables slated to open soon after. Both openings reflect the increasing consumer demand for fitness experiences that combine physical intensity, mindfulness, recovery, and community connection in thoughtfully-designed spaces.

Since its founding in 2002, CorePower Yoga has grown into a leading force in modern wellness, now operating more than 220 studios nationwide and welcoming millions of student visits annually. Known for its physically intense workouts rooted in the mindfulness of yoga, CorePower Yoga combines movement, breathwork, heat, and music into a modern studio experience that allows students to seamlessly move between performance, strength, recovery, and community as part of their wellness routine.

Opening Monday, October 19, the Midtown Miami studio will bring CorePower Yoga's signature experience to 3401 N Miami Avenue in Midtown Miami (3401 N Miami Avenue), extending the brand's reach to a thriving neighborhood just steps from Wynwood and the Design District. The studio features two practice rooms, infrared heat panels, locker rooms with two showers each, and three restrooms to support students before and after their practice.

Slated to open soon after, the new Coral Gables flagship will be located on the second floor (known as "fitness row") of The Plaza Coral Gables (2811 Ponce de Leon Boulevard), a transformative mixed-use development and open-air lifestyle destination with dining, retail, lodging, entertainment and luxury residences. The studio will anchor CorePower Yoga's growing Florida footprint and bring the brand's full studio experience to the heart of one of Miami's most vibrant neighborhoods. It will feature two practice rooms accommodating more than 70 yoga mats, with high ceilings overlooking an open-air courtyard. The studio also offers 90 minutes of validated parking in the Plaza's garage, elevated amenities, curated retail offerings, and a communal lobby space designed to foster connection before and after class.

Together, the two new Miami locations will create new opportunities for residents to experience CorePower Yoga's unique blend of strength-based mind-body workouts. The new Midtown Miami and Coral Gables studios will join CorePower Yoga's existing Brickell studio, further strengthening the brand's presence across the Miami area and expanding access to its signature wellness experience throughout the community.

Both studios will offer CorePower Yoga's full portfolio of signature classes, empowering students to personalize their practice and move across yoga flow, strength training, cardio conditioning, mobility, and recovery-focused classes, based on their goals and experience level. Class offerings include the brand's most popular formats such as Yoga Sculpt, a heated, high-energy class that combines yoga, cardio and strength moves with handweights; CorePower Strength X, a 45-minute HIIT-style class combining functional strength training with energizing breathwork; CorePower Yoga 1 (C1), a foundational Vinyasa flow designed to introduce core yoga poses, and CorePower Yoga 2 (C2), a heated power Vinyasa flow designed to build strength, endurance, and flexibility; and Hot Power Fusion (HPF), which blends traditional hot yoga and power yoga moves with high heat intensity.

To celebrate the new locations, CorePower Yoga will welcome the local community with special opening programming and opportunities to experience its signature classes. For a limited time, new students can also sign up for a Founding All Access Membership, offering 25% off monthly dues and access to CorePower Yoga studios nationwide, plus virtual Live and On Demand classes and exclusive member benefits such as monthly Buddy Passes and retail discounts.

For additional information, class schedules, or membership details, visit CorePowerYoga.com or follow CorePower Yoga on Instagram.

About CorePower YogaCorePower Yoga shares the transformative power of yoga with every mind, every body, everywhere through physically intense workouts rooted in the mindfulness of yoga. Since 2002, the brand has grown into the nation's largest yoga studio company, with more than 220 locations across 23 states and Washington, D.C., digital livestream and on-demand platforms, and thousands of passionate teachers guiding students through movement, mindfulness, and community. By combining strength, sweat, recovery, and human connection, CorePower Yoga creates modern wellness experiences designed to support students both on and off the mat. For more information, visit CorePower Yoga.

#96. An AI agent sent a stranger to a man’s house without telling him—and exposed the privacy risks of AI assistants

Matt Robb wanted to sell his computer keyboard.

So he made a listing on Facebook Marketplace and, as an experiment late last month, he put Meta’s new artificial intelligence agent Muse in the driver’s seat.

“I kind of went into it like a guinea pig,” said Robb, a Toronto-based content creator who regularly reviews consumer tech. He had seen Muse’s plush-toy-looking avatar pop up on Instagram and decided to see if the AI agent could spare him some online bargaining.

Muse got to work. But within a day, Robb got an alarming update: A buyer he didn’t know had shown up outside his house late at night. How? Muse had struck a deal on its own and shared Robb’s home address after agreeing to a pickup. It even sent an automated “Yep, I’m here!” message from his account when the buyer arrived—all without Robb’s knowledge.

“Not only did it give my address when the guy asked and it accepted the offer, but it literally was almost like teasing the guy [about me being there when I wasn’t],” said Robb, who also detailed the experience in his now widely shared social media posts. “That really baffled me.”

Many have welcomed AI agents into their online lives and raved about how personalized assistants like Muse can handle everyday tasks with ease, from snagging a dinner reservation or planning a trip, to organizing email inboxes. But like other AI bots, the agents are only as good as the information they have access to. They perform better the more they know about a user—and perhaps also that person’s friends, family, and even colleagues. That raises privacy concerns.

Robb and the buyer eventually made amends, and Meta reached out to talk through what went wrong. But the episode showed real-world risks that can arise from sharing extensive personal information with the technology.

“Using an AI agent is similar to handing someone your keys and a to-do list,” said Veronica Rivera, assistant professor at Georgia Tech’s School of Cybersecurity and Privacy. “How helpful they are, and by extension how risky, depends on which keys you hand over.”

Since its September launch, downloads of Meta’s Muse app have skyrocketed. And competition is only growing. OpenAI recently rolled out its own lineup of “always on” AI helpers, called dots, which can be integrated into ChatGPT and workplace platforms like Slack and Microsoft Teams.

Older generative AI chatbots, like the standard version of ChatGPT, respond to specific prompts. At the user’s request, they can write essays, generate new images or music, or even write lines of code.

Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s dots go a step further to perform day-to-day tasks on a person’s behalf. AI agents are powered by the same large language models as chatbots, but they run in a loop. That allows an agent to take proactive steps, even when the user isn’t looking.

“One of the things that makes these AI agents really appealing is that they are unprecedentedly useful,” said Rivera, who is also a Microsoft-funded Computing Research Association Trustworthy AI Research Fellow.

But the convenience comes with the price of sharing more details about your life.

Once AI agents obtain users’ information, it’s very difficult to fully withdraw access, said Ebrahim Bagheri, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.

“If you provide access to your credit card to an agent, the agent now immediately has access to all of the historical transactions…they will immediately—within less than seconds—ingest all of that data,” Bagheri said. And while users can later withdraw access, Bagheri said there’s “no taking back” data the agent has already seen, and how developers store historical data can be murky.

Both Meta and OpenAI outline privacy policies for their new AI agents, which operate on their own dedicated cloud computers. You can turn off memory sharing between dots and ChatGPT, but information the agent previously received isn’t automatically deleted. OpenAI gives users an option to request access to, delete, or correct personal information, although rights can vary depending on where you live.

Meta’s Muse gives users options to delete message history and other information, too. For day-to-day use, the agent prompts users for access permissions, and Meta has said Muse learns about a user and who they interact with “based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share.” But the company says that all stays secure for each user.

But the tech giant also notes that Muse can still “make mistakes or take unexpected actions.”

In Robb’s case, he learned the disclosure of his address came down to “always allow” permissions he granted when he first let Muse on his Facebook Marketplace profile, where he had shared his pickup address. But he warned others could similarly misunderstand the extent of that access—and said he initially thought the AI agent would check with him before sharing that information or accepting offers, regardless.

His AI agent didn’t follow the rest of his instructions without error, either. For another item Robb was selling, Muse seemingly suggested he would accept a price $100 below the previously set minimum. When reached by the Associated Press, Meta acknowledged the agent’s error without offering further comment.

Robb later largely disconnected Muse from his apps. In an interview earlier this month, he said it could have been a far worse situation, especially “if some stranger turned up to someone more vulnerable’s house.” Still, Robb said he expects these agents to be fine-tuned, and he would consider re-enabling Muse in the future. He’s since been testing another AI agent: Grok Bot from Elon Musk’s X, which launched in beta in August.

Other tech companies have become wary of the influx of AI agents. Earlier this month, Apple said it would introduce new controls for its Mac operating system in response to AI agents’ broader access of apps like mail, messages, and even browsing history without users’ “full knowledge and understanding.”

“As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” Apple wrote in an Oct. 2 update.

Apple didn’t specify any developers or agents by name, but the update arrived after Inc. magazine columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse watched notifications on his Mac—including Messages—without him giving the agent that specific access.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone has maintained such integration is “entirely opt-in,” writing on social media last month that users would have to enable both the Apple security feature “Full Disk Access” and a Messages connector through Muse. Aten said he didn’t grant the agent those permissions.

Even those who do not join the AI agent boom aren’t necessarily shielded. Consumers who don’t download an AI agent might still interact with others who do. And beyond potential confusion when AI sends messages on behalf of a user, experts warn of ripple effects when it comes to privacy.

“When your agent reads your inbox or your texts, it’s also reading what your friends and family sent you, even if they never explicitly agreed to that,” Rivera said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.
