#97. Amazon’s NBA coverage adds Prime 360 — AI replays that ‘fly the camera through’ the action

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 15, 2026 at 4:27 pmOctober 15, 2026 at 4:27 pm

Amazon is bringing a new AI-powered camera system to the court as the tech giant gets ready to tip off its second season of basketball coverage on Prime Video.

Called Prime 360, the technology uses an array of high-resolution cameras positioned around the arena to capture plays from multiple angles. Amazon’s proprietary AI models then process the footage to create highlight replays that the company says traditional cameras can’t replicate.

The feature will appear during live games and as an analysis tool on the pregame, halftime and postgame shows for select broadcasts. Amazon said it built the system with a team of producers, engineers and AI scientists, using its in-house AWS Trainium chips.

“Think of it like a video game camera,” Josh Green, an associate producer, said in an Amazon video describing the tech (below).

The cameras are calibrated and synchronized, and their footage is sent to the AWS cloud, where each play is reconstructed as a 3D scene — opening up possibilities beyond a normal replay.

“I want to see this play again, and you could actually fly the camera through the play,” said Wade Wakashige, a director of product. The view gives fans at home “something that the customer in the arena can’t see,” he added.

Introducing Prime 360 🎥Prime Video's proprietary, AI-powered technology that utilizes an array of high-res cameras around the court and AWS Trainium chips to deliver cinematic highlights you've never seen before! pic.twitter.com/mOlikDb45u

Prime Video is also adding a fantasy basketball integration with Yahoo Sports. Viewers who link their accounts will see their fantasy rosters and real-time stats on screen during games. They’ll also get recommendations for live and upcoming games featuring players on their teams.

Amazon debuted “NBA on Prime” last October with a Celtics-Knicks game — reviewed by GeekWire — the first under an 11-year deal that gives the company exclusive rights to select regular-season and playoff games. Bloomberg reported that Amazon is paying about $1.8 billion annually for the rights.

This season, Amazon says it will stream more than 100 regular-season and postseason games. In the playoffs, that includes the Play-In Tournament exclusively, select first- and second-round games, and, for the first time, exclusive coverage of the Eastern Conference Finals.

Several tech-driven extras from the first season are back. Fans can again track their active FanDuel bets during broadcasts, though they still can’t place wagers through Prime Video. The Prime Vision alternate stream returns as well, serving as a testing ground for AI-powered stats and graphics, such as flagging offensive players in position to score, that can graduate to the main broadcast.

The “NBA on Prime” season opener is Oct. 23, with a doubleheader: the defending champion New York Knicks host the Boston Celtics at 4 p.m. PT, followed by the Houston Rockets against the San Antonio Spurs in Austin at 6:30 p.m. PT.

The programming is included with a Prime membership, which costs $139 a year or $14.99 a month. Games stream in English and Spanish on the Prime Video app and the web.

Microbiotica, a Cambridge, UK-based biopharma company developing orally-dosed precision microbiome medicines, raised £36M ($48M) in Series C financing.

The round was led by British Business Bank, with participation from Tencent, IP Group, Cambridge Innovation Capital, Flerie Invest, and Seventure Partners.

#99. NiCE bets the company on AI, data and accountability, and the legacy business buys it time

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Every company in the customer experience ecosystem now claims to be an artificial intelligence company. Last week, at NiCE Ltd.’s annual industry analyst summit, the company demonstrated what happens when an AI strategy shifts the organization’s center of gravity.

A year after closing the Cognigy acquisition, NiCE is no longer a contact center-as-a-service or CCaaS provider with AI bolted on. It’s an AI platform that happens to include the industry’s deepest CCaaS and workforce engagement stack. Even before the Cognigy purchase, I felt NiCE led the CCaaS industry, and the event only reinforced that view.

During his keynote, Chief Executive Scott Russell (pictured) spoke at length about how the deal transformed the company. “Most acquisitions that companies make expand the portfolio and the capability,” he said. “This one changed where we build from. It changed the nature of who we are as a company.” Jeff Comstock, president of CX product and technology, said Cognigy is “now the underlying substrate for all of our conversational and agentic AI across the entire platform.”

What I found equally interesting is that NiCE isn’t using Cognigy solely to lock in CXone customers. Philipp Heltewig, Cognigy’s co-founder and now NiCE’s chief AI officer, said that the standalone motion of selling Cognigy on top of Genesys, Five9 or Amazon Connect “is equally important to us as the integrated motion.” Russell noted that he has yet to see a rival’s AI running on NiCE, whereas Cognigy runs on theirs.

Cognigy has a large customer base on competitive platforms, and it can be tempting to shut that down and force other vendors to scramble for new partners. It’s the right thing for NiCE to keep selling Cognigy that way because it’s best for customers, and that’s always the best path.

NiCE’s real asset is no longer the routing engine or the ability to offer multiple channels. That’s table stakes. NiCE’s strength and competitive moat is its decades of interactions, analytics, and screen recordings originally captured for compliance, which multimodal models can now reason over. Comstock demoed a system that observed a human agent process a refund across voice, screen, and telemetry, then built an AI agent from that observation, including a $250 supervisor-approval guardrail it inferred on its own.

Speaking of the AI startups that partner with NiCE, Russell said, “They need NiCE data. They need our workloads. They need our interactions. They need our intents.” In the Q&A, he added: “There’s no doubt the power of our data is a huge value, not just the interaction data, but the contextual real-time data, the human behavior behind it, the screen record.”

The numbers support that statement. Prospects that get an automated insights readout based on their own data book nine times more AI than those that don’t, and application programming interface volume off the platform is up 7.5 times in two years. Asked whether NiCE would package that intelligence for sales, marketing and the C-suite, Russell said, “Yes, it’s coming, just not right now.” That’s the long-term story. Systems of record capture what happened; NiCE captures how it happened.

Historically, part of what NiCE did was help customers understand and manage their customers’ journeys. At the event, Russell made an interesting comment, saying, “Companies can no longer own the customer journey.” Consumer AI agents don’t sleep, don’t give up and don’t care about your interactive voice response tree.

Demand, once limited by human patience, is about to surge. Dave Meyer of Hyatt said it’s already happening, starting in Asia. “You have bots talking to bots,” he said, “We don’t have any historical baselines.” His advice is not to “fear the bots,” because “there’s a customer behind every single one of these inquiries.”

Banking isn’t there yet. Mia Carrera, head of customer excellence at Citi, said, “When you’re dealing with your money, there’s no tolerance for error,” though attitudes are shifting.

“The race we are in is not about the smartest agent,” Russell said. “I see some of these announcements about these AI players, and I roll my eyes.” Accountability must shift from design time to runtime, with humans and AI agents held to the same standard.

From a company perspective, one of the most important points came during the analyst Q&A, when Russell was asked why 50%-plus AI growth isn’t showing up in overall revenue and whether AI expands NiCE’s market or cannibalizes it. Russell said reported revenue blends very different growth profiles: workforce management, analytics, Actimize and public safety don’t grow like CCaaS and AI. “If you look at CXone and NiCE Cognigy, those numbers will blow you away,” he said. “I am obsessed with long-term, durable growth, not with what happened last or this quarter.”

“That 52% year-over-year ARR is not from pilots and POCs,” Russell said. It counts only multiyear commitments, and backlog is growing faster. The bottleneck is deployment, which is why Heltewig’s 30-day time-to-value goal is so important.

This is a point many miss, and it explains why the stock has moved sideways since the Cognigy acquisition. The timing of AI revenue is uncertain because enterprises move slowly. NiCE’s large, sticky installed base gives it time to navigate the transition. Pure-play AI startups lack that cushion, and Russell said customers increasingly realize that many of those startups’ economic models “don’t stack up.”

When I asked about outcome-based deals, Russell said premium customers are defaulting to enterprise license agreements that mix seats, consumption, and outcomes. “Predictability is right now even more important than outcome,” he said. Seats never monetized efficiency; now, “With the AI workloads, we clipped the ticket on everyone.” If seats decline, spend shifts to AI workloads rather than leaving.

That said, investors dislike uncertainty, and anything Russell can do to clarify when AI creates a step function in the company’s growth will help. It’s worth noting that this is an issue not just for NiCE but for the entire CX industry. AI will likely reduce the number of human seats sold, but the revenue upside from AI usage should dwarf that. How and when this happens remain unknown, so many investors sit on the sidelines.

Treat interaction data as a strategic asset. Call recordings, transcripts, quality scores and screen recordings were once compliance artifacts stored until legal needed them. Now they’re the raw material for building, testing, and tuning AI agents, as NiCE’s demos showed. Information technology leaders should inventory where that data lives, how long it’s retained,and who can access it. Every platform contract, NiCE or otherwise, should guarantee that the enterprise can retrieve that data in a usable form. Whoever controls the interaction data will control how fast you can automate, so don’t let it be locked inside a vendor’s walls.

Plan for agent traffic now. Personal agents aren’t a 2028 problem. Hyatt is already seeing them, and the company’s biggest challenge is the lack of a historical baseline to plan against. Start by measuring how much inbound traffic is machine-generated, what those agents are asking for, and when they appear. Then work with security teams to determine how you’ll verify that an agent truly represents a customer and what it’s allowed to do on that customer’s behalf. Capacity planning also needs a rethink, since a single viral post can send millions of agents to your front door at once.

Budget for change management. Every customer on stage said the technology was the easy part. Hyatt’s Meyer agreed, favoring a 70/30 split between change management and deployment. Jermain Smith, senior director of customer support at Valvoline, noted that the company more than doubled containment and cut one group’s staff by about 30% through attrition alone. It got there in part by adjusting agent metrics before rollout, so employees weren’t penalized when the AI took over coupon and pricing calls. Citi took a similar approach, making it clear that frontline agents wouldn’t be held responsible when the AI running in the background made a mistake. IT should own the deployment, but it needs human resources, operations and frontline managers in the room from day one.

Get the knowledge base right first. Russell made a point that’s easy to overlook: Human agents can work around inaccurate or outdated knowledge articles through training and experience, but AI agents can’t. They’ll confidently repeat whatever they’re given. Before scaling AI agents, audit the knowledge content they’ll rely on, assign owners and put a process in place to keep it current. This unglamorous work often separates a stalled pilot from a production deployment.

Measure resolution, not containment. Containment is the metric most companies start with, and it’s easy to inflate. A customer who gives up and hangs up counts as “contained.” Hyatt is moving toward measuring whether the customer’s original intent was resolved, along with the accuracy of the information the AI provides. Citi treats accuracy as the metric that matters most. Define what a resolved interaction means for your business before you deploy, and ensure your vendor reports against that definition.

Negotiate for predictability. Outcome-based pricing sounds great until success makes it expensive, and the definition of a completed task can vary widely. Russell said most large customers are choosing predictable models, and that’s the right instinct for now. Look for enterprise license agreements that let spend move across seats, consumption and outcomes as your mix of human and AI agents changes. Also, model token costs before committing, since several customers saw costs balloon and had to switch models mid-deployment.

NiCE did what it said it would a year ago. The open questions are about execution: how quickly backlog turns into revenue, whether 30-day time to value holds in regulated enterprises, and how aggressively NiCE pushes to monetize its data.

NiCE’s advantage isn’t any single agent. It’s an installed base that funds the transition and a data asset no AI startup can replicate. Many of its traditional peers lack the resources or the data platform to deliver the depth of insight. If personal agents drive the demand surge Russell expects, enterprises will need a platform to absorb, govern, and learn from it. NiCE is betting it’s that platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#100. Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation.

The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth.

Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma.

The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting.

The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management.

Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass, a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills.

“In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement.

Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes.

The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding.

As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets.

Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company.

“Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”

— With additional reporting from Connie Loizos

#102. A two-person Seattle startup lands $1M to reinvent energy-hungry chips suitable for space

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 15, 2026 at 2:51 pmOctober 16, 2026 at 8:11 am

Seattle-based TriMagnetix has landed new funding and commitments totaling $1 million to continue developing a semiconductor chip that, according to initial lab testing, consumes 800 times less energy than a traditional chip to process the same amount of data.

The startup uses nanomagnetic technology that requires only electrical pulses rather than the constant power stream traditional chips need, dramatically reducing electricity consumption and heat generation. The design also makes the chip resistant to radiation, and it’s built to integrate with existing computing infrastructure.

The startup has made additional progress beyond the new funding:

Earthbound data centers struggling to curb energy use and heat output are seeking more sustainable chips, but the startup is particularly interested in satellite applications.

The Pacific Northwest, home to companies including Starcloud and SpaceX, is the “satellite capital of the world,” said Lucas Hahn, co-founder, president and chief strategic officer of TriMagnetix.

Satellite companies have told him they want semiconductors that are energy efficient and resistant to the radiation experienced in space, Hahn said. That makes TriMagnetix’s devices “a no-brainer.”

In addition to Hahn, the startup’s other employee is Madison Hanberry, who launched the TriMagnetix in 2023. Hanberry, who has served as chief of research and development, is transitioning to CEO. His sister, Aspen White, is also a co-founder.

The chips made so far by TriMagnetix are not the high-performance graphics processing units, or GPUs, used for applications such as AI and 3D animation. Nor are they simpler central processing units, or CPUs.

“It’s replacing specific compute in certain devices at a very low level,” Hahn said. “So not quite CPU yet, but it is at the core level doing similar things.”

TriMagnetix has contracted with the Washington Nanofabrication Facility at the University of Washington to use the site’s fabrication equipment. It aims to have a product available for commercial sales within the next year.

The round was led by Acequia Capital with participation from Athenaeum Ventures. Actuate Ventures has also committed to the round. The combined total from the three firms is $1 million. Last year, the startup received a $200,000 investment from climate venture fund SNØCAP.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#104. Neural Concept launches MCP to help AI agents operate commercial CAD tools

Switzerland-based artificial intelligence-native engineering company Neural Concept SA today launched Model Context Protocol Bridge to help AI agents operate commercial computer-aided design and simulation tools.

The capability will also help large engineering organizations automate complex software environments that are fundamental to designing and simulating physical products. This is an important part of manufacturing and proving prototypes before they are prepared for the real world.

In a typical simulation cycle, running solvers is the only step that doesn’t require human engineers. It’s largely already automated through retrieving proper physical geometry, cleaning it up and turning it into a virtual simulated mesh.

Founded in 2019, Neural Concept serves leading original equipment manufacturers and engineering organizations in industries throughout automotive, aerospace, energy, consumer, electronics, semiconductors and defense. It integrates an AI-augmented engineering platform and deep learning directly into computer-aided design and computer-aided engineering workflows.

With the new MCP Bridge, the platform will give AI agents access to the tools that make this happen, as well as the engineering know-how to use them, while companies retain control and ownership of their software and data.

“For the first time, the software that shapes every physical product can be operated by AI at enterprise scale,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Pierre Baqué.

Ideally, Baqué added, the opportunity is to reduce the tedium for engineers, who can then take on harder problems and work faster. This comes at a time when manufacturers are looking to shorten development lifecycles with fewer engineering experts available.

If an agent can handle an approved task in design and simulation software, every hour it takes is an hour handed back to an expert for more critical work. In one customer case, an engineer using MCP Bridge cleaned up the geometry of a wheel rim in three minutes, compared with a day using a manual process. That work is needed to get a physical product from physical to virtual model preparation and into simulation.

Thiat process, virtual model preparation and simulation, shifts engineering from reaction, physical trial-and-error into proactive data-driven digital environments by creating “digital twins.” These digital twins can be simulated in high fidelity, but only if they are “cleaned up” to act, look and react like their real-world counterparts with real-world physics before manufacturing happens.

That preparation works off spec sheets, materials guidelines and vast amounts of data. It can be extremely tedious, long work that requires extensive validation.

Once it’s done, engineers can test thousands of design scenarios simultaneously in virtual labs instead of waiting for real-world physical prototypes. However, getting one set up and into a rough draft an expert can refine can take weeks or more; an AI agent working in computer-aided engineering software can cut that time to hours. An engineer can fine-tune the result.

“AI agents have completely changed the way I work,” said Ciro Alosa, an electromagnetic design engineer at Traton SE, a subsidiary of Volkswagen Group that manages its heavy truck, bus and light commercial vehicle brands. “I can run more work in parallel, and going from a research paper to a validated script in our simulation toolchain now takes a couple of days.”

#107. Leaked list shows what Microsoft, Amazon and other tech giants are giving for the White House ballroom

by Todd Bishop on Oct 15, 2026 at 2:19 pmOctober 15, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Microsoft committed $10 million to President Trump’s White House ballroom project, and Amazon and T-Mobile each chipped in $5 million, according to an internal donor list obtained by the Washington Post and reported by the newspaper Thursday morning.

The commitments are drawing scrutiny because the ballroom donations aren’t subject to campaign finance limits or disclosure requirements. The money goes through a nonprofit, the Trust for the National Mall, into a White House account the president directly controls.

Of the $333 million raised so far, the vast majority came from companies and wealthy people with interests before the federal government, the Post found, raising concerns among experts that companies could be buying influence with the administration, or feeling pressured to give.

The White House publicly named Microsoft, Amazon and T-Mobile among the ballroom’s donors last October but didn’t disclose the amounts. Other donors asked to keep their names out of it entirely, the Post found, including a subsidiary of mortgage lender Rocket, which committed $10 million weeks after a federal agency approved its acquisition of Mr. Cooper.

The Seattle-area companies have a wide range of dealings with the government as suppliers, regulated businesses and targets of federal scrutiny. Microsoft and Amazon are two of the federal government’s largest technology providers, and T-Mobile requires regulatory approval across its business, from wireless spectrum to acquisitions.

Amazon is facing an FTC antitrust trial next year, focused on its treatment of third-party sellers on its online marketplace. The FTC and 22 states also sued Amazon in August, accusing it of rigging ad auctions to overcharge advertisers.

Microsoft is at odds with Vice President JD Vance and the Labor Department over claims that the company laid off American workers while sponsoring foreign workers for permanent residency, leading the department to suspend the company from the program.

Apple and Nvidia were among the top contributors at $25 million each, according to the list of 67 donations above $10,000. Microsoft’s $10 million puts it in the next tier with Palantir and Lockheed Martin, while Amazon and T-Mobile joined Meta, Cisco and ServiceNow at $5 million.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle told the Post that the donors are “a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People’s House better for generations to come.”

A Microsoft spokesperson said the company didn’t have a comment beyond what has been publicly reported. We’ve contacted Amazon and T-Mobile for comment.

#109. Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans to focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and biological computing, it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

#110. Microsoft’s Brad Smith pushes back on Vice President JD Vance’s visa fraud accusations

by Todd Bishop on Oct 15, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 15, 2026 at 10:51 am

Microsoft President Brad Smith says someone apparently “failed to inform the vice president accurately about our numbers” before the Trump administration cut off the company’s ability to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.

In an interview with Politico, published Thursday, Smith rejected Vice President JD Vance’s accusations of fraud and called his claim that Microsoft replaced laid-off Americans with foreign workers “completely off base.” He said Microsoft has “always been committed to a high integrity and high compliance” approach to immigration.

“We will stand by our record,” Smith said. “And I hope that folks at the White House might look again and look at what we think is a more accurate picture.”

At a White House news conference last week, Vance said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year while receiving 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.

“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said, after asserting that there “has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft.”

Critics of the visa programs say tech companies have used them to displace U.S. workers, and that the job ads companies must run before sponsoring workers for green cards often appear in places few American job seekers will see. Labor Department records show Microsoft’s required print ads ran mostly in The Seattle Times.

Smith said most of Microsoft’s recent visa and green card applications were for people already working at the company, many of them for years, because of long green card backlogs. He also said Microsoft hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year, a number he said was “left out of the narrative.”

The Microsoft executive also rejected the idea that the company pays visa holders less. “It doesn’t matter whether you came on a visa or you’re an American worker,” he said. “Everybody has the same compensation system.”

He warned that the crackdown could send “the most talented next wave” of engineers to other countries. Five of the six tech leaders President Trump honored with national medals last week, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, came to the U.S. as immigrants, Smith noted, and their companies together account for more than 25% of the value of the S&P 500.

The suspension doesn’t stop Microsoft from hiring foreign workers on H-1B visas. Those are temporary work visas, typically granted for three years at a time and generally limited to six.

Amazon led in H-1B approvals for new employment in fiscal 2025, with 4,644, followed by Meta with 1,555 and Microsoft with 1,394, according to an analysis of USCIS data by the National Foundation for American Policy.

What Microsoft lost is access to a key step toward permanent residency. The program, known as PERM, is run by the Labor Department. Companies use it to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency, also known as a green card. The employer has to advertise the job and show the department that no qualified, available U.S. worker can fill it.

PERM is commonly used for employees already working in the U.S. on temporary visas, including H-1Bs.

The interview didn’t address Microsoft’s outsized use of PERM. The company had more PERM cases decided than any other employer in fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026, according to a GeekWire analysis of Labor Department data. Other big tech companies, including Amazon and Google, sharply reduced their PERM filings after early 2023.

#112. Motive brings agentic AI to physical operations with agents that act before problems escalate

ANALYSIS by John Furrier

Motive Inc., the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence platform provider for physical operations, today announced the launch of Agents, a new capability that automatically responds to safety, maintenance and operational issues before they escalate into accidents, costly breakdowns or business disruptions.

The new Agents platform moves beyond alerts to automatically contact drivers, initiate maintenance and coordinate operational responses. The launch advances Motive’s strategy to bring agentic AI to the physical economy.

Motive’s technology uses operational data already collected through their platform to identify potential problems and initiate corrective actions. Agents can contact drivers, create maintenance work orders, alert managers and coordinate responses across fleet operations without requiring personnel to manually process every notification.

The launch targets one of the biggest challenges facing transportation, logistics, construction and other physical industries: Organizations have more operational data than ever, but acting on that information still requires significant manual coordination.

Motive estimates that companies lose approximately $46 billion to preventable operational problems, including vehicle downtime, compliance violations and unnecessary idling. According to the company’s 2026 ROI Report, 42% of surveyed organizations cite operational inefficiencies, including excessive administrative work, as a leading concern.

“Our customers don’t need another alert. They need action,” said Hemant Banavar, chief product officer at Motive. “The data that prevents collisions and breakdowns already lives in Motive. Agents put it to work the moment it matters, so teams can grow without adding headcount.”

Agents are available now to Motive customers. The company is demonstrating the new capabilities this week at the American Trucking Association’s Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Motive plans to expand the technology in early 2027 with natural-language agent creation, allowing customers to describe a workflow in plain English and have AI build the corresponding automation. That future capability represents a progression beyond the rule-based and AI-assisted workflows available today. Motive has not provided independently validated performance results for the newly launched Agents platform.

The announcement builds on technology introduced earlier this year, including the company’s Atlas AI assistant, AI-powered automation tools and expanding edge computing capabilities.

The Motive announcement is a good example of what I see emerging as one of the most important trends in enterprise AI: the transition from systems that generate insights to intelligent systems that actually do work.

For years, enterprise software has focused on collecting information, improving visibility and giving people dashboards to manage their businesses. The cloud era made that data more accessible. Generative AI made it easier to query, summarize and interpret. Agentic AI introduces a different opportunity: closing the gap between understanding what’s happening and taking action. This will be very important in the physical economy.

The deeper opportunity isn’t simply automating individual tasks. It’s eliminating the operational latency between detecting a problem, making a decision and executing a response.

This is where agentic AI could change the unit economics of physical operations. Companies have spent years investing in sensors, cameras, telematics and operational software. Those technologies generate enormous amounts of information, but much of the responsibility for converting that information into action still falls on people.

Agents introduce the possibility of compressing that coordination layer.

When intelligence can initiate an approved operational response instead of simply generating another alert, the economics begin to change. Fleet managers can potentially oversee more vehicles, maintenance teams can respond earlier, and organizations can improve utilization without adding proportional administrative overhead.

The real prize in physical AI may not be automating the workflow. It may be redesigning the operating model around intelligence that continuously turns signals into action.

During a recent interview on theCUBE’s NYSE Wired: Physical AI & Robotics program, Motive Chief Product Officer Hemant Banavar discussed the company’s evolving architecture. “The next era of AI is about action and not insights,” Banavar said.

He was describing an industry that had spent years deploying telematics, cameras and monitoring devices but had created a new problem in the process: too much data and too little time to respond.

Banavar outlined a real-world scenario involving a fatigued driver. Motive’s computer vision technology could detect signs of fatigue and issue a warning. If the condition persisted, an automated workflow could initiate a conversation with the driver, encourage a safe stop and alert the fleet manager. “Imagine now nobody needs to be watching a dashboard in real time,” he explained.

The technology is designed to turn a sequence of disconnected activities — monitoring, detecting, notifying, communicating and coordinating — into an integrated operational workflow. This matters because the strategic value of agentic AI isn’t simply automating an individual task.

In our recent interview, Banavar also explained why AI in physical operations has fundamentally different requirements from AI in traditional digital environments. He emphasized that accuracy in physical AI can be a matter of life and death, unlike many digital AI applications where an incorrect response may have limited consequences.

A slightly incorrect email generated by a language model is inconvenient. A safety system that fails to recognize a dangerous operating condition can have serious consequences. That places a premium on real-time processing, reliable models and the integration of intelligence directly into physical environments.

Motive has been investing in edge AI technologies, including its AI Dashcam Plus and AI Omnicam Plus, which extend computer vision and processing capabilities inside and around vehicles.

Banavar discussed the company’s relationship with Qualcomm, whose chips power these devices. He said Motive’s latest hardware can run three times more computer vision models than competing devices in its comparison, increasing the number of conditions the system can detect.

The performance comparison is Motive’s claim, but the architectural implications are meaningful. Motive is combining processing at the edge with cloud-connected operational systems and AI-driven workflows. The edge detects events. The platform provides operational context. Agents initiate approved actions. Atlas enables direct communication with people.

This integrated stack could become an important competitive differentiator as agentic AI moves into industries where reliability, real-time decision-making and safety are critical.

One of my recurring themes on theCUBE is that the real opportunity in AI isn’t just technological innovation. It’s the ability to produce measurable economic value.

During my July 2025 interview with Nyanya Joof, then Motive’s regional vice president for the U.K. market, at the RAISE Summit in Paris, we discussed the economics of physical AI and the opportunity to bring intelligence to industries that have traditionally relied on manual processes.

I characterized the opportunity as practical AI — not another demonstration of a powerful language model, but technology that can deliver measurable operational improvements.

Joof provided several examples. Phoenix Global, a metals and mining company, had reduced safety incidents by 40%, according to Joof, while improving its operational performance.

Ernst Concrete, an 80-year-old construction materials business, had deployed Motive’s AI cameras and video coaching after experiencing costly safety incidents. Joof said the company achieved $6.5 million in savings and a 2,000% return on investment over 13 months.

Motive also reported significant reductions in collisions and accident-related costs among Motive customers, along with improvements in vehicle uptime and administrative productivity.

In the physical economy, companies can measure AI’s value in cost per mile, vehicle uptime, accident rates, fuel consumption, maintenance expenses and labor productivity. Those metrics create a more direct connection between technology investments and business outcomes than many early generative AI productivity applications have demonstrated.

Agents could potentially extend those benefits by reducing the time and human intervention required to resolve problems once detected.

Another important theme from my conversation with Joof was how AI could transform the role of frontline workers.

Much of the AI debate has focused on replacing white-collar jobs. But physical AI offers a different narrative: using intelligence to augment people operating vehicles, machinery and industrial equipment.

A driver who previously had to rely on personal experience or contact a supervisor can now receive contextual guidance from an AI assistant. A fleet manager who previously spent hours reviewing alerts and contacting drivers can increasingly focus on exceptions, higher-value decisions and operational improvements.

This creates an interesting shift in the nature of frontline work. AI can make specialized knowledge more accessible at the point of activity, potentially improving productivity and safety while reducing repetitive administrative demands.

The objective isn’t necessarily removing the human from the process. It’s changing where human judgment is applied. Agents will need clear operating policies, reliable escalation mechanisms, transparency and human accountability. The industry has considerable work ahead in demonstrating how autonomous systems can operate safely and predictably in the physical world.

The Motive launch connects to a larger thesis we’ve been developing around the evolution of enterprise computing and systems of intelligence.

Traditional systems of record were designed to capture business information. Systems of engagement improved how people interact with that information. Systems of intelligence introduced AI-powered analysis, context and recommendations.

Now agentic AI is adding an execution layer. Instead of merely showing managers what happened or recommending what they should do, AI systems can initiate the next operational step within defined business policies.

Motive provides a concrete example of this evolution in the physical economy. The company’s early approach is relatively constrained: Customers define triggers and actions, while AI interprets operational conditions and assists in executing the workflow.

The longer-term roadmap moves toward goal-oriented agents that determine how to achieve business outcomes. That’s a much bigger architectural transition, and it introduces important questions about governance, explainability, human oversight and accountability.

But the strategic opportunity is clear. The competitive advantage in enterprise agentic AI may increasingly come from the combination of domain-specific data, real-time context and the ability to execute reliable actions.

Foundation models will continue improving. But the models themselves are only part of the value chain. The systems that understand a business’s unique operating environment and can take appropriate action may ultimately capture more durable value.

For Motive, its integrated hardware, software and AI strategy provides a foundation for pursuing that opportunity. The challenge now is proving that Agents deliver incremental improvements in operational outcomes while maintaining the reliability required for physical-world applications.

The bigger story isn’t another AI agent entering the market. It’s the emergence of a new operating model where intelligence becomes an active participant in how physical businesses function.

For Motive, the opportunity is to turn years of investment in edge computing, computer vision and operational data into a system that not only understands what’s happening but can coordinate what happens next. The competitive test will be whether that integration produces measurable improvements beyond conventional automation — fewer accidents, lower downtime, better asset utilization and greater operating leverage.

My takeaway: The physical economy could become one of the most compelling proving grounds for agentic AI because the outcomes are tangible, the economics are measurable and the consequences of execution are immediate.

The next wave of AI value won’t be measured by how many agents companies deploy, but by how much operational friction they eliminate and how effectively intelligence translates into real-world outcomes.

#114. Meet the five companies competing in the Startup Battlefield finals at Disrupt 2026

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Over the past two days, 20 startups have been pitching onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, presenting live demos and answering tough questions from our expert judges. Now it’s time to unveil the five companies that will be competing in the Startup Battlefield finals.

This year’s Battlefield spanned four categories — space and physical AI, energy and manufacturing, health tech and life sciences, and enterprise and security — and our finalists are working on everything from miniature human organs to fighting scams to computing in space.

The finals will kick off tomorrow (Thursday) at 11:30 a.m. Pacific — you can watch them onstage at Disrupt or on the livestream here. The founders will be presenting for another panel of expert judges who will pick the winner; that winner gets to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000, equity-free.

Apate deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, with different ages, genders, and accents, speaking various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

Flox Intelligence has built a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently than the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away. Instead, it uses edge devices with perception systems trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.

Intero Biosystems is developing human intestinal organoids — lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut — as another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. Its organoids differ from simpler models that replicate only part of the gut. They contain multiple cell and tissue types found in the human intestine, which the company believes makes them a more human-relevant model for testing drugs and other compounds.

Industrial Next builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks, without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor. In fact, some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones.

Satlyt is building software designed to allow many satellites to share the work of large computing jobs in space. The startup has already flown its software on two demonstration missions, with an initial focus on finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft. Those spacecraft typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise, with communication, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings. The next goal: to show that it can create a shared computing cloud between two satellites.

#115. Startup Spotlight: Zeacon aims to turn website visitors into buyers with AI-powered video

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by John Cook on Oct 15, 2026 at 9:57 amOctober 15, 2026 at 9:57 am

Businesses spend heavily to attract visitors to their websites, but traffic doesn’t necessarily translate into sales. Bellevue, Wash.-based Zeacon is building AI tools to help companies connect their marketing content with customer behavior and understand what actually drives conversions.

Co-founded by Kris Naidu and Jay Gounder, Zeacon uses AI to generate videos, personalize website content and track how visitors interact with it. The platform is also designed to identify bot traffic and analyze how both people and AI agents navigate websites — an increasingly important capability as AI changes how people discover and interact with businesses online.

Zeacon’s goal is to help companies move beyond traffic and content creation to understand what turns visitors into customers. As Naidu and Gounder see it, the real measure of success isn’t how many visitors a website attracts, but how many convert.

We caught up with Kris Naidu for our latest Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your elevator pitch:

We help businesses deploy AI agents that optimize their entire digital funnel, with an initial focus on video. Our AI agents can autonomously generate video content without prompting, publish it across social media and websites, personalize the experience for each website visitor and identify bots, while continuously analyze and optimize performance.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

We are obsessed with helping businesses turn the attention they already paid for into sales. Brands invest in advertising and great video content, but the website where customers actually buy often doesn’t connect with those investments. Zeacon brings that content onto the website, personalizes it to the visitor, and connects engagement to buying behavior. We can also create new videos from product photos and website data based on what converts. The question driving us is simple: How can we help this business sell more while taking work off its team?

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How much opportunity exists in what they already have. Businesses have videos, product photos, website traffic, and customer data. What’s missing is the connection between them. A marketing team wants to know: Which content helps people buy? Where are we losing customers? What should we create next? That reinforced our belief that the real value is turning information into a decision they can act on which we can provide with our platform.

How has artificial intelligence changed the way you build your company?

AI changed what we could take off the customer’s plate. Zeacon can understand website and product information, generate video from pictures without prompting, choose relevant content for a visitor, and help teams ask questions about performance in plain English. We’re building those capabilities together: create, personalize, measure, and learn. Each result can inform the next decision. That’s a much bigger opportunity than making content faster which we can also do but it means helping a business continuously improve how it sells.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That revenue alone does not tell you how valuable an AI company is. Revenue matters it proves customers will pay. But data deserves equal attention because it determines what the system can learn and how useful it becomes. At Zeacon, we care about the connection between visitor behavior, content, and conversion. The advantage comes from the quality of that data and our ability to turn it into better customer outcomes. Investors should ask what a company is learning with every deployment, alongside what it earns that will help them understand the true growth value.  Upfront value without long term vision effects companies and we were always focused on the end goal which was delivering a product that adds value not only in the near term but cannot be easily replaced.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Deciding what to say no to. When your technology opens up several opportunities, it’s tempting to pursue all of them. But customers need you to solve their problem well. Our focus is helping businesses use video and data to improve their website experience and grow sales. We have to judge opportunities against that purpose, even when they’re exciting. The data helped us understand the entire flow of users for our customers that when we had our moment.  We realized it just was not about providing outcomes for sales but helping the customers fix issues within their website journey and using the content to help fill gaps for the desired outcomes.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Focus. Get close to your customers, understand the problem they will pay you to solve, and keep delivering against it. Do not confuse more features with more value. Make something customers use, trust, and want to keep. It is hard but being focused is the key to winning.

Zeacon is recognized for creating a new business science on relating content and user behavior to actual business outcomes.

#116. Fortanix extends Confidential AI to Kubernetes workloads through Confidential Containers

Data security company Fortanix Inc. today extended its Fortanix Confidential AI platform to support the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s Confidential Containers project, so enterprises can run artificial intelligence workloads on Kubernetes inside hardware-based trusted execution environments.

The release goes after the exposure that comes during inference, when model weights and the data fed to them have to be decrypted in processor memory. Privileged administrators and cloud operators with access to the infrastructure can potentially reach them at that point.

Fortanix published survey figures last week on how AI leaders view that risk. Atomik Research polled 300 of them at large U.S. companies on Fortanix’s behalf, and 93% said traditional encryption does not protect data while AI is processing it. Security concerns had led 41% to block a deployment completely.

Fortanix’s answer builds on Confidential Containers, which reached incubating status at the CNCF in July. The open-source plugins the company is writing for the project verify that a container is genuine before it gets anywhere near an encryption key. That check runs through Fortanix Confidential Computing Manager, which attests the CPU and GPU together so an inference job spanning both is covered in full.

The company’s Data Security Manager hands over the keys only if the result satisfies the customer’s security policy. They go nowhere but the protected environment.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Anand Kashyap said moving AI into containers “doesn’t change the threat,” since models and agents still touch a company’s most sensitive data while they run. With the plugins in place, deploying a container into a confidential computing environment takes one click on supported hardware and Kubernetes platforms.

Fortanix is pitching the update at regulated industries that need confidential AI to hold up in production. Key release runs on a cluster, so losing one server does not block it. Customers with sovereignty requirements can run the platform on-premises or fully air-gapped, and the company says that also lets an enterprise host a frontier lab’s proprietary model next to its own data without putting the lab’s intellectual property at risk.

“Attestation is a protocol. Trust is an operation,” said Anuj Jaiswal, Fortanix’s chief product officer. Having attestation and key management on one platform spares enterprises from building the trust layer themselves when they adopt standard Confidential Containers, he said.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Intel Corp. and CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. are among more than a dozen companies Fortanix lists as supporting the work. John Fanelli, vice president of enterprise software at Nvidia Corp., said Fortanix is building on open standards for attestation and secure key release “at production scale.” Nvidia and Fortanix launched a joint on-premises confidential AI platform last October.

Fortanix Confidential AI for Confidential Containers is available now. The company plans to demonstrate it on Nvidia GPUs with confidential computing enabled at Nvidia GTC Berlin, which runs Oct. 20-22.

#117. Expert Orthodontists Dr. Erik Higginbottom & Dr. Kyle Higginbottom Compare Braces & Invisalign in HelloNation

The article explains how treatment needs, daily habits, appearance, and patient responsibilities can influence the choice between orthodontic options.

EASTON, Md., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should you consider when choosing between braces and Invisalign?

HelloNation has published an article featuring insights from Expert Orthodontists Dr. Erik Higginbottom and Dr. Kyle Higginbottom of Higginbottom Orthodontics in Easton, MD. The article explains how patients can compare treatment methods based on orthodontic needs, personal preferences, and daily responsibilities.

The HelloNation article explains that braces use brackets and wires to guide teeth into new positions over time. Because braces remain attached throughout treatment, patients do not need to remember to replace them after meals or brushing. They do, however, require adjustments to eating and cleaning routines.

Invisalign works differently by using removable trays that gradually move teeth according to a treatment plan set up by the orthodontist. These clear aligners are changed as directed while progress is monitored during regular appointments. Patients must wear them consistently for the recommended amount of time to keep treatment progressing. Compliance is KEY.

The orthodontic problem is an important consideration when comparing these approaches. Different bite concerns and tooth positions can require different types of movement. An orthodontic evaluation allows an orthodontist to assess those needs and determine which options can produce the necessary movements.

Treatment goals also influence the decision. Some patients may need relatively straightforward teeth straightening, while others have more complex bite or positioning concerns. The article notes that braces can offer advantages for certain movements, while clear aligners can be appropriate for many other cases.

Daily habits are particularly important with Invisalign because the trays are removable. Patients need to keep track of the trays during meals and replace them afterward. Following the recommended wear schedule can play an important role in treatment progress.

Oral hygiene requires attention with either approach. Patients with fixed appliances must carefully clean around brackets and wires where food and plaque may collect. Removable trays allow patients to brush and floss normally, but the trays themselves also require cleaning. Maintaining good oral hygiene remains important throughout treatment.

Eating habits differ as well. Patients with fixed appliances may need to avoid hard, sticky, or chewy foods that could damage brackets or wires. Clear aligners are removed during meals, allowing patients to eat their usual foods before cleaning their teeth and replacing the trays.

The article also discusses comfort and appearance. Both methods apply controlled pressure to encourage tooth movement, so temporary soreness can occur. Removable trays are designed to be less noticeable, while some patients may prefer a fixed treatment that does not depend on remembering to wear an appliance.

Treatment time cannot be determined by the method alone. The length of orthodontic treatment depends on case complexity, required tooth movement, individual response, and patient cooperation. Regular appointments allow an orthodontist to monitor progress and determine whether adjustments are necessary.

Cost may also influence the decision, but the article recommends considering fees alongside treatment needs. Pricing can vary based on complexity, treatment length, and the method selected. Patients should understand what is included when comparing costs.

An orthodontic evaluation provides a foundation for making that comparison. Tooth position, bite alignment, treatment goals, and expected movement can all be reviewed before a suitable approach is selected. The article concludes that both methods can provide effective orthodontic treatment when chosen for appropriate cases.

Braces vs. Invisalign: What Should You Consider When Choosing? features insights from Dr. Erik Higginbottom and Dr. Kyle Higginbottom, Expert Orthodontists of Easton, MD, in HelloNation.

#118. Gudea leverages AI to help organizations prevent social media crises before they erupt

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post — whether it involves AI-generated misinformation, hate speech, or a damaging rumor — can quickly snowball into a much larger public controversy.

Gudea, a company that tracks how stories and rumors spread online that describes itself as the “storm tracker for the internet,” is using AI to help organizations spot trouble brewing online before it turns into a crisis.

Unlike traditional social listening platforms, which only track metrics such as mentions, hashtags, and impressions, Gudea aims to show organizations who is driving a conversation, how information is moving, how quickly a story is gaining traction, and where it could be headed. Rather than simply tallying posts, its AI analyzes behavior, relationships, and the pathways through which information travels across more than 500 mainstream and fringe websites and platforms, including X, Reddit, and TikTok.

Instead of simply telling a company that mentions are rising, Gudea aims to provide the context behind that growth so decision-makers can determine how and whether to respond.

Gudea pitched its mission Wednesday afternoon on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company made the case that companies need to take a more proactive approach to protecting their reputations.

“These big industries don’t understand that there are things they can do proactively to defend their reputation and their brand,” CEO and founder Keith Presley said. “A lot of the chief communications officers and chief media or marketing officers, they’re using legacy tools to try to figure out what’s happening. Those tools were only ever designed to tell you the number of hashtags or number of impressions.”

Gudea was founded in 2023 by Presley, Jonathan Sperber, and James Thomin. Presley brings more than 15 years of experience spanning political campaigns and defense, including building the infrastructure for Andrew Yang’s presidential campaign. Sperber, the company’s chief strategy officer, has a background in disinformation research. Thomin, Gudea’s CTO, holds a PhD in chemical engineering and has spent roughly two decades working in AI and machine learning.

Presley called the company’s path to becoming a startup unusual.

“We’re one of those weird startups where I never wanted to do a company,” he said.

The team began with the George Washington Initiative, a nonprofit established after the 2020 election. The organization adapted strategies and tactics that the intelligence community has used overseas to disrupt online networks tied to groups such as Al Qaeda and ISIS. It applied them to domestic information campaigns.

The goal was to identify the online environments where information campaigns were taking shape and disrupt the pathways that allowed those narratives to reach wider audiences.

However, the team found that existing tools didn’t show how information was actually moving across people, groups, and platforms. That gap became the opening for Gudea.

Three years after its founding, Gudea has nearly 40 clients. According to Presley, its customer base includes a Fortune 50 telecommunications company, a Fortune 50 retailer, “one of the world’s largest AI labs, one of the world’s largest bands,” public relations and crisis communications agencies, and government agencies.

With the rise of generative AI, Presley believes that the need for Gudea’s technology has only grown, as the company looks to expand its customer base.

AI tools have dramatically lowered the cost and effort required to generate content and coordinate online campaigns. What once required a larger organization can increasingly be carried out by a single person with a laptop and access to the right software.

“When we first started in 2021, and then as a company in 2023, we maybe saw one out of four things we looked at have inauthentic activity around it,” Presley said. “Now it’s probably nine out of 10 things that we look at have this inauthentic activity.”

Looking further ahead, Gudea plans to expand its ability to understand where narratives originate and how they spread. One major upcoming initiative is geolocation for narratives. Slated for next year, the technology is intended to allow users to identify where conversations are happening with far greater precision, down to the city-block level, Presley explains.

The company also wants to give customers greater access to the tools behind its analysis. For example, a company could eventually run an advertising campaign through Gudea’s AI model before launching it and get a better idea of whether the strategy is likely to produce a negative outcome or not.

Last week, Gudea announced that it had raised $7 million in seed funding in a round co-led by Mudita Venture Partners and Silicon Road Ventures. The investment brings the startup’s total funding to approximately $15 million.

Castries, Saint Lucia, October 19th, 2026, FinanceWire

PrimeXBT, a global multi-asset broker and crypto asset service provider, has introduced a new VIP Welcome offer, giving all new clients automatic VIP4-tier status for their first 14 days. Activated upon registration with no additional action required, the offer provides immediate access to lower trading costs and enhanced conditions without first meeting the usual trading-volume requirements.

During the welcome period, clients receive 15% discount on Forex and CFD spreads on broker’s PXTrader 2.0 platform, with further reductions of up to 50% on Gold and Bitcoin CFD spreads. VIP4 tier also includes 33% off Crypto Futures taker fees, 10% off Exchange spreads, 24/7 priority support and access to 10% cashback on eligible trading costs through the Rewards Center. Trading volume on MT5 counts towards VIP qualification, but VIP fee and spread discounts only apply on PXTrader 2.0.

PrimeXBT’s VIP Tiers program offers five levels of progressively lower fees and enhanced conditions, with VIP status normally earned based on trading volume over the previous 30 days. Tier upgrades are automatic, and traders can track their progress in real time. The VIP Welcome offer gives all new clients immediate access to VIP 4 without first meeting these volume requirements. After the 14-day welcome period, clients who meet the relevant thresholds can maintain VIP 4 or progress to VIP 5.

“Small differences in spreads and fees can be easy to overlook on a single trade, but they add up over time and can have a substantial impact on costs, particularly for high-volume traders,” said Jonatan Randin, Senior Market Analyst at PrimeXBT. “The VIP Welcome offer gives new clients the opportunity to experience our premium trading conditions from day one, alongside the charting and risk-management tools they need to plan and manage their positions.”

#120. Lime tops 10.5M Seattle rides in 2026, rolling past last year’s e-bike and scooter total two months early

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 15, 2026 at 9:25 amOctober 15, 2026 at 10:46 am

Lime riders in Seattle have already outpaced last year’s entire ridership numbers, logging more than 10.5 million trips into October — surpassing the city’s 2025 full-year total more than two months ahead of schedule.

Powered by a massive surge during the summer’s FIFA World Cup matches in Seattle and a record-breaking Seahawks Super Bowl parade, the milestone highlights how deeply e-bikes and scooters have embedded themselves into Seattle’s daily commute and transit network.

The summer soccer tournament alone accounted for more than 1.7 million trips, headlined by an all-time single-day high of 83,000 rides on June 19 for the USA vs. Australia match — a record notably boosted by Seahawks legend Marshawn Lynch joining the “march to the match.”

That single-day mark shattered the previous high-water mark of nearly 60,000 rides set during the Seahawks parade in February. Four of Lime’s top five all-time ridership days in Seattle occurred during the World Cup stretch.

“We’re extremely proud of our partners at SDOT, who have spent years building a program and infrastructure that compelled our CEO to call Seattle ‘the next micromobility-first city,'” Lime’s Hayden Harvey, a regional director of government relations, said in a statement. “We’re also grateful to our riders, the Seattleites who choose day in and day out; rain or shine, two wheeled transportation instead of four.”

The record-setting volume reflects Lime’s position as the only game in town. After rival operators exited the market, Lime became the exclusive vendor in the City of Seattle’s micromobility share program.

Lime has since scaled its footprint to 15,000 active devices that are serviced and staged out of a sprawling warehouse south of downtown in Georgetown.

#121. Motive Technologies revs up new AI Agents to automate fleet management

Motive Technologies Inc. is pushing the needle for fleet management automation with the launch of a new artificial intelligence offering called Agents today.

As the name strongly hints at, Motive’s Agents are autonomous AI agents designed to take a more proactive approach to fleet operations by anticipating problems before they occur and taking action to prevent them, without constant human supervision.

San Francisco-based Motive is the developer of a comprehensive fleet management software platform for trucking companies. Its platform comes with multiple sensors that can be installed into individual vehicles, so the system can track their location, fuel levels and other data, such as the temperature of refrigerated loads – basically anything that might be useful to monitor. Those sensors send all that data back to the company’s cloud-based platform, providing tons of useful information for managers trying to keep their fleets organized.

Motive has long excelled at tracking and monitoring fleets, and says now is the time to move beyond just passive monitoring and start taking action where possible. It’s turning to AI to do that.

Fleet operations teams have unparalleled visibility into their fleets thanks to Motive’s platform, but many struggle to take action on the insights it provides quickly enough. That’s because, while data can provide those teams with warnings, it’s still up to humans to do everything else, such as chasing down and investigating alerts, calling drivers individually and verifying any fixes manually.

This problem was made clear in Motive’s recently published 2026 ROI Report, which found that 42% of its customers cite operational inefficiencies relating to administrative work as a major problem. The lag in response time can be very expensive, with Motive estimating that fleet operators lose about $46 billion annually due to issues that could, and should be prevented, such as unplanned vehicle downtime, unproductive engine idling and compliance violations.

That’s why Motive believes its new Agents can save customers an awful lot of money. The Agents are designed to do more than just flag specific problems and notify a human manager to solve them. According to Motive Chief Product Officer Hemant Banavar, they can actually predict problems will happen before they arise, and take action autonomously to ensure they don’t.

“Our customers don’t need another alert,” Banavar explained. “They need action. The data that prevents collisions and breakdowns already lives in Motive. Agents put that data to work the moment it matters, so teams can grow without adding headcount.”

Banavar said Motive’s existing customers will be able to deploy Agents in minutes by following a guided workflow and ready-to-use templates it has created. Once they’re set up, they’ll be able to resolve issues regarding compliance, maintenance and safety without any human involvement.

For example, if one of the Agents detects early signs of driver fatigue, it will alert Atlas, the company’s in-vehicle assistant. It will then speak to the driver and tell them it’s time to take a break, and even direct them to the nearest place where they can safely park the vehicle and rest.

That’s not all the Agents can do. They can also warn drivers of severe weather conditions before they occur. With regard to maintenance, they actively monitor each vehicle and when they spot signs of wear and tear, they can automatically create a work order and mark the vehicle as being out of service while it’s being repaired. In every case, customers will be able to specify the exact conditions that would trigger a maintenance order.

Motive’s Agents can also help fleets to save on money that’s wasted to engine idling, which burns through fuel and wears down engines over time. The company will flag excessive idling when it occurs and prompt the driver through AI Dashcam Plus to shut the engine down. It takes into account ambient temperature conditions too, so drivers who are purposely idling the engine to keep the air conditioner or heater running won’t be penalized for doing so.

Existing customers can access and deploy the Agents starting from today, and this is just the start, Banavar said. The company is planning to bring much greater autonomy to fleet operators in future. Early next year, it will enhance Agents with a new feature that allows teams to create their own Agents simply by describing the task they need them to do.

Ultimately, Motive wants to take automation to such an extreme that a fleet operator can simply tell it what their specific business objectives are, Banavar said. When customers set a simple goal, such as “more on-time deliveries” or “fewer collisions,” the Agents will determine the best way to achieve that objective and issue the necessary instructions to get it done.
