#145. DeepSeek releases updated V4.1-Flash model it says completes tasks faster

Chinese artificial intelligence startup Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd. has released an updated version of its V4.1-Flash model that it says completes tasks faster.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 arrives a little over five weeks after the company launched the original V4.1-Flash as the smallest model in a new architecture family. Its model card on Hugging Face calls the release a “minor update” that “reduces task execution time and output length.” DeepSeek did not say by how much.

Price was the selling point in September, with off-peak application programming interface rates starting at 15 cents per million uncached input tokens. After that release, Bloomberg reported Saturday, shares of Chinese rivals MiniMax Group Inc. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. fell in Hong Kong.

The update resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering test in DeepSeek’s own testing, up from 74.2% for the September version. Anthropic PBC’s Claude Opus 5 sits at 74% in the same table. Seven of the 11 benchmarks DeepSeek published still go to Anthropic’s model, and the margin on Humanity’s Last Exam runs to almost 14 points.

DeepSeek said it tuned the update for agent software, including its DeepSeek Harness tool and two Tencent Holdings Ltd. products, the CodeBuddy coding assistant and WorkBuddy, a desktop agent for office work. WorkBuddy has offered V4.1-Flash since DeepSeek released the model on Sept. 10.

Agent builders got a second release from DeepSeek. The company opened its in-house search engine to outside developers through a Search API that returns up to 50 ranked web results per query. A separate Fetch API converts a single web page to Markdown. Both cost 75 cents per 1,000 successful requests, and calls made through DeepSeek Harness, Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex are free until Nov. 1.

The releases follow a nearly five-hour API outage on Oct. 15 that Yicai Global counted among DeepSeek’s worst this year. The company apologized afterward, and users received credits pegged to what they had spent the week before. DeepSeek also said it would remove single points of dependency in its systems to keep the failure from recurring. Some experts quoted by Bloomberg blamed a shortage of computing capacity.

The updated model is live now in DeepSeek’s web and mobile apps. API customers reach it through the existing deepseek-flash model ID at unchanged prices, with the change log recommending Harness version 0.2.1-rc.1 or later. The weights are on Hugging Face under the MIT license.

#146. Prime Intellect acquires Moondream, a vision AI startup founded in Seattle by AWS vets

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Oct 14, 2026 at 11:15 amOctober 14, 2026 at 2:20 pm

Prime Intellect, a San Francisco-based AI cloud company valued at $1 billion, has acquired Moondream, a startup founded in Seattle by Amazon Web Services veterans that makes small, open-source AI models for understanding images.

Terms weren’t disclosed. Moondream has fewer than 10 employees, according to The Information, which first reported the deal Tuesday. Prime Intellect announced the acquisition later in the day in a blog post and on X.

Moondream emerged in 2024 with a $4.5 million pre-seed round from Felicis, Microsoft’s M12 GitHub Fund and Seattle-based Ascend. Its original model was small enough to run on phones and other devices.

The startup’s co-founders Jay Allen and Vik Korrapati are joining Prime Intellect to lead its inference work — running AI models after they’re trained — and to expand its efforts in vision and computer-using AI agents, the company said.

Prime Intellect is largely buying Moondream for its team’s skill at making models run faster, CEO Vincent Weisser said, according to The Information.

Moondream built Photon, an inference engine that compiles each AI model into a single program on the GPU, known as a megakernel, reducing the chip’s idle time between tasks. Engineers have historically written megakernels by hand, the report said.

“We share the conviction that specialized models can outperform much larger generalists on the tasks that matter to a business,” Weisser said in an email to GeekWire, adding that Prime Intellect will bring its evaluation, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning platform to Moondream.

Prime Intellect is one of a wave of “neoclouds” that provide computing power for AI developers and help them run open-source models. It raised $130 million in a Series A round led by Radical Ventures in July and said at the time that it had passed $100 million in annualized revenue.

Moondream was one of Prime Intellect’s earliest customers, Weisser said.

Prime Intellect will keep using the Moondream name for small, efficient AI models that handle images and other types of data, and the models will remain open, Weisser said. Its latest model, Moondream 3.1, is available through Prime Intellect’s inference service.

Moondream’s own cloud service will shut down Nov. 13, the startup said in a blog post. It will refund unspent credits and help customers move to Prime Intellect.

Korrapati, Moondream’s CTO, spent nine years at AWS. Allen, its CEO, spent seven years at AWS and previously worked at Porch, Zynga and Microsoft.

Moondream said earlier this year that it was moving to San Francisco. Korrapati announced the move in January in an online post calling AI “the biggest platform shift we’re going to see in our working lives.” Allen’s LinkedIn profile still lists him in Seattle.

Updated with comments from Prime Intellect CEO Vincent Weisser and details from Moondream’s announcement, including the planned shutdown of its cloud service.

#148. Newsweek names Encompass Health America's Most Awarded Leader in Inpatient Rehabilitation for seventh consecutive year

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Encompass Health today announced it has been named America's Most Awarded Leader in Inpatient Rehabilitation by Newsweek for the seventh consecutive year. A record 78 Encompass Health hospitals in 32 states were included on Newsweek's America's Best Physical Rehabilitation Centers 2026 list, more than any other inpatient rehabilitation provider in the nation.

According to Newsweek, "The facilities recognized on this list exemplify the best patient care practices in inpatient physical rehabilitation and set an example for others."

The ranking is based on four data pillars: quality metrics published by the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; results from a national online survey conducted by Newsweek among experts in the field; accreditation data provided by the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities and the Model Systems Knowledge Translation Center; and Google reviews, an indicator of patient satisfaction.

"Being recognized by Newsweek as America's Most Awarded Leader in Inpatient Rehabilitation for the seventh consecutive year reflects the extraordinary dedication of our teams across the country and their commitment to helping patients achieve meaningful recoveries," said Encompass Health President and CEO Mark Tarr. "With a record 78 hospitals recognized this year, this honor is a testament to the high-quality, compassionate care our teams provide every day and the trust patients and families place in us during some of the most important moments of their recovery journeys. We are committed to honoring that trust by helping patients achieve the best possible outcomes."

Encompass Health hospitals provide essential rehabilitation services that help patients recovering from strokes, brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, amputations and complex orthopedic conditions regain functional ability, independence and quality of life. Patients receive a minimum of three hours of intensive physical, occupational and/or speech therapy five days each week, as well as frequent physician visits and 24-hour nursing care. An interdisciplinary team of highly specialized nurses, therapists and physicians creates customized treatment plans to meet each patient's unique recovery goals.

With a national footprint that includes 178 hospitals in 39 states and Puerto Rico, the Company provides high-quality, compassionate rehabilitative care for patients recovering from major injuries or illnesses, using advanced technology and innovative treatments to maximize recovery. Encompass Health is recognized by Newsweek as America's Most Awarded Leader in Inpatient Rehabilitation and is ranked among Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies™ and Forbes' America's Best Companies. It is also recognized by Becker's Healthcare and Modern Healthcare as a top healthcare employer. #151. ServiceNow AI Control Tower: Selling a penthouse while building the frame

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

ServiceNow Inc. is making one of the more consequential and visible bets in enterprise artificial intelligence. The company says AI Control Tower can discover and govern any agent, work across models and clouds, track cost and value, and shut down behavior that violates policy.

That sales pitch plays directly to ServiceNow’s greatest asset – its installed base. Information technology and service management or ITSM, configuration management database or CMDB, risk workflows, security operations and years of operating context give the company a distribution and data advantage most AI and governance vendors do not have.

Our research suggests that moat is real. But proprietary customer data shows a more nuanced picture. Control Tower is already strong as a governance workflow and system of action. It can inventory AI assets, connect risks to owners, route approvals and remediation, and preserve an audit trail. What the field study has not broadly validated is the claim that Control Tower is a complete technical governance and runtime enforcement plane across the heterogeneous enterprise.

In this Breaking Analysis episode, we use a methodology similar to our CoreWeave analysis, and pressure-test management’s statements against 15 in-depth interviews with ServiceNow customers conducted with our data partner, Qualitate. We ask the following question: Is Control Tower becoming the enterprise AI control plane – or is it limited to the governance system of action?

Access the full slide deck here with survey data in the appendix.

ServiceNow may not need to own every technical control to build a very large business bolstered by AI governance. It can create enormous value by owning the workflow around those controls – inventory, accountability, approvals, exceptions, remediation and audit history.

But its marketing pitch is allowing customers to think the the market is collapsing three jobs into one convenient phrase: AI governance.

The first is governance workflow and accountability. This is where ServiceNow is strongest.

The second is AI lifecycle evidence – model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability and drift. ServiceNow can coordinate that evidence, but customers often generate it elsewhere.

The third is runtime enforcement and AI security – intercepting an action, blocking a deployment, constraining an agent or revoking access in real time. Our survey indicates this layer is frequently external, custom or human.

The nuance is that approving a model and assigning a remediation ticket are valuable. But they are not the same as technically validating the model, proving lineage or blocking the action.

ServiceNow’s opportunity is to connect all three. It is not best-of-breed in each today according to its own customers. Broadly, buyers should be cautious of claims that ServiceNow AI Control Tower is a platform that is universally end-to-end.

Control Tower sits inside a broader ServiceNow agentic AI strategy built on five connected pillars as shown below.

First is a model-agnostic posture: Any model, agent, cloud, data source or system of record.

Second is the shift from chat assistants to autonomous workers that plan, execute and adapt across workflows.

Third is centralized governance through AI Control Tower – discovery, ownership, access, observability, value and remediation.

Fourth is AI cost and value management: Token economics, model selection, budget control and ROI.

Fifth is pricing and packaging. Foundation, Advanced and Prime tiers seed AI broadly, move customers up the stack and add consumption on top of subscriptions.

These pillars reinforce one another and describe ServiceNow’s advantage and momentum. More agents create more governance demand. Model choice creates complexity. Governance addresses complexity and creates more reasons to stay on the platform. And more usage drives more consumption.

Our focus today is the key link in that flywheel chain: Can AI Control Tower can extend ServiceNow’s workflow advantage into technical governance and runtime control?

Management’s “right-to-win” argument is not that ServiceNow builds the best foundation models. It is that ServiceNow already knows how work moves through the enterprise.

Bill McDermott describes the moat in one word: context.

ServiceNow says its platform supports roughly 100 billion workflows and nearly 8 trillion transactions. Amit Zavery said more than 500 customers were live with AI Control Tower in the first six months. And ServiceNow reported AI ACV above 1 billion dollars in Q2, with a full-year target of $1.5 billion.

The CMDB knows assets, services, owners and dependencies. ITSM and change management know how work is routed and approved. IRM understands controls, risks, issues and evidence.

A best-of-breed specialist will likely have deeper model analytics, but it often lacks the operational graph that identifies the owner, business service or the path to remediate an issue.

The installed base gives ServiceNow a right to compete. It does not, by itself, prove that every technical control is present or every runtime path is governed.

TheCUBE Research commissioned a study through its partner, Qualitate, which conducted the fieldwork from Sept. 15-21, 2026.

The final base is 15 completed large-enterprise interviews totaling 575 minutes. Eleven respondents were in North America and four in Europe. Five came from financial services, four from healthcare, three from technology and telecommunications, and three from public sector, manufacturing or other industries.

The sample was senior: three executives or vice presidents, 10 directors or functional heads, and two senior managers.

Every respondent had an existing ServiceNow footprint. The study is a deliberate qualitative study of expansion, coexistence, implementation and control boundaries inside real accounts. Eleven of the 15 customers had either installed, piloted or were actively evaluating ServiceNow AI Control Tower.

There’s of course a bias toward the ServiceNow installed base. That is by design and it’s useful because management’s premise is it has an installed-base premise. We are testing the environment where Control Tower should have its greatest advantage.

Our methodology specifically separates direct experience from management claims. This is not a survey with 15 customers supplied by ServiceNow.

This next chart speaks to the heart of the episode.

All 15 respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational integration or incumbency advantage.

Fourteen of 15, however described runtime enforcement as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or not proven at enterprise scale. The one exception was a limited financial-services pilot that successfully tested ServiceNow’s blocking capability for at least one model and one agent.

Twelve of 15 identified a model-specific evidence gap – validation records, lineage, bias, explainability, drift history or AI-specific regulatory artifacts.

And twelve of 15 tied governance value or switching cost to the wider Now Platform – mainly ITSM, CMDB, change management and SecOps.

Our research shows that the same ServiceNow architecture creates both the moat and the boundary limits. Specifically, ServiceNow is hard to displace because governance work is embedded in operations. But the value story degrades when the CMDB is immature, the AI estate sits outside ServiceNow control paths, or regulators require technical evidence generated elsewhere.

One respondent called ServiceNow more like a governance orchestration layer than the actual governance of AI. We would challenge that a bit: It is real governance, but strongest at orchestrating accountability and action.

Regarding CMDB – when we first started covering ServiceNow in 2013, ServiceNow management would constantly push customers to consolidate on a single CMDB, which today is the norm. This has given ServiceNow a tremendous incumbency advantage but customers encounter friction.

A senior engineering manager at a large North American financial services company summed it up like this:

The CMDB dependency is bigtime on this because it must be cleaned up quite often, and that is the reason there are a lot of surveys that have been sent within the organization to actually clean up the CMDB on a regular basis. And a lot of auditing around is to be done as part of that.

The interviews suggest that AI governance is separating into three operating layers, with different buyers and budgets as shown below.

The first is governance workflow and accountability: Here we mean inventory, ownership, approvals, exceptions, issues, remediation and audit history. ServiceNow has the clearest advantage here.

The second is AI lifecycle evidence and regulatory proof: We’re talking about functions like model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability, drift and performance history. Hyperscaler-native tools, model platforms and specialists often supply this layer. Players here include IBM with Watsonx.governance, Fiddler AI; or a company like Credo AI which is strong at regulatory mapping and audit trail.

The third is runtime enforcement and AI security: Gateway policies, permission checks, agent identity, deployment gates and the ability to block or constrain actions. Security and AI platform budgets usually fund it. Palo Alto Prisma AIRS and Cisco AI Defense are good examples here.

This explains why architectures remain multi-vendor even when vendors claim end-to-end governance. There are three different activities involved including:

The question for ServiceNow is can it own every layer? Or will it become the policy authority and hub for evidence that connects these three layers and acts as the system of action?

This is where the field study we did with Qualitate strongly validates management’s story and at the same time highlights some notable weaknesses.

An AI asset can be connected to an application, business service, owner and dependency in the CMDB. IRM can attach controls, risks, issues, evidence and exceptions. ITSM, change management and Action Fabric can route the finding, track remediation and preserve the audit history.

Note: Action Fabric is ServiceNow’s interoperability and governance framework that lets external AI agents like Claude execute multistep workflows inside ServiceNow in a headless manner — similar to the way we reported on Salesforce’s Headless 360 – bypassing the traditional interface.

One respondent put it like this: Day one ServiceNow, day one workflow. Another said the CMDB matters because an AI risk can be connected to the application and business-service owner.

That is important because model-risk tool may detect drift or bias, but if the organization cannot assign, prioritize, remediate and prove what happened, the control has limited operational value.

This is why “just ticketing” is the wrong criticism. Operational accountability is part of governance.

The more accurate description in our view is that ServiceNow is exceptionally well-positioned to be the system of action for AI governance. The question is how much technical evidence and enforcement it can bring into that system.

This next diagram shows what actually flows when the architecture works as advertised.

AI Control Tower discovers the asset and establishes ownership. The CMDB supplies application, service and dependency context. IRM brings policy, risk, control, evidence and exception records. ITSM and Action Fabric turn the finding into assigned remediation work.

That internal path is ServiceNow’s sweet spot.

The limits show up when the organization needs technical model evidence or a live intervention at runtime. The technical validation may come from a model platform or specialist vendor. Blocking may occur in an application programming interface gateway or security product. The telemetry then has to return to Control Tower as evidence.

In several of our customer interviews, that connection was incomplete or fuzzy. Different teams owned governance, model tooling and security. Data models and workflows did not align automatically.

ServiceNow does not have to be the box that blocks every action. But it should define policy, identify the owner, send the decision to the right enforcement point, receive telemetry and preserve the audit trail.

Bill McDermott stated on CNBC’s “Mad Money” in July 2026, that ServiceNow possesses a kill switch to halt rogue AI agents and prevent disruptions, contrasting it with incidents like OpenAI’s agent escaping a test environment and hacking Hugging Face.

Buyer beware on this claim. Our survey exposes the limitations of this assertion.

Only one respondent reported a very positive pilot and that was limited. In this case, at least one model and one agent were tested for blocking, auditors were satisfied, and the respondent gave high marks. So that case directly supports management’s claim in a selected environment.

But the other 14 respondents described runtime control as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or not proven at scale.

What has not been validated – and appears to be a gap – is universal coverage across Azure OpenAI, custom agents, SaaS copilots, third-party models, shadow AI, multiple clouds and non-ServiceNow workflows.

One security practitioner estimated that only 30% to 40% of total AI activity could realistically pass through ServiceNow control paths today.

Our assessment is the kill-switch claim is overstated. It is not yet proven as a universal enterprise runtime control plane.

ServiceNow is strong at procedural proof – showing who approved a use case, which control was completed, who owns the exception, whether remediation occurred and what the audit history looks like. Several respondents said auditors accepted the ServiceNow record.

The gaps become more obvious in high-risk or regulated use cases. Survey respondents indicated ServiceNow gaps in many areas related to what we’re calling technical proof, including: Validation methodology, test dataset, model versions, training-data lineage, bias and fairness results, explainability, drift and performance history, prompt and response evaluations, hallucination and toxicity tests, permission evidence and a record of what the agent did at runtime.

Those artifacts are most often generated by alternative platforms – for example. IBM, hyperscaler-native governance tooling, other model platforms, MLOps systems, privacy and AI governance specialists, or traditional model-risk tools.

Control Tower can still become the place where that evidence is captured, evaluated, linked to policy and operationalized. But ServiceNow is currently out over its skis in our view, using “end-to-end” language. Our survey data suggests that, today anyway, ServiceNow is weaker at showing the complete evidence path for a real model or agent across a heterogeneous environment.

Buying indicators become clearer when we assess two variables: ServiceNow footprint depth and the intensity of AI or model risk. The four quadrants below explain this dynamic in simple terms.

Where ServiceNow is deeply embedded and regulation is modest, Control Tower has its best expansion opportunity – the lower right on this chart. This is the consolidation sweet spot for ServiceNow and probably represents the largest total available market.

The upper right shows where regulation is high and ServiceNow is deep, customers often preserve ServiceNow as the system of action but add independent lifecycle evidence and runtime controls. Coexistence is likely. That’s also a fairly large chunk of the market.

Where regulation is high and the ServiceNow footprint is shallow, the field is open to independent AI governance and model-risk tools.  That is shown on the upper left.

Where both are limited, hyperscaler-native controls or lighter specialists may be good enough – lower left.

Our analysis also exposes three different buyer-personas.

The vendor that speaks to only one persona may win the feature argument and still lose the account.

ServiceNow’s commercial strategy is worth exploring. This spring, ahead of ServiceNow Knowledge, the company replaced its legacy package tiers (Standard, Professional, Enterprise, Pro Plus and Enterprise Plus) with three AI-native pricing and packaging tiers: Foundation, Advanced and Prime.

Foundation, Advanced and Prime give customers an upgrade path, but some customers bristle. Management reports price uplifts of roughly 20% to 30% in the lower AI tiers and more than 30% in Prime, with subscription commitments paired with usage-based meters.

Our survey supports the momentum in ServiceNow ACVs. It shows that the operating model drives higher invoices. But the data also exposes some meaningful customer friction.

Twelve of 15 respondents said pricing, packaging or total-cost were acute concerns. Thirteen described significant configuration, integration or staffing friction.

As shown above, eight respondents supplied actual data comparing expectations to actual costs. Seven of the eight said costs came in above expectations, and one described the rollout as broadly on budget.

The cost overruns were not from licensing issues alone. They included partners, data normalization, CMDB hygiene, custom workflows, integration engineering, permanent specialists, administration and external controls.

One respondent said: We expected to need ServiceNow specialists, but we underestimated how permanent that would be.

Some verbatim quotes from the customers regarding pricing:

“the packaging is frustrating” “We expect costs to increase”

“Our costs came in 30% above our original expectation”

Importantly, this does not mean the value is poor. Some customers justified the extra cost. The issue is predictability. Customers should force ServiceNow to sell a bounded outcome, make integration assumptions explicit and show the full operating cost.

The broader market is fragmenting into different budget layers as shown below. Control Tower touches them all but ServiceNow faces credible competition in each.

Runtime enforcement and AI security include Palo Alto Networks, Guardrails AI, Kong, Lakera, HiddenLayer and Protect AI.

Hyperscaler-native governance includes Microsoft Purview and Azure AI, Bedrock Guardrails and Vertex AI governance.

Specialist or AI governance leaders include IBM, OneTrust, Credo AI, Holistic AI and ModelOp. Traditional GRC and model-risk tools include Archer, AuditBoard, MetricStream, LogicGate and Navex.

Notably, 12 of fifteen respondents were evaluating or deploying separate runtime controls, usually from cybersecurity or AI platform budgets.

The obvious opportunity for ServiceNow is to orchestrate and preserve evidence across all these tools. The risk is that the vendor owning the enforcement point also captures the telemetry, the security buyer and eventually the policy decision. ServiceNow could receive a ticket after the fact instead of controlling the loop.

The answer is potentially openness with authority: Customers choose any enforcement technology while Control Tower remains the policy system, accountability layer and durable evidence system of record to support the overall system of action.

This scorecard below summarizes our test.

The incumbency and context moat is most definitely supported by our survey. All fifteen respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational or installed-base advantage.

Model-agnostic orchestration is directionally supported. Customers value broad connectivity, but connector breadth is not the same as control depth.

The end-to-end governance claim is a stretch in our view. Control Tower is strong on inventory, accountability and procedural evidence but model-specific artifacts are frequently generated elsewhere.

The kill-switch claim is also overstated in our view. It is supported for selected pathways but definitely not yet as a universal runtime control plane. One positive pilot is good, but 14 respondents describing external, custom or limited enforcement suggest immaturity.

Execution watch: Cost transparency is an issue. Value management is a credible promise. The packaging creates attach and consumption opportunity but implementation remains a source of friction.

The field is most definitely not saying Control Tower is vaporware. Claims that it’s just a bolt-on are overstated; but its scope is currently limited.

The bottom line is ServiceNow is strongest where governance turns into actual work. It is less proven where governance becomes mathematical model evidence or a real-time intervention across a heterogeneous estate.

From an investor and strategic perspective, the bull case is compelling.

AI Control Tower creates a new attach point into a sticky and powerful installed base. It converts CMDB context into a governance system of action. The model-agnostic posture gives optionality across labs and hyperscalers. And the commercial model creates subscription uplift plus consumption.

But there are areas of concern that we describe below.

Based on our customer surveys, runtime claims are ahead of broad field validation. Model-specific evidence still depends on adjacent tools with better depth. Implementation friction can slow adoption and create cost overrun surprises. Security vendors, deep governance experts and hyperscalers can capture control points and budget.

We believe the business can be excellent without ServiceNow owning every technical control. Orchestration is the strongest position because buyers rarely want to replace every model platform, security product or cloud control. They want a common policy, accountability and action layer.

The company’s valuation has fluctuated substantially peaking in late 2024 at around $230 billion dipping to the mid-$80 billion range in April of this year. It’s market cap is now on the rise again at around $146 billion as of this writing. The market cap debate will rest on how successfully ServiceNow can convince investors that it’s an AI winner; which in part, will depend on the company’s ability to monetize the closed loop we described earlier.

If Control Tower becomes the policy authority and evidence hub, the moat expands. If it only receives alerts after other products make the important decisions, the strategic value is more limited. Our bet is on the former because of the company’s footprint.

The research does not say Control Tower lacks value. Quite the opposite. Customers consistently value ServiceNow’s workflow, CMDB context, accountability and ability to turn a governance finding into work. But orchestration is not the same thing as technical enforcement, and that distinction is where buyers can get into trouble. In fourteen of the fifteen interviews, broad runtime enforcement was external, custom, human-mediated, limited to selected pathways or not yet proven at enterprise scale.

Start by mapping the control sequence. For one specific model or agent, name the policy owner, the source of model-level evidence, the exact enforcement point, the telemetry path and the remediation owner. Do not accept an architecture in which every arrow disappears into a black box control plane.

Next, test a real violation. Pick a high-risk use case – for example an agent that can access sensitive data, move money, change infrastructure or interact with customers. Trigger a policy breach and show where the action is blocked or constrained. Then verify that the event comes back into the governance record, creates the right case, assigns an owner and preserves the evidence an auditor would need and accept.

Third, price the full operating model – not just the Control Tower license. Include IRM and CMDB dependencies, data normalization, connectors, implementation partners, external runtime controls, AI uplifts, service fees and the recurring specialists needed to maintain the system. Our interviews show that those operating costs are where many programs moved significantly beyond their original expectations.

Finally, protect optionality. This is fundamental to your AI sovereignty. Architect around open APIs, explicit integration responsibilities, service levels and have compensating controls for an exit path. Buyers should have a shared accountability model with their vendors and internal stakeholders. Understand who owns the policy, who owns the enforcement point and who is accountable when a handoff fails.

The buyer gate should be no production-scale growth until one real violation is detected, blocked, recorded and remediated end to end. ServiceNow can be the system of action without being the only control. The buyer’s job is to prove that the entire system works as a system.

#152. Steve Ballmer’s USAFacts pits Ben Shapiro against Scott Galloway in YouTube debate special

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 14, 2026 at 9:37 amOctober 14, 2026 at 9:38 am

USAFacts — the nonpartisan civic data initiative founded by former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer — is stepping out of its usual spreadsheet-and-report routine and onto the debate stage, launching its first-ever YouTube debate special titled “The American Dream at 250: Data doesn’t argue. They do.”

The 75-minute program pairs conservative commentator and Daily Wire founder Ben Shapiro with progressive author and NYU Stern professor Scott Galloway to hash out escalating cost-of-living pressures and the viability of homeownership — all while tethering their arguments to official government numbers. PBS NewsHour co-anchor Geoff Bennett moderated.

Ballmer steers the effort from the organization’s Fact Desk, leaning into USAFacts’ core mission of grounding national political flashpoints in verified government numbers rather than partisan rhetoric.

“Americans can disagree about the role of government in their lives, but productive debate begins with a shared understanding of the numbers,” USAFacts President Lauren Woodman said in a news release Wednesday, explaining that the project is designed to give the public a common factual baseline to evaluate competing policy choices.

The debate focused on three core economic questions, using federal data as a launching pad:

Capitalism vs. government intervention: The debaters tackled whether free markets or government programs are better equipped to preserve the American Dream and address mounting economic pressures.

The scale of government: They sparred over whether Washington is currently doing too much or too little to intervene in the everyday lives and finances of citizens.

The housing crisis and homeownership: The discussion zeroed in on whether homeownership remains a realistic milestone of the American Dream for younger generations, and whether the government should step in to make housing more attainable.

Founded by Ballmer in 2017 with $10 million of his own money, Bellevue, Wash.-based USAFacts operates like a reporting unit for the public sector, aggregating statistics from over 70 federal sources.

The organization is best known for publishing annual corporate-style “10-K” reports on government revenue and spending, as well as running a data-driven “State of the Union” companion timed to the president’s annual address to Congress.

#153. Origin Raises $20M in Funding

Origin, a San Francisco, CA-based full-stack physical AI company building general-purpose robots for interior construction, emerged from stealth with $20m in total funding.

The round was co-led by Accel and Zacua Ventures with participation from Unilazer Ventures, Schema Ventures, Z21, ISAI and Imad Ventures, alongside angel investors from Anduril, Skild AI, 1X and Tesla.

The company intends to use the funds to deploy OG-1, its flagship robot, and build out its fleet, support large-scale pilots with customers in the U.S. and Europe—including large drywall finishing contractors in the U.S., with additional pilots scheduled in Germany, Sweden, France and Saudi Arabia—and extend the platform to new interior trades.

Founded in early 2025 by Yogesh Ghaturle, Ashish Daga and Tushar Makkar, Origin is building robots to help crews increase capacity, deliver consistently and turn that demand into revenue. OG-1, the company’s flagship robot, is designed to perform multiple interior construction trades on a single platform. Today, it autonomously completes wall-finishing workflows without human intervention. It applies compound, sands and primes walls to a professional finish. OG-1 can work long shifts and  handle complex tasks, from targeted spraying and finishing high walls to handling difficult areas like corners, pillars, soffits and edges, and it’s already delivering the quality expected of a skilled professional.

Built for rough, chaotic construction sites and uneven surfaces,  OG-1 moves on a three-wheeled platform and has a 360-degree view of its surroundings. It can work at heights of up to 14 feet and handle contact-rich tasks, such as sanding, using real-time force control to keep consistent pressure against the wall. OG-1 is designed to work safely alongside construction crews while other trades continue on sites, without requiring a separate cordoned-off work area.

OG-1 is powered by Origin’s Construction Action Model, a foundation model built specifically for construction. It brings together three core components:

Together, these components enable OG-1 to apply compound, sand, prime walls or do other construction tasks, adapting to changing site conditions. The model is trained using high-fidelity simulation and deployment data from live job sites. It enables OG-1 to generalize across different construction tasks and environments, transferring learned capabilities between workflows and adapting to variations in site conditions. Origin uses data from ongoing deployments to improve the model’s capabilities, performance and generalisation across tasks and environments over time.

Today, OG-1 is being deployed across commercial spaces, multi-family apartments, data centers, hotels and warehouses. Origin’s platform is ready for manufacturing at scale, and the company is targeting 150 robots deployed by the end of 2027. It plans to support additional interior trades like taping, drywall installation, drilling & conduit installation, using the same hardware platform and Construction Action Model.

#154. Microsoft’s wild ride: Stock hits new record after a year of ups and downs

by Todd Bishop on Oct 14, 2026 at 6:27 amOctober 14, 2026 at 6:28 am

In less than four months, Microsoft has added roughly half an Amazon to its market value.

The tech giant’s stock has gained about $1.4 trillion in value since early summer, rising from $352.83 on June 25, its lowest close in more than a year, to a record close of $543.45 on Tuesday, giving it a market value just above $4 trillion. The increase over that period is nearly as much as Tesla is worth.

As stock turnarounds go, it’s extraordinary. In January, Microsoft lost $357 billion in a single day, the biggest one-day drop in its history, as investors worried about the company’s AI spending and its reliance on OpenAI. By midsummer, Microsoft was the worst performer this year among the big tech stocks known as the “Magnificent Seven,” according to Morningstar.

The rebound accelerated in late July, when Microsoft reported that Azure, its cloud platform, grew 43% and topped $100 billion in annual revenue. The stock jumped 15.5% the next day. It has mostly kept climbing since, as Microsoft rolled out a revamped Copilot app, a new AI push for Windows and new AI chips.

Microsoft isn’t rising alone. The broader stock market has also been hitting record highs, led by AI stocks. The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time last week, even as the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield reached its highest level since 2002.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been making a broader pitch along the way. In an essay posted on X in July, he warned that companies relying on outside AI labs “pay for intelligence twice, once with money, and again with something even more valuable,” meaning their own knowledge.

He urged businesses to keep control of that knowledge and avoid tying themselves to any one AI model. Microsoft sells access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others, along with its own.

Last weekend, he took up a related theme, calling on X for an “emergency brake” on advanced AI models. That means “separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work,” he wrote. “We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start.”

The message also fits Microsoft’s business interests. As companies use AI models from multiple providers, the advantage could shift to companies like Microsoft that run the cloud and workplace software where businesses keep their data.

Microsoft reports its next quarterly results Oct. 28.

#155. Banaraswala Raises $2M in Seed Funding

Banaraswala, a New Delhi, India-based provider of quick-service restaurant formats and traditional regional cuisine, raised $2m in seed funding.

The company intends to use the funds to accelerate its pan-India physical footprint expansion, fund ongoing culinary innovations in Banarasi molecular cuisine, broaden its multi-city product portfolio, and scale up its network of company-owned and franchise locations.

Led by Founder Vibhanshu Mishra, Banaraswala develops a specialized fast-casual dining experience under the “Ghat se Ghar Tak” brand identity, engineered to standardize, modernize, and commercially scale the authentic recipes and food culture of Varanasi for mainstream consumer markets.

The startup currently operates three physical outlets across Delhi alongside digital storefront integrations on major food delivery platforms, and has finalized market-entry timelines to scale to 50 active outlets across Rajasthan, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, and Delhi-NCR by March 2027.

#156. Booking Holdings unveils AI travel startup Vayo, based in Seattle, with a planned $100M investment

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Oct 14, 2026 at 6:00 amOctober 14, 2026 at 6:32 am

Booking Holdings is launching a new Seattle-based travel startup called Vayo, led by serial entrepreneur Mike Fridgen, betting that AI agents built for travel can do a better job of planning and managing trips than general-purpose assistants from the likes of OpenAI and Meta.

The travel giant — parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable — says it plans to invest $100 million in the venture, depending on Vayo’s progress and market conditions.

Vayo, which is opening a waitlist for a free private beta Wednesday, offers AI agents that connect to a user’s inbox to pull in flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. They then monitor the bookings for price drops, openings at sold-out hotels and other changes.

If a flight is delayed, Vayo flags what that means for the hotel check-in or dinner reservation. It also recommends restaurants and activities based on past trips. Vayo users can make restaurant reservations now, with flight and hotel booking expected in the next few weeks.

The venture is part of a broader effort by Booking Holdings to adapt to the rise of AI agents. Big tech companies and startups are developing general-purpose agents that can plan trips and make bookings, potentially bypassing traditional online travel sites.

The company is pitching Vayo as a personal travel agent “built for trips, not tasks.”

“We are out to build the leading consumer experience in travel — nothing less,” said Fridgen, the company’s CEO and co-founder, who previously led Madrona Venture Labs, the Seattle startup studio, and was CEO of Decide.com, the price-prediction startup acquired by eBay.

Vayo’s website promises neutrality. “Our only agenda is yours,” it says. “Vayo is part of Booking Holdings, but it works for you, not for any one site. If the better room is on the hotel’s own site, or the right stay is on another platform, that’s where Vayo will send you.”

A return to travel: It’s the latest travel venture for Fridgen, who was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, co-founded travel startup TripHub, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at Farecast, the airfare-prediction startup acquired by Microsoft, after which he led Bing’s travel and shopping search businesses.

Vayo’s CTO and co-founder is Allen Chen, who was previously CTO of Fanatics Collectibles and before that a partner in Boston Consulting Group’s AI practice. A serial entrepreneur himself, Chen co-founded two Seattle software startups, CloudPress and DataBlade, which were acquired by News Corp. and BCG, respectively.

The startup’s head of growth is Ian Fliflet, the former chief growth officer at OfferUp, the mobile marketplace for buying and selling used goods locally. Fridgen said Fliflet helped build OfferUp’s growth from the start and was at the top of his list for the role.

Vayo has about 20 employees, all working in person in downtown Seattle, and has been building the product for about six months. The company’s name is pronounced VAY-oh, as in “vacation.”

For Booking Holdings, the new venture marks a return to Seattle, home to its biggest rival, Expedia Group. Booking.com opened a Seattle office in 2012 and moved it to Bellevue the following year, with plans for as many as 350 jobs. It closed the Bellevue office in 2020, amid the pandemic.

A startup inside a giant: Given the team’s entrepreneurial experience, why build inside a travel giant instead of raising venture capital for an independent startup? For one thing, the arrangement gives Vayo access to Booking Holdings’ travel inventory, infrastructure and capital, while letting the team operate like a startup, Fridgen said in an interview.

Vayo has a unique opportunity to succeed with the backing of the world’s largest online travel company in “a very crowded, very noisy category with a lot of competitors,” he said.

Fridgen was already working on a consumer travel idea when his plans lined up with Booking Holdings’ interest in investing in new ventures. “It was really a meeting of the minds,” he said.

In a footnote in its news release, Booking Holdings said the $100 million investment will be “subject to continued advancement of the product and market conditions.” Fridgen said Vayo’s team will share in the value it creates, without giving details on the ownership structure.

Booking Holdings is also backing Lola, a separate AI startup from Kayak co-founders Steve Hafner and Paul English, which launched last month. “It’s a portfolio approach,” Fridgen said, describing Lola as focused on everyday experiences, such as things to do on a weekend at home, while Vayo is “mile-deep in travel scenarios.”

In a statement, Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel described travel as one of the most complex consumer experiences, with too much of the work still falling on travelers to manage.

Fogel said he’s confident in the Vayo team “and their ability to move with purpose, capitalize on early learnings and adapt at pace as they explore what the next generation of personalization in travel can look like.”

How it works: Vayo is initially targeting frequent leisure travelers who plan trips for family and friends, often in Google Docs, Notion or spreadsheets. That group makes up about 5% of travelers but roughly 30% of travel spending, Fridgen said.

In a demo, Fridgen showed how Vayo built his upcoming trips — to Amsterdam, to Philadelphia to visit his son in college, and to Guatemala for the holidays — within about a minute of connecting to his email. The company says Vayo reads only travel confirmations, not the rest of a user’s inbox.

In this demo video, Vayo plans a trip to Japan, landing a hard-to-get dinner reservation, repricing the flights to save $180 and booking a room at a sold-out hotel when one opens up. (Vayo Video)

Vayo also looks for patterns. For example, it noticed that Fridgen travels to Philadelphia every March, during his son’s sports season, and suggested a mountaineering trip after he climbed Mount Rainier with his daughter this summer.

When the fare dropped on one of his Alaska Airlines flights, Vayo automatically captured the difference as a credit and notified him, Fridgen said. For hotels, it currently prompts users to rebook. During the demo, he reserved a restaurant table through OpenTable without leaving Vayo.

Behind the scenes, Vayo runs numerous AI agents at once, using different models for different jobs. “At any given moment, we have all of these agents working on a user’s behalf,” Chen said. “We are picking the best models that are best suited for those tasks.”

The company has built its own system on top of off-the-shelf AI models, but Chen said the company will probably need its own custom models for some tasks soon.

Vayo connects directly with Booking Holdings brands including Booking.com, Kayak and OpenTable, and has signed a partnership with ticketing platform SeatGeek. Because it pulls travel confirmations from a user’s email, it can also track bookings made anywhere else, including directly with airlines and hotels.

Fridgen said users will be able to book flights and hotels in Vayo in the coming weeks, followed by features for planning trips with travel companions and a native mobile app.

Vayo is free during the private beta. Fridgen said the company hasn’t settled on a business model. A subscription is one possibility as the startup learns which features people are willing to pay for, he said. Fliflet noted that travel also offers traditional revenue from commissions on bookings.

Agents and platforms: Vayo is entering a crowded field of AI travel apps, including trip planners from startups and the big online travel sites. However, Fridgen said he sees general-purpose personal AI agents — such as Meta’s Muse and fast-growing San Francisco startup Instinct — as Vayo’s main competitors.

A growing number of agents have run into resistance from the sites they use. Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from its store last month, and Resy locked out a user whose Instinct agent repeatedly pinged the site for a table.

Vayo is taking a different approach, relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, Fridgen said. Those direct relationships make the service more reliable for customers and avoid the risk of being blocked, he said.

Fridgen said Vayo wants to work with companies across the industry, not just Booking Holdings brands. The startup doesn’t have a direct relationship with Expedia, but is open to one, he said. “The only way this can live up to its promise as an orchestrator of your travel life that you’ll trust is if it has all the options,” he said, “and that’s what we’re going for.”

#157. Microsoft reveals cutting-edge MAI-Base-2 model with 2T parameters

Microsoft Corp. has developed a new large language model that it says is significantly more efficient than leading open-source alternatives.

The company’s artificial intelligence research group detailed the algorithm on Thursday.

MAI-Base-2 is not a full-fledged LLM but rather a base model, a kind of no-frills prototype. Developers turn base models into LLMs by putting them through several additional rounds of training. That extra training usually focuses on adding reasoning features and safety guardrails.

The most capable open-source base model on the market today is DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. Microsoft says that MAI-Base-2 outperformed it on a series of internal benchmarks that contained science, programming and math questions. Furthermore, MAI-Base-2 is up to 12 times more hardware-efficient by certain measures.

MAI-Base-2 features a mixture of experts, or MoE, architecture, which means that it only uses a subset of its artificial neurons to process prompts. That’s more efficient than activating the entire neural network. MAI-Base-2 has 2 trillion parameters and activates 80 billion of them when it receives a prompt.

A language model’s artificial neurons are organized into clusters called layers. Microsoft’s previous-generation base model mixed MoE layers with modules based on a less efficient design called FFN. MAI-Base-2 is made up entirely of MoE layers, which is one of the contributors to its performance.

Microsoft trained the model for 38 days using 16,000 of Nvidia Corp.’s GB200 chips. The training dataset used in the project comprised 50 trillion tokens. About a fifth of the tokens were used to train a computer vision module integrated into MAI-Base-2. The module makes the model better than its predecessor at tasks such as understanding scientific charts.

Developers train LLMs by observing the manner in which they complete tasks and providing feedback on how they can improve. That feedback, which is generated algorithmically, takes the form of a mathematical object called a gradient. The gradient travels through the layers of the model being trained and re-calibrates each one to boost its output quality.

Gradients change every time they pass through an LLM layer. Under certain circumstances, those changes cause bugs that can disrupt the training workflow. Microsoft employed a method called gradient clipping to prevent that issue from affecting MAI-Base-2. It also used Muon, a popular open-source AI tool, to speed up the training workflow.

Microsoft will license MAI-Base-2’s weights to “trusted partners” through its Azure cloud platform. Additionally, it will use the model to power a new series of LLMs. The company plans to share more information about those models in the near future.

#160. Reflection AI open-sources Beam’s weights, post-training recipes

Startup Reflection AI Inc. today made the weights of Beam, its first large language model, available on Hugging Face.

The company also released technical resources that will enable developers to customize the algorithm.

Originally introduced last week, Beam is one of the industry’s most advanced open-source LLMs. It features about 500 billion parameters, yet approaches the performance of models four times its size on some benchmarks. It also uses significantly less computing power and memory.

Reflection AI trained Beam over two months using several thousand high-end graphics cards. Such large-scale training runs are prone to errors that can decrease model quality. According to Reflection AI, its engineers addressed the challenge by developing a set of custom reliability optimization algorithms.

The company’s error mitigation efforts placed particular emphasis on avoiding training-inference mismatches. Those are bugs that emerge when there are slight inconsistencies in the configuration of an AI training environment’s components.

Reflection also developed a system that can automatically fix certain data quality errors. When such bugs emerge, the system reverts the training run to an earlier stage and continues from there instead of starting over from scratch. The company says that its optimizations enabled it to train Beam with practically zero cluster downtime.

Beam’s newly released weights are available in multiple versions. There’s a standard edition and several scaled-down variants that keep information in smaller units of data. That arrangement, which is known as quantization, trades off some output quality for increased hardware efficiency.

The weights are available alongside training recipes, code templates that enable users to fine-tune the model. A vibe coding startup, for example, could create a fine-tuning workflow that enhances the model’s programming capabilities. The recipes are joined by tools that can be used to measure how customizations change Beam’s capabilities and safety guardrails.

Reflection AI has also released a drafter model for Beam. It can be used to implement speculative decoding, an inference approach designed to lower hardware usage. The basic idea behind the method is to use a lightweight LLM, the drafter model, to generate the initial version of a prompt response. Beam checks the output for errors before displaying it to the user.

Performing inference in a hardware-efficient manner requires developers to use a software tool called a serving engine. Adapting an LLM to a given serving engine can involve a significant amount of work.

Today’s release includes ready-to-use Beam configurations for several popular serving engines. Developers also have access to fused kernels, code snippets that compress multiple inference calculations into a single operation to speed up processing.

Reflection AI plans to follow up the launch by releasing additional training recipes in the coming days. They will enable Beam to refine its own output quality using an approach known as self-distillation. Additionally, the company intends to share some of the lessons it gleaned while developing the model in the form of contributions to open-source AI tools.

#162. Getty Images to keep Seattle HQ as it goes private through bankruptcy

by Todd Bishop on Oct 13, 2026 at 5:53 pmOctober 13, 2026 at 6:15 pm

Getty Images, the stock-photo giant with a presence in Seattle dating back to the dot-com era, plans to keep its headquarters in the city and avoid layoffs as it heads into a prearranged bankruptcy intended to cut its debt and take the company private.

A Getty spokesperson confirmed the plans in an email to GeekWire, citing “no expected impact on employees.” The company has about 300 employees in Seattle, out of nearly 1,650 worldwide as of the end of last year.

Getty is best known for its news, sports and entertainment photography. Its operations were profitable last year, with $84 million in operating income on $981 million in revenue, but it posted a $206 million net loss after interest and other costs.

The company has been weighed down for years by debt, now totaling nearly $1.5 billion, much of it going back to its years under private equity ownership starting in 2008. It returned to the public markets in 2022 through a SPAC deal that valued it at $4.8 billion.

A failed $3.7 billion merger with rival Shutterstock, announced in January 2025, deepened its financial crisis, as Getty spent more than $100 million on fees and financing. Getty abandoned the deal this summer after U.K. regulators required Shutterstock to sell its editorial business as a condition of closing, which Getty viewed as a deal-breaker.

Getty’s creative stock-photo business has shown signs of vulnerability, with revenue down 2.6% in Q2, as it competes with AI-generated images and the boom in smartphone photography.

Under the restructuring, members of the Getty family and affiliates of Koch Equity Development will invest up to $533 million and own the company together, Getty announced Monday. Koch Equity Development, the investment arm of Koch Inc., has been a minority investor in Getty since 2018, the spokesperson said. It owned 27.5% of Getty’s shares as of April, according to a regulatory filing.

The deal will “enable us to accelerate investment into the business and better position Getty Images for long-term success,” Getty CEO Craig Peters said in the announcement.

Getty plans to file for Chapter 11 in the coming weeks, aiming to emerge by year-end.

Bondholders agreed to retire $270 million in unsecured debt, and most secured lenders agreed to reduce interest payments and push out repayment. Public shareholders are expected to be wiped out. The NYSE suspended trading in the stock Sept. 29, after shares fell to 12 cents.

Mark Getty and Jonathan Klein co-founded the company in London in 1995. In 1998, Getty acquired Seattle-based stock-photo company PhotoDisc, and it moved its HQ to Seattle in 1999.

In 2016, Getty became the distributor of images from Corbis, its longtime Seattle-based rival, after Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates sold Corbis to China’s Visual China Group.

Getty’s current offices are in the Union Station complex near Lumen Field.

#163. Seattle voters view economy as weakening in survey that reveals short-lived World Cup euphoria

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 13, 2026 at 1:46 pmOctober 13, 2026 at 1:46 pm

Seattle embraced the global spotlight and rode a wave of economic euphoria when the FIFA World Cup came to town this summer, but according to new voter data out Tuesday, the city let that momentum slip away just as downtown businesses and major tech employers grapple with an ongoing economic squeeze.

The eleventh edition of The Index, a semiannual survey tracking voter sentiment commissioned by the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, reveals a sharp erosion in public confidence regarding the city’s economic trajectory.

According to polling of 700 Seattle voters conducted from Sept. 23 to Oct. 1 by public opinion research firm Fulcrum Strategic Group, 68% believe the city’s economy is getting weaker, 22% think it’s staying the same, and just 10% say it’s stronger.

While voters point to persistent quality-of-life concerns like public safety, homelessness and affordability, the findings underscore growing anxiety over Seattle’s business climate, at a time when major tech employers continue to evaluate their regional footprint and shift jobs across Lake Washington.

Seattle Metro Chamber President and CEO Joe Nguyen said the World Cup brought an energy and excitement downtown that was real and positive. But after a few months, there’s been no sustained honeymoon, and 65% of voters feel Seattle is losing positive momentum on public safety and quality of life.

“We demonstrated as a region what is possible when we all work together, and folks are already feeling that shift away,” Nguyen said during a media briefing Tuesday.

While chief concerns in the survey center on crime and public safety, economic health follows closely behind. In addition to widespread pessimism about the city’s overall trajectory, 71% of respondents agree that businesses are closing down or leaving for nearby cities because the cost of doing business in Seattle has gotten too high. Furthermore, 95% of those surveyed say it is difficult for small businesses to operate in the city.

When it comes to major employers — the tech giants and large corporations such as Amazon that anchor the regional economy and bear the brunt of taxes like the city’s JumpStart payroll levy — the survey reveals a striking disconnect.

The survey found 70% of voters recognize large businesses as essential to Seattle’s success, defying the narrative that the local electorate is anti-business. Andrew Thibault, partner at survey conductor Fulcrum Strategic Group, called it “the most interesting section” in the whole survey.

“Voters here deeply understand that their quality of life is connected to the health of the business environment and our ability to afford the things that we want to afford, like transit and schools, and environmental protections,” Thibault said. “All of those depend on a healthy business environment.”

But a significant knowledge gap persists around tax contributions. Voters estimated on average that large businesses pay just 37% of the city’s total tax revenue, with three-quarters believing that figure sits below 50%. In actuality, businesses pay 68% — more than two-thirds — of all city taxes, according to a recent tax analysis from the Chamber.

Underlying economic anxiety is playing out directly in City Hall’s budget debates. As major employers and tech giants navigate a shifting economic landscape — including recent reports showing downtown Seattle shedding 13,000 jobs in a single year while neighboring Bellevue’s tech hub expanded — voters are demanding a tighter rein on city spending.

The Index reveals that 66% of Seattle voters distrust the city to spend tax dollars responsibly, and nearly eight in 10 support requiring City Hall to prove existing spending is producing results before asking residents or major employers to pay more.

Those sentiments carry heavy weight as the city grapples with its budget. Facing what officials call “seismic shifts” in the tech sector, Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed budget attempts to close a massive deficit through spending cuts while freezing the rates for corporate levies like the JumpStart payroll tax.

For Nguyen and the Chamber, the message from voters is clear: City Hall must focus on tangible delivery with existing resources rather than continuous policy shifts and progressive tax increases.

Pointing to the city’s reliance on core revenue streams like business and occupation (B&O), sales, and JumpStart taxes, Nguyen emphasized the risk of over-targeting a concentrated corporate base.

“Finagling with it too much creates a problem where the people who are reliant upon paying the taxes are also the ones being targeted,” Nguyen said. “So if they leave, it creates a multiplier effect in the wrong direction.”

#165. What to expect during Dell’s ‘Cyber Resilience’ event: Join theCUBE Oct. 27

Data protection and cyber resilience have emerged as foundational control layers for enterprise AI.

This was one of the clear messages from the discussion at Dell Technologies World in Las Vegas earlier this year. Cyber recovery capabilities are linked to resilience, AI governance, data integrity and operational trust, all essential requirements in an environment where the reliability of AI systems depends on the data pipelines, runtime controls and recovery processes supporting them.

Cyber recovery will be at the center of the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, broadcasting Oct. 27–28 on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The Summit will feature a Dell Technologies-led day 1 flagship program, titled “From AI to Quantum: A New Era of Cyber Resilience,” airing Oct. 27. One of the guests on the program will be Rob Emsley, director of cyber resilience marketing at Dell Technologies Inc., who has spoken in the past about how enterprise security staff must continually refine their incident response skills and familiarize themselves with core defensive principles.

“We train our sellers and our partners about three keywords when it comes to cyber resilience: secure, detect and recover,” Emsley said. “Secure is about reducing the attack surface. Detect is about detecting and responding to threats. [Recovery] from cyberattacks, at the end of the day, is what the customers expect when they need it.”

The broadcast will also reach North America, EMEA and APJ audiences Oct. 28–29. TheCUBE Research analysts Dave Vellante, Krista Case, Christophe Bertrand and Scott Hebner will examine how Dell and its industry partners are rethinking architecture, policy and operating models to make AI more reliable in real-world conditions. (* Disclosure below.)

Earlier this year, Dell made a series of announcements designed to connect its AI Data Platform, PowerProtect portfolio, CyberSense capabilities and automation stack into a more unified architecture. The emphasis was on data access, AI-ready data pipelines, cyber resilience and policy-aware AI operations designed for enterprise-scale environments.

“Dell’s announcements reflect that cyber resilience and AI infrastructure platforms are expanding beyond backup and recovery into metadata visibility, recovery validation and contextual understanding of enterprise data,” said theCUBE Research’s Case. “Organizations should pay close attention to how vendors establish governance and validation for AI environments.”

This expansion beyond backup and recovery illustrates how agentic AI is changing the protection needs for many organizations. As agents become more capable of accelerating cyberattacks, enterprises must adopt defensive strategies more rapidly as a result.

“The threat is evolving more quickly than ever with agents, and that’s why having this secure, isolated, immutable layer — which is a core differentiation for how we build our portfolio — is necessary,” said Simon Jelley, vice president of product management at Dell, during a conversation with theCUBE. “Governance is necessary, but governance, as unfortunately we know, is never 100% guaranteed.”

Along with protecting against AI-fueled attacks, Dell and its customers are also discovering the benefits of using autonomous tools to safeguard critical data and systems. Dell has been using Claude Mythos Preview and other frontier AI models to aggressively find and fix product vulnerabilities. Generating highly unpredictable test scenarios can uncover hidden architectural weaknesses, according to Jelley.

“The reality is you need it to be randomized, and again, that’s where you’re leveraging those on demand environments to be able to spin up quickly — randomize the test set,” Jelley explained. “AI is going to actually be a contributor to helping there, in terms of randomizing the vulnerability. It’s definitely both a risk and a tool in terms of how we help our customers.”

Dell’s approach highlights a key element in the development of new approaches to building cyber-resilient infrastructure. As theCUBE Research analysts have noted, survey data reveals that enterprises are facing security challenges in AI deployments, and this has been a central part of Dell’s focus on building cyber resiliency.

“Cyber resiliency risk is not just on the data, what you have to go through every day; it’s also starting to appear in the actual AI infrastructure itself,” said theCUBE Research’s Bertrand. “Security or cyber exposures … this is what people are saying is, on top of cost, their first operational challenge when it comes to implementing AI. There is no AI without a secure infrastructure, and that means data that is also recoverable, that it is secure and is of course compliant.”

#166. Microsoft forms ‘Xbox Labs’ to explore game remixes, ports and other new frontiers

by Todd Bishop on Oct 13, 2026 at 12:23 pmOctober 13, 2026 at 12:23 pm

Xbox is creating a new team to experiment with technologies that are changing how games are made, ported and played — including some that run counter to how the game industry and its business have traditionally worked.

Microsoft Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Xbox Labs on Tuesday in a memo to employees, describing it as “a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.”

The group will be led by Scott Van Vliet, Xbox’s chief technology officer since May. Sharma said the team will build in the open and measure success “by whether more people are playing and creating.”

Sharma pointed to recent examples of games being decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never designed for, as well as Windows PC games translated to run on Apple Silicon or inside a web browser. She called these “unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.”

The memo never uses the term AI (or SI), but it frames the effort in part around AI agents.

“Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software,” Sharma wrote. “Games share many of those same properties.” She said people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing Xbox games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.

Sharma came to Xbox in February from Microsoft’s CoreAI division. In her first memo as CEO, she said games would be “crafted by humans, and created with the most innovative technology provided by us,” and pledged not to “flood our ecosystem with soulless AI slop.”

In May, she pulled Gaming Copilot from mobile and canceled its console launch, saying Xbox would “retire features that don’t align with where we’re headed.”

Microsoft last month cut 268 roles in Xbox Game Studios and moved work on the next Halo game to Activision. It was the latest round in a reset Sharma announced in July, which called for about 3,200 job cuts by the end of this fiscal year, roughly 20% of the Xbox workforce. The company said at the time that the restructuring was about 75% complete.

Xbox’s priorities aren’t changing, Sharma wrote in her new memo, describing Labs as “a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.”

#168. RapidCanvas raises $29M to develop custom AI applications for enterprises

Software development startup RapidCanvas Inc. today announced that it has raised $29 million in funding.

Vertex Ventures SEA & India led the Series B round with contributions from Hitachi Ventures, Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures. The deal follows a $16 million investment in 2024.

RapidCanvas develops custom artificial intelligence applications for companies with between $100 million and $1 billion in annual revenue. Its engineers write software with the help of an automation toolkit called the RapidCanvas Enterprise AI Platform. According to the company, it automates about 60% of the work usually involved in building AI applications.

The toolkit’s first component, the Enterprise Context Engine, collects business data from clients’ internal systems. It uses that information to improve the AI applications delivered by RapidCanvas.

If an application receives a prompt that contains a company-specific term or business metric, the Enterprise Context Engine can clarify what it means. That makes the underlying AI models less likely to make mistakes.

The tool also maps out how a company’s employees perform business tasks. AI applications can use that knowledge to identify the best way of automating repetitive work. If the Enterprise Context Engine has incomplete or inconsistent information about how a task is performed, it asks a human for help.

The second component of RapidCanvas’ automation platform is a library of prepackaged application modules. They cover common tasks such as user authentication, document processing and vulnerability detection. The modules remove the need for RapidCanvas engineers to build client applications from scratch.

Once an application is ready, RapidCanvas verifies that it works as intended using a tool called Operational Harness. The tool evaluates each use case that the application automates against task-specific reliability criteria. For example, Operational Harness can check how well AI-generated document summaries align with the source material.

RapidCanvas’ engineers start client projects by identifying an AI use case that can deliver a quick return on investment. After the customer verifies that the company’s approach works, AI is applied to additional tasks. Tech-savvy clients can optionally use RapidCanvas’ internal automation tooling to build software on their own.

The company delivers its development tooling and professional services through a single subscription. It has so far built software for more than 75 clients in verticals such as the manufacturing, finance and retail sectors. RapidCanvas says that its annualized revenue has grown eightfold over the past 18 months.

“Vibe coding has made it easy to start building with AI. Getting AI into production reliably and safely still remains the biggest gap,” said RapidCanvas co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Rahul Pangam. “Our growth over the past six quarters is evidence that AI in enterprises is moving beyond pilots into production and real operations.”

RapidCanvas will use its newly raised funds to grow its go-to-market and AI engineering teams.

#169. Apple challenges Amazon’s Echo and Ring with its new smart home lineup

by Todd Bishop on Oct 13, 2026 at 10:47 amOctober 13, 2026 at 11:06 am

Apple is going after Amazon’s smart home business on several fronts at once.

The iPhone and iPad maker on Tuesday unveiled HomeView, a $299 smart display that competes directly with Amazon’s Echo Show, along with a lineup of cameras, a video doorbell and a smart lock made by LG Electronics. That puts Apple in the core categories of Amazon-owned Ring for the first time.

Apple also announced a new Apple TV 4K and the HomePod mini 2, which will go up against Amazon’s Fire TV and Echo speakers.

Amazon made its own move into Apple’s territory last week, unveiling premium Alexa Tablets, including a Pro model that competes more directly with the iPad.

The new Apple HomeView has a 7-inch screen and comes in a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version. It recognizes up to six household members by their faces and switches to each person’s messages, calendar and apps.

It runs Siri AI, Apple’s rebuilt version of its voice assistant, which the company calls “profoundly more capable and conversational.” Pre-orders started Tuesday, and the device ships Nov. 13.

Amazon’s big lead: About two-thirds of U.S. smart speaker owners have an Amazon device, compared with about a quarter for Google and 7% for Apple, according to the latest data from Consumer Intelligence Research Partners, covering the 12 months ending in June. Apple’s share has stayed in the mid-single digits for years.

CIRP’s Michael Levin and Josh Lowitz wrote that Apple may go after people who don’t own a smart speaker rather than try to convert Amazon and Google customers. Only 57% of recent Apple buyers have a smart speaker of any kind, the firm found.

The HomeView is aimed at people already using Apple devices. Setup and the personal features require an iPhone or iPad. It won’t be sold in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t available there.

Apple is also hinting that its AI won’t stay free. A footnote in the HomeView announcement says certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models are subject to daily limits, with expanded access “available for a fee in the future.” Amazon’s Alexa+ is free with Prime or $19.99 a month on its own.

Competition for Ring: The new Apple Home Collection, designed with LG and Schneider Electric, includes a $249.95 LG video doorbell with two cameras, LG indoor, outdoor and floodlight cameras priced from $199.95 to $399.95, and a $349.95 LG deadbolt that unlocks automatically as its owner approaches, using ultra-wideband technology.

The accessories are set for release starting in December, with some arriving in early 2027.

Camera video history requires an iCloud+ storage plan, and Apple says there’s no separate camera subscription. Apple’s retail stores will also offer installation by ADT for an extra charge.

The LG lock was announced a week after Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a hand-turned dial that revives a dead battery. It’s due in the first quarter of next year. Ring also announced five new cameras priced from $69.99 to $219.99.

The LG lock includes a backup key slot. “If you have to have a key, it’s like, well, why have a smart lock?” Ring founder Jamie Siminoff told GeekWire last week.
