#171. The agentic AI era is forcing security and resilience into a single discipline

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For two decades, security and data resilience have been neighbors who share a fence but rarely a budget. Security kept bad actors out, while resilience brought the business back when they got in. Agentic artificial intelligence is tearing down that fence, yet most organizations haven’t noticed.

Last year, I wrote that Veeam Software Group GmbH’s acquisition of Securiti AI positioned it as the industry’s first AI resiliency company. At VeeamON 2026 in May, the company foreshadowed what that would look like.

At its recent VeeamON Global Launch virtual event, Veeam announced a product: Veeam Intelligent ResOps, or iResOps, with Microsoft 365 as the first generally available workload. Whether you call it AI resiliency or resilience operations, the idea is the same. When software agents act on data at machine speed, you can’t secure what you can’t recover, and you can’t recover what you don’t understand.

Chief Executive Anand Eswaran (pictured) opened with an example that should make every chief information security officer squirm a little. A company in Spain recently told its regulator that an AI agent, acting largely on its own, breached it by finding a flaw in a live application and modifying personal data and billing records. Eswaran framed the 72-hour disclosure requirement as an engineering problem. “Somebody has to answer three questions: Which records did it change? What did it change them to? And what were they before?”

That’s at the heart of the need to converge these historically separate markets. Ransomware encrypts, and exfiltration steals, but both are detectable events with established playbooks. Modification is different. “You can disclose a theft. You cannot disclose your way out of a modification,” Eswaran said. “You have to reverse it, and you can only reverse what you can identify precisely.”

Eswaran described three eras: backup and recovery, where the rule was to assume failure; cyber resilience, where the rule was to assume breach; and the agentic era, where the rule is to assume drift. All three now apply at once. He also made a distinction I think is underappreciated. Agents are often temporary, but “the data is not temporary, and the data drifts too. It goes stale. It gets reclassified. It gets poisoned.” A perfectly entitled agent can still do real damage by reasoning over the wrong data.

Most of the industry’s approach to agent risk starts with the agent: registries, runtime guardrails, and scoped credentials. Those matter, but Eswaran pointed out their limits. “You can govern the agents you choose. You cannot register the ones that you do not know about.”

Veeam argues that the only vantage point that doesn’t require knowing the actor in advance is the data, because every agent eventually touches it. According to Veeam’s Data Trust & Resilience Report 2026, 88% of organizations are using or piloting AI agents, yet only 7% qualify as truly AI-ready, and more than 82% have unknown agents in their environments.

Identity follows the same logic. Eswaran noted that even perfect identity hygiene only restores who can act. It doesn’t restore what has already changed. One function closes the door, and the other must clean up the room, so they can’t remain separate.

One of the most important points in Eswaran’s keynote was clarifying the difference between a recovery point and a recovery map. “A recovery point tells you what you can restore,” he said. “A recovery map tells you what to restore first, what changed, and what not to bring back.” This distinction is important because recovery is often an “all or nothing” process, which increases cost and time, both of which are precious commodities in the AI era.

The map he referred to is the DataAI Command Graph, brought over from Securiti, which connects data, users, permissions, agents, activity and protection status across live and backup environments. iResOps for Microsoft 365 is an add-on to Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft 365 that requires no data migration. It discovers Copilot and other agents, shows what sensitive data each can access, flags redundant, obsolete and trivial data, or ROT, and lets teams undo an agent’s changes, file by file.

Rehan Jalil, president of products and technology and former CEO of Securiti, positioned it as an end to the pain caused by fragmented tooling. “Customers don’t want silos of tools with conflicting sources of truth. They want visibility, controls, and resilience in one place,” he said. “You know what is sensitive, what is critical, and what an agent touched. You protect exactly what needs protection, and you restore exactly what broke.” In data sciences, there’s an expression that “good data leads to good insights,” but it’s also true that silos of data lead to fragmented insights, which causes inconsistent insights.

IResOps for Veeam Data Platform and Okta are in private preview, with GitHub, Azure DevOps and Google IAM previews planned for the fourth quarter. Okta is a smart early target because, as Veeam notes, it lacks native point-in-time restore. Developer tools are too. As Jalil put it, “One force push can rewrite main’s history.”

Veeam said preview customers found that a quarter of a 40-terabyte estate didn’t need to be in production and that there were 25 agents on a single tenant, two of which were actively modifying data.

Robert Davis, director of information technology infrastructure and operations at Construction Resources, a Home Depot company, said organizations need to know where data came from and where it’s going “before people have a case of Copilot gone wild.” He added that ROT is “not just a housekeeping problem; it’s about compliance and legal protection, and it cuts down on Copilot’s hallucinations.”

Steve McIntyre, senior vice president of data protection, analytics and cloud security at Fidelity Investments, put it plainly: “If you have an event, you have to assume that you have to recover the data as well,” and identities must be revalidated so “we’re not just reopening ourselves” to the same attack.

The launch of iResOps is what Veeam has been working toward since it closed on Securiti. However, other vendors are musing about this. For example, Microsoft is building agent governance into Microsoft 365. Veeam’s credible angle is that it starts with recovery, with more than 550,000 customers, and adds data security posture management rather than the other way around. As Eswaran said, it has spent 20 years as “the company you call when everything else is broken.”

The risk is the one McIntyre raised. Customers are wary of an “Uber platform” that aims to replace everything, and they’ll favor vendors that ingest context from tools they already own. IResOps will succeed as much on how well it integrates as on how much it consolidates.

The bigger lesson goes beyond Veeam. The resilience question is no longer “Can I recover?” It’s “Can I prove exactly what happened and undo only that?” That’s AI resiliency, and companies that keep security and resilience in separate silos won’t be able to answer it.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#172. Microsoft’s top science exec is leaving to fulfill a childhood dream: Joining a Formula 1 team

by Todd Bishop on Oct 13, 2026 at 10:27 amOctober 13, 2026 at 10:27 am

When Peter Lee announced two weeks ago that he was leaving Microsoft, he said only that his next job would fulfill “a dream I’ve had since childhood.”

The dream, it turns out, comes with a pit crew.

The longtime Microsoft Research leader, who is leaving his post as president of Microsoft Science after more than 16 years at the company, plans to join the Mercedes Formula 1 team in a newly created AI advisor role, according to a report by Fortune.

As a career turn, it isn’t as much of a surprise as it might seem. Lee raced karts and Formula Ford as a kid, and he was once a licensed auto body technician, he told GeekWire last year. He had a replica 1955 Porsche 550 Spyder converted to electric and was in the middle of converting a 1968 Ford Mustang GT Fastback last year.

He called cars “a great laboratory” for AI models that decide an agent’s next move.

“The thing I’ve always loved about cars, and why I love to work on cars, is you actually finish something,” he said in that interview. “That never happens in software.”

At Mercedes, he’ll focus on using AI to tackle physics problems for the team’s car, breaking down organizational and data silos, building financial and predictive models, and advising the team on how F1’s regulators might govern AI. He’s expected to join on a one-year contract with an option for a second. His exact title is still being worked out, according to the report.

“I’m completely thrilled, and I’m in disbelief that they would think of me for something like this,” he told Fortune.

His exit is part of a broader wave of senior departures from Microsoft this year, including LinkedIn and Office chief Ryan Roslansky and communications chief Frank Shaw.

#174. UW receives $12M gift from Taiwan-based chip company led by alumnus Arthur Chiao

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 13, 2026 at 9:00 amOctober 13, 2026 at 8:36 am

The University of Washington’s College of Engineering has received a $12 million gift from a semiconductor company whose chairman earned a master’s degree from the school more than 45 years ago.

The donation is from Winbond Electronics Corporation America, a U.S. subsidiary of Taiwan-based Winbond Electronics Corp. Arthur Y.C. Chiao is Winbond’s chairman and CEO and has been with the company since 1987. He earned his master’s degree in electrical engineering from the UW in 1980.

The gift will create the Winbond Endowed Fund for Excellence in the College of Engineering to support student scholarships, faculty recruitment and retention, research and interdisciplinary collaboration.

“Arthur Chiao’s vision, leadership and lifelong commitment to the University of Washington make this gift especially meaningful,” Nancy Albritton, dean of the College of Engineering, said in a statement.

Chiao envisions the new fund “as a catalyst for breakthrough discoveries” that will allow the college to “pursue bold initiatives and respond to evolving opportunities in engineering, technology and fields of future strategic importance,” according to a UW release. That includes semiconductors, AI, quantum tech and advanced manufacturing.

The College of Engineering is among the UW’s largest colleges, enrolling 10,136 students last fall and employing a faculty of 350. The college says it is the fifth-largest producer of electrical and computer engineering graduates in the U.S.

“Seattle is a gateway to the Pacific Northwest of North America, and the University of Washington will play an important role in connecting future technology innovation between North America and East Asia,” Chiao said.

The gift comes amid a push to bring chipmaking closer to home. Taiwan is the global center of manufacturing for the most advanced semiconductor chips, and the United States has been working to reduce its dependence on East Asian chip production. In 2022, Congress passed the CHIPS and Science Act to incentivize domestic fabrication, R&D work and workforce training.

#175. What to expect at Dell Technologies New York Symposium: Join theCUBE Oct. 20

Most financial institutions today don’t suffer from a lack of customer data; the problem is how to turn the data they have into something useful.

The challenge lies in sifting through CRM logs, channel interactions, transaction streams and market signals that are frequently siloed. The solution is technology that can connect and unify data, understand context and act in real time. Moving beyond AI models and bringing these three capabilities together is the goal of the AI data infrastructure that Dell Technologies Inc. offers its financial clients.

“In many cases, the model is not the next constraint, the data is,” said Arthur Lewis, president of the Infrastructure Solutions Group at Dell. “That is the problem that the AI Data Platform was built to solve. Within the Dell AI Factory, it is the data foundation that curates, connects and serves enterprise data to fuel the AI, and especially agentic AI.”

How Dell’s platform creates a more efficient data path from raw enterprise information to AI-ready context in the financial services industry will be a central focus of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium on Oct. 20. Dell executives and industry experts will join analysts from theCUBE Research to discuss the growing role of agentic AI, AI-powered PCs and modernized infrastructure in shaping the financial sector’s future. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s AI Data Platform provides a four-engine architecture with a storage layer that helps modernize data infrastructure and create efficiencies for financial institutions.

The platform includes a Data Orchestration Engine that uses the latest machine learning models and normalizes product documentation, while orchestrating retrieval requests and assembling the information needed for intelligence reports. A Data Processing Engine based on Apache Spark handles feature engineering, customer segmentation, and training for affinity scoring.

Dell’s Data Search Engine, powered by Elasticsearch, provides grounded retrieval through vector and keyword searches across product knowledge bases. The Data Analytics Engine exposes the Iceberg lakehouse as a governed SQL query surface that agents can call directly. Any MCP-compatible agent framework can discover available data products and execute governed queries without having to build a custom adapter.

A key part of Dell’s approach involves making structured and unstructured enterprise data accessible to AI agents while preserving the business context needed for reliable responses. The company’s Unified Semantic Layer is designed to address this challenge by connecting information across disparate sources.

“The semantic layer gives structured and unstructured information consistent business meaning, so a term means the same thing everywhere it appears,” said Vrashank Jain, lead product manager for the AI Data Platform at Dell. “It uses open models to fix the hardest part of building semantic layers: generating entities, definitions and finding meaning at-scale with human-in-the-loop for verification.”

#176. Nouscom Raises €120M in Series D Funding

Nouscom, a Basel, Switzerland-based clinical-stage biotech company developing neoantigen-targeted immunotherapies, raised €120M ($135M) in Series D funding.

The round was co-led by M Ventures and Revelation Partners, with new investors Angelini Industries, the European Investment Bank, and Neva SGR, alongside participation from existing international investors including 5AM Ventures, Andera Partners, Angelini Ventures, Bpifrance, CDP Venture Capital, EQT Life Sciences, Indaco Venture Partners, Panakes Partners, Versant Ventures, and XGEN Ventures.

The company intends to use the funds to advance its lead asset, NOUS-209, through a global, registration-enabling clinical trial for cancer interception in Lynch Syndrome (LS) carriers.

Led by CEO Marina Udier, Nouscom is a clinical-stage biotech developing neoantigen-targeted immunotherapies to treat cancer from early interception to late-stage metastatic disease. Its lead asset, NOUS-209, is an investigational neoantigen-based cancer immunotherapy designed to target mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) and microsatellite instability (MSI) tumors.

#177. Flexport and AI startup Freightmate settle trade secrets suit ahead of trial

by Todd Bishop on Oct 12, 2026 at 5:03 pmOctober 12, 2026 at 5:54 pm

Freightmate AI has settled a trade secrets lawsuit filed by San Francisco-based freight forwarder Flexport on terms that will keep the Bellevue, Wash.-based logistics software startup’s products on the market.

“We’re glad to have this resolved,” said Bryan Lacaillade, Freightmate’s CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “I’m incredibly grateful to our team, customers, and partners for their support throughout this journey, and we’re excited about what’s ahead for Freightmate.”

The case raised a question that could become more common as employees leave big companies to start AI ventures: whether everyday business documents count as valuable trade secrets when they can be fed into AI models.

Lacaillade and fellow co-founder Jason Zhao, both former Flexport employees, acknowledged in a stipulated court judgment that they and the company acquired approximately 2,000 confidential Flexport shipping documents and used some portion of them. But they denied Flexport’s claim that Freightmate’s product was built on them, and the court ultimately made no finding of liability.

The documents included bills of lading, arrival notices and other paperwork from about 70 Flexport shipments. Court filings show that Lacaillade and another co-founder, Rishab Gadroo, each ran five to 10 of the documents through OpenAI’s GPT-4o model in 2024 to test how well it could pull out standard information.

Flexport argued in court filings that the use went further, saying the documents helped shape the prompts Freightmate wrote for its AI system, giving the startup a head start.

Freightmate responded in its own filings that it built its product independently, and that the documents weren’t trade secrets in the first place.

The companies notified the court of the settlement Oct. 5. The case had been set for a jury trial starting Oct. 19 in U.S. District Court in San Francisco before Judge Rita Lin.

Financial terms of the settlement weren’t disclosed. The judgment says Flexport’s claims for monetary damages were resolved in a confidential agreement, and each side will cover its own legal fees as part of the resolution. Flexport had sought a court order that could have barred Freightmate from selling its main product for a period of time.

“We’re satisfied with this result,” said Courtney Heger, Flexport’s vice president and head of marketing and communications, responding to GeekWire’s email inquiry. She said the judgment includes key admissions that were backed up by a detailed forensic review conducted during the case. That review’s findings weren’t made public.

Lacaillade and Zhao joined Flexport from Amazon in 2021 and left in 2024 to start Freightmate, which came out of stealth that June with a $650,000 pre-seed round from Wischoff Ventures. It raised a $5 million seed round led by Fuse in January 2025.

Freightmate has 17 employees, Lacaillade said in a follow-up email. The company sells AI-powered freight forwarding software, along with add-on tools that pull data from shipping documents and handle customs paperwork and invoices. Its customers include some of the world’s largest freight forwarding and logistics companies.

Flexport sued in March 2025, alleging that the founders secretly planned the startup while still at the company, as GeekWire reported at the time.

As part of the stipulated judgment, Zhao acknowledged that he acquired Flexport confidential information, including trade secrets, and both founders agreed that they knew or should have known that acquiring the shipping documents violated their agreements with Flexport.

They didn’t admit Flexport’s other allegations. Lacaillade said in an email that the stipulated facts “were agreed to as part of resolving the case” and only for purposes of the lawsuit.

He underscored that Freightmate and its founders deny liability, that nothing else in the judgment is an admission, and that it preserves Freightmate’s right to compete and to independently develop and sell its software.

Going forward, the judgment calls for a neutral forensic examiner to search Freightmate’s systems and cloud storage for Flexport documents. If any exist, the examiner will oversee their deletion, along with any product changes needed to remove Flexport data. Lacaillade said Freightmate is cooperating fully with the review, which is due to be completed by Jan. 30, 2027.

The startup’s focus, Lacaillade said, is on its customers and on building the company.

#178. Physics AI pushes chip design beyond traditional simulation

Vinci4D Inc. is bringing a new approach to semiconductor design grounded in fundamental physics equations.

The company provides simulation software for chip designers, offering an alternative to traditional simulation methods, including finite element analysis, a technique engineers use to study the physical behavior of objects. Instead, Vinci4D’s technology uses pretrained physics models to accelerate simulations and analyze multiple physical phenomena simultaneously.

“Vinci is changing how design and analysis is being done from the ground up,” said Karthik Aravamudhan (pictured), global client director at Vinci4D. “The whole industry is talking about agentic AI and how the workflow automation, the orchestration, happens. That means more simulations, more analysis, a lot more that needs to happen under the hood. Vinci is trying to attack that problem.”

Aravamudhan spoke with theCUBE’s Christophe Bertrand at SEMICON West, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Vinci’s approach to physics-based simulation and its implications for semiconductor design and agentic AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Physics foundation models could play a growing role in semiconductor engineering, according to Aravamudhan. He highlighted the strategic shift from Design Technology Co-Optimization to System Technology Co-Optimization, which involves thinking of chip design as one part of a larger system.

“[Vinci] fundamentally tries to solve the problem from the foundational physics level,” Aravamudhan said. “When you’re designing, you’re trying to understand what the package looks like. While you’re designing the package, you’re trying to understand what the board looks like. So, you’re designing a whole system; you’re not just designing one portion of it anymore.”

Vinci trains its models on physics equations rather than customer data, reducing the need to expose proprietary design information during model training. Its technology also aims to reduce the time and cost of simulations by analyzing multiple physical phenomena simultaneously.

“An average customer today in the whole semiconductor ecosystem tries to solve for a certain physics,” Aravamudhan explained. “It could be thermal, it can be mechanical and it can by any[thing]. They try to solve one physics at a time because that’s the only way it has been known to be possible. That takes a whole long time. What Vinci tries to do with these foundational physics models is try to solve these physics true to what it is and to solve multiple of these at the same time.”

Vinci recently closed a $250 million Series B funding round at a $1.5 billion valuation, co-led by Advent International, Temasek and Xora. The startup now plans to expand its reach beyond semiconductors into other hardware industries, including automotive and aerospace applications.

“The funding gives us … the foundation to go after bigger [things],” Aravamudhan said. “From the different physics that we can solve, from having a go-to-market team and a go-to-market approach, it gives us so many different dimensions we can start focusing on. With these big names backing us, it certainly helps a lot and it shows their belief not only in Vinci, but their belief in the technology.”

#179. Knowledge graphs fuel AI innovation for financial services at Raymond James Financial

Knowledge graphs are becoming a critical context and reasoning layer for agentic AI, helping enterprises connect data and ground agents in key areas of business expertise.

For diversified financial services companies such as Raymond James Financial Inc., graph technologies have become an important part of developing trustworthy infrastructure to support AI. The technology has been particularly helpful in building unique solutions, according to Jeff Griffith (pictured, left), vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James.

“Using something like a data graph lets us harness the power of AI in dynamic ways,” Griffith said. “People already know how to go get the things that they’re getting every day. But it’s when you want to cross those domains or do some unique thing that this has a lot of value.”

Griffith spoke with John Furrier, executive analyst for theCUBE Research, at the recent GraphSummit event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. He was joined by Naveen Mahankali (right), vice president of technology at Raymond James, and they discussed how knowledge graphs and AI are changing the business landscape. (* Disclosure below.)

As a Neo4j customer, Raymond James uses graph technologies that give developers a way to represent the relationships, dependencies and business context that AI applications need to reason effectively. Accuracy is a critical requirement in the financial world, and Raymond James uses its knowledge graph to help agents work with data from trusted systems and evaluate results against established sources.

“We have golden sources, we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” Mahankali told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”

Raymond James’ work with AI is creating new efficiencies within the organization. Looking ahead, Mahankali sees opportunities for AI to reduce the time and effort financial advisors spend sourcing information for clients.

“One of the things we’re trying to do is we’re letting AI query the data dynamically so that our financial advisors get what they want without clicking on screens and without looking at a fixed dashboard,” he said. “They can do more analysis rather than just looking at the data that they already see in other applications. They can do product analysis versus how accounts are balanced and things like that by asking a question.”

The implementation of AI agents is also changing everyday processes within Raymond James itself. In January, the company launched Raimond, its proprietary digital AI operations agent.

“We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith said. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people, how everyone works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”

#180. Vinci pushes the boundaries of chip design with physics AI

Physics AI is bringing a new approach to semiconductor engineering, where increasingly complex designs make physical behavior harder to predict. Advanced accelerators combine multiple chips, memory and packaging components, creating tightly coupled engineering challenges.

Vinci4D Inc. uses physics AI to bring simulation into engineers’ everyday design work. Its approach addresses a familiar engineering tradeoff, according to Dinesh Panneerselvam (pictured), head of technical solutions at Vinci.

“Oftentimes, what I see in the field is engineers have to choose between accuracy or fast physics,” he said. “They don’t get to do both. What Vinci does is bring them both at the speed at which they’re designing.”

Panneerselvam spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand at SEMICON West, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed physics-based simulation, earlier design exploration and protecting customer data. (* Disclosure below.)

Vinci combines a physics foundation model with a GPU-native physics kernel in an approach it calls Continuous Physics Reasoning. The combination produces repeatable results with solver accuracy, according to Panneerselvam.

“In a product development world, the team that understands the physics — or the behavior of their product early on — they win the race,” he said. “That’s exactly what Vinci is providing. That means you design at your architectural level. We provide what the performance is.”

The model is trained on Vinci’s own data rather than customer data. Deployment behind the customer’s firewall keeps proprietary design information with the customer, Panneerselvam explained.

“The way we have designed our platform, it works right into your workflow,” he said. “You don’t have to change any of your current workflows. We ingest your design files as is and start building the model. There is so much automation built in that there’s very little manual input.”

Physics AI could also support the development of physical AI, including robots and humanoid systems. Vinci’s simulation approach could help engineers understand how those products would behave before committing to a particular design, according to Panneerselvam.

“Customers are able to open doors for new innovation — things that they haven’t imagined before,” he said. “For example, you have an engineering intuition for a product, and it stops there. What Vinci and products like Vinci allow is basically [to] explore beyond that. We call it the art of the impossible, and you can move into that space.”

Vinci is exploring applications in automotive and aerospace engineering as it expands beyond its semiconductor base. Its $250 million Series B funding round will support development across additional physics disciplines and industries, including planned capabilities in electromagnetics and fluid dynamics, Panneerselvam explained.

“The bottom line is physics doesn’t change,” he said. “It’s just the applications that we have to build. The physics remains the same.”

#181. Band launches desktop app for developer collaboration and control of multiple AI coding agents

Artificial intelligence agentic collaboration platform for multi-agent systems Thenovi AI Ltd., also known as Band, announced Thursday the launch of Band for Developers, a platform and new desktop application that allows software engineers to manage multiple coding agents at once.

As software developers continue to adopt agentic AI, autonomous coding assistance platforms that can generate application code with little or no human intervention, more engineers are beginning to lead entire teams of agents. These agents have also become more specialized, gaining access to larger parts of the development lifecycle, including coding tools, sessions, machines, validation, testing and integration.

Although more agents are working together on projects, individual agents often remain isolated from one another and are only aware of each other from the codebase – or via repositories such as GitHub and tickets posted to trackers such as Jira. This often means developers must pass session context between agents and coordinate handoffs so agents don’t collide or overlap.

“Developers are going from working with one coding agent to leading teams of them, but the tools around those agents haven’t evolved to support that,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Arick Goomanovsky. “We’re seeing engineering teams undergo a fundamental transformation as they adopt multiple agents across different harnesses.”

Band provides a desktop application that lets developers see their entire team of agents with a bird’s-eye view of them at work, including projects, ownership, blockers, questions and progress.

That lets developers move from high-level views to projects or jump to a specific agent when intervention is needed. Afterward, the engineer can shift back to the broad picture in the dashboard without moving contextual information between individual agents.

For example, if a specific agent gets stuck because another is working on a key function or apparatus in the software it needs to move forward – and it has a question about how it will work – the developer can note that it should wait until it completes, or tell the waiting agent to go ahead with prototyping. That gives development teams greater control over fleets of agents working across the entire codebase while staying aware of where each agent is, similar to how a development team might operate.

The company added a desktop application that complements its command-line interface and integrates with AI agents in the development environments developers already use.

Weekly AI agent usage for professional developers has reached mainstream for local and remote cloud agents, according to JetBrains s.r.o.’s Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026, with 90% of professional developers using at least one AI coding agent at work weekly and 68% using them daily. It’s harder to peer into developer adoption of multi-agent systems, or swarms, but across other use cases, multi-agent workflows have been steadily adopted, with Databricks Inc.’s 2026 State of AI Agents report showing  327% growth from September 2025 to early 2026.

“Running more agents only helps if developers can actually manage the work those agents create,” said Engineering Manager Amit Gazal.

#182. AI safety and financing worries multiply but everyone’s still racing full speed ahead

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

The drumbeat over how safe artificial intelligence is — or more to the point, isn’t — just keeps louder.

In the wake of weeks of incidents involving rogue agents, with likely more to come, more government officials are calling for regulation, even if President Trump says it’s not needed. Several states are suing OpenAI over harms to kids. And even many people in tech are calling for more controls, including several hundred AI researchers worried about cybersecurity issues and Microsoft President Brad Smith, who says AI is less regulated than a carton of milk.

One big issue: Who gets to say any particular AI is safe? That’s the question Dave Vellante explored in his latest Breaking Analysis. He concluded that “we should advance the evidence and engineering for control alongside the capability of the models. For policymakers, that means an independent standard with consequences. For businesses, it means granting more authority only when the deployment earns trust.” Indeed, for some companies, AI agents in particular just may not be the answer at all, wrote Intellyx’s Jason Bloomberg.

Meanwhile, investors are starting to vote with their dollars on AI, increasingly worried that revenue growth for AI, namely for leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic, might not continue as fast as it has this year. Though Anthropic revealed to investors 45% revenue growth from the second to the third quarter, that constituted a slowdown, which could bring its planned public offering valuation from $2 trillion to a slightly less incredible $1.5 trillion. And investors had more to worry about, namely CoreWeave’s debt load, which knocked down the stocks of neoclouds and their suppliers this week.

And it’s not just public investors who are getting antsy. As Intel’s and Broadcom’s CEOs pointed out this week, capital is becoming a brake on expansion for AI, especially as interest rates keep creeping up.

Nonetheless, AI companies from Nvidia and Meta to startups such as Reflection AI are forging ahead with new models. In particular, they’re increasingly offering open-source or open-weight models as enterprises aim to create customized models for their businesses. Look for SiliconANGLE to explore that realm of AI soon.

And the AI picks-and-shovels crowd isn’t slowing down either. At the Open Compute Project’s Summit in San Jose this week, Cisco Systems, Nvidia, Intel and many other suppliers debuted technologies to enable AI to scale up, out and across faster.

Tech earnings season gets underway next week. Besides Netflix and Tesla, there’s IBM, Meta, SAP, SpaceXSI and more, setting the table for the big cloud/AI players Alphabet and Microsoft the following week.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Icon, one of the biggest players in 3D printed real estate, raised $200M Series D financing

120ft raises angel funding to build autonomous microfactories run by humanoid robots

William Draper, pioneering Silicon Valley venture capitalist, died at 98 (per the Wall Street Journal).

Database pioneer Jeff Naughton from Celonis, Google and UW-Madison joined Snowflake as a Technical Fellow to “advance data systems for the agentic enterprise.”

OpenAI again is shaking up data center leadership, with xAI exec Uday Ruddarraju to lead and Sachin Katti to leave.

Longtime marketing exec Rachel Thornton, most recently at Adobe, joined AMD to lead marketing for Enterprise and Data Center AI.

Agentic customer experience platform ASAPP appointed Jeremy Stinson chief marketing officer.

Enterprise Java firm Azul named Matt Camassa, formerly in sales at TeleSign and Sift, chief revenue officer.

XCENA hired Steve Fingerhut, formerly with companies such as Qualcomm, Pliops and Intel, as chief business officer to lead commercialization of its MX1 computational memory.

After nearly seven years in infrastructure at Google, Bikash Koley has joined AI infra firm Crux AI, a Blackstone/Google joint venture, as chief technology and product officer.

Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics hired former Ford EV chief Doug Field (per TechCrunch).

Sierra Ventures hired Nkechi Iregbulem from MVP Ventures as head of inception.
